# Overview



This page introduces the **Comparative SAE Atlas** — a research repository that runs ten single-cell foundation models through the same pipeline, opens each model's internal features with sparse autoencoders, and compares what the models encode. It covers the project's purpose, the ten models under study, the repository layout, the two-stage pipeline architecture, and the reproducibility engineering that makes every published number verifiable. By the end you will know what lives where, how the pieces connect, and which page to read next.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L9)

## What This Project Is

The core question is simple to state: when ten different gene-expression foundation models read the *same cells*, do they learn the *same biology*? The project answers this by running every model on one shared corpus of 6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells, training one sparse autoencoder (SAE) per network layer — 172 dictionaries in all — annotating the resulting features with a single calibrated method, and then comparing the models on four questions: what each model encodes, what they share, which to use for a given task, and whether their features predict biology the models were never shown. The results are published as an interactive web atlas (served from `index.html` in this repository) and as 59 audited result files.

![Figure 1: The comparative SAE atlas overview schematic](https://github.com/Biodyn-AI/atlas-comparison/blob/main/outputs/atlas/comparative/figures/Fig1_overview.png?raw=true)

A crucial design rule shapes everything downstream: a difference between two models can only be trusted if the *data* is identical. Earlier single-model atlases were built on different corpora, so any difference between them could have been the data rather than the model. This repository's first recorded decision was therefore to give all ten models exactly one corpus, drawn with a fixed seed, plus a second disjoint held-out draw for replication tests.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L9), [DECISIONS.md](/docs/DECISIONS.md#L6-L19)

## The Ten Models at a Glance

The comparison spans a 300-fold range of model sizes (10M to 3B parameters) and deliberately diverse designs — different input encodings, training objectives, and pretrained priors — which is what makes the comparison informative. Note the `reads a cell as` column: models differ fundamentally in how they convert a cell's gene-expression vector into tokens.

| model | params | layers | reads a cell as | objective | prior | species |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIDO.Cell | 10M | 8 | expression, all genes | MLM | none | human |
| scGPT | ~50M | 12 | binned expression | MLM | none | human |
| tGPT | ~120M | 8 | rank order | autoregressive | none | human |
| scFoundation | 100M | 12 | expression, read-depth aware | MAE | none | human |
| GeneCompass | 104M | 12 | rank order plus value | MLM | knowledge graph | human, mouse |
| MaxToki | 217M | 11 | rank order | autoregressive (Llama) | none | human |
| Geneformer-V2 | 316M | 18 | rank order | MLM | none | human |
| UCE | 650M | 33 | ESM2 protein tokens, sampled by expression | masked | ESM | multi-species |
| C2S-Scale | 2B | 26 | rank-ordered gene names as text | autoregressive | text (Gemma-2) | human, mouse |
| Tahoe-x1 | 3B | 32 | binned expression | MLM | none | human |

> [!TIP]
> Because the models span species (UCE, GeneCompass, C2S-Scale are multi-species), the shared human-only corpus means the atlas says nothing about the models' cross-species abilities — a deliberate trade-off of the one-corpus design, recorded in the decision log.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L49-L62), [DECISIONS.md](/docs/DECISIONS.md#L6-L19)

## Repository at a Glance

The repository splits cleanly into five zones: the interactive site, the frozen results, the GPU pipeline, the local analysis pipeline, and the documentation that ties them together.

```
index.html, data/            the site: a 12 MB page plus the feature maps it fetches on demand
outputs/atlas/comparative/   the 59 result files and 7 figures every number is read from
pipeline/atlas_h100/         the GPU stage: adapters, SAE, extraction, per-model analyses
pipeline/scripts/            the local stage: matrices, controls, prediction tests, assembly, audit
pipeline/atlas_template.html the site's markup; index.html is built from it
pipeline/legacy/             earlier builders, kept for provenance, used by nothing
docs/DECISIONS.md            what was decided, why, what it cost, where it lives
docs/METHODS.md              methods in brief, with pointers into the code
docs/REPRODUCE.md            how to check the numbers, rebuild the site, re-run the analysis, re-extract
docs/RESULTS.md              every result file: written by, read by, what it holds
requirements.txt             the local analysis environment (Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3.4)
```

Two things are deliberately *not* in the repository: the manuscript and supplement (shared separately — the audit needs them dropped into `outputs/atlas/comparative/`), and the 1.2 GB of per-run feature catalogues and external inputs, published as release assets and fetched by a checksummed download script. The SAE weights (~17 GB) and activations stay on the GPU host entirely.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L11-L35), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L1-L5)

## How the Pipeline Is Organized

The architecture is a strict two-stage design, and understanding the boundary between the stages is the key to navigating this repository. **Stage 1 (GPU)** turns model checkpoints into small JSON *feature catalogues*: each model's adapter reads the shared corpus, residual-stream activations are extracted at every layer, a TopK sparse autoencoder is trained per layer, and each layer's catalogue records the top-20 genes per feature. **Stage 2 (local, CPU-only)** needs only those catalogues — every matrix, null model, prediction test, figure, and the website itself is built downstream of them. The diagram below shows the full flow:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Shared corpus<br/>6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells, seed 0"] --> B["Model adapters<br/>one per model"]
    B --> C["Layer-wise activations<br/>residual stream, all layers"]
    C --> D["TopK SAE per layer<br/>172 dictionaries, k = 32"]
    D --> E["Feature catalogues<br/>top-20 genes per feature, JSON"]
    E --> F["Stage 2: local analysis<br/>matrices, nulls, controls, prediction tests"]
    F --> G[("Result files<br/>outputs/atlas/comparative/")]
    G --> H["Site assembly<br/>index.html + data/explorer.json"]
    G --> I["Figures, supplement tables"]
    G --> J["audit_all.py<br/>312 checks against paper + site"]
    H --> J
    I --> J
```

The two stages even run under different environments: extraction used Python 3.12 with PyTorch on an NVIDIA H100, while everything downstream runs on a laptop under Python 3.13 with NumPy 2.3.4 (pinned in `requirements.txt`). This means a reader can reproduce *all* published analyses without ever touching a GPU — the catalogues ship as release archives.

> [!TIP]
> Every script in the local stage reads and writes under a single `ATLAS_BASE` environment variable (default: your repository root, set via `export ATLAS_BASE=$(pwd)`). If a script can't find its data, this variable is the first thing to check.

Sources: [atlas_h100/README.md](/pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L1-L22), [scripts/README.md](/pipeline/scripts/README.md#L1-L5), [METHODS.md](/docs/METHODS.md#L85-L89), [REPRODUCE.md](/docs/REPRODUCE.md#L8-L17)

## Core Concepts for New Readers

Five terms recur on every page of this documentation. The table below defines each in one sentence, in the order you are likely to meet them.

| Concept | What it means here |
|---|---|
| **Feature (SAE feature)** | One direction in a sparse autoencoder's dictionary; a feature's identity is the ranked list of genes that most activate it (top 20 kept per catalogue) |
| **Feature catalogue** | The per-layer JSON file listing every feature's genes — the atomic artifact the whole local stage consumes |
| **Annotator** | The procedure that maps a feature's genes to a named biological concept; a *permissive* version (top-5 genes, five databases) failed a random-gene null, so every cross-model claim uses the *calibrated* version (top-10 genes, curated pathway, ≥3 overlap) |
| **Null model** | A synthetic control (random genes, degree-matched genes, cell shuffles, rewired graphs) that every claim must beat — the failed and passed controls are reported side by side |
| **Held-out corpus** | A second cell draw (seed 1, 5,581 cells) sharing no cells with the corpus, used to test whether findings replicate on data the pipeline never touched |

Sources: [METHODS.md](/docs/METHODS.md#L21-L56), [DECISIONS.md](/docs/DECISIONS.md#L61-L80)

## What the Atlas Found (Headlines)

The findings section of the README is unusual in scientific code repositories: it reports the controls that *failed* alongside those that passed, and every number is audited against the result file that produced it. Four headlines summarize the story:

- **A naive "universal core" is an artifact.** The permissive annotator suggests 1,977 concepts shared by all ten models — but *random* genes share 3,570 under the same construction (z = −24.2). The claim does not survive its null.
- **A calibrated backbone is real, but modest.** Under the calibrated annotator, 96 concepts are shared by at least 8 of 10 models — 27.5× the uniform random-gene null — and they replicate on the disjoint held-out draw. Yet a no-model dictionary built purely from gene-gene co-expression recovers 73–95 of those same 96 concepts: the backbone is mostly the co-expression structure of the data, not something the models add.
- **Known regulation is recovered by only 4 of 10 models** (UCE 10.2×, Tahoe-x1 9.4×, C2S-Scale 5.5×, Geneformer-V2 2.5× over a degree-matched null against TRRUST), and co-expression from the same cells does about as well.
- **No new biology, and the reason is the evidence:** only 98 of 4,272 predicted pairs were never co-mentioned in literature, and the resources cannot confirm links about understudied genes.

The detailed claims — and equally important, the **retracted** ones — are catalogued in [Key Findings and Retracted Claims](4-key-findings-and-retracted-claims).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L64-L118)

## Why Everything Is Audited

The repository's most distinctive feature is its reproducibility engineering. The published catalogues are the *second* run: three faults in the first release (a position cap that let some models see 32 cells while others saw 6,000, filler genes in top-gene lists, and an unseeded SAE) were discovered and the entire extraction was corrected and re-run, with the changes documented as decision 16 in the log. Three mechanisms keep the current numbers honest:

1. **The audit** — `audit_all.py` runs six modules performing 312 checks that re-derive every number in the paper, supplement, figures, and website from the result files, and reports whether it is safe to submit.
2. **Checksummed archives** — the 1.2 GB of per-run outputs ship as release assets with SHA-256 checksums, downloaded and verified by `fetch_runs.sh`.
3. **The decision log** — `docs/DECISIONS.md` records every methodological choice in order: what was decided, why, what it cost, and where it lives in the code.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L27-L45), [REPRODUCE.md](/docs/REPRODUCE.md#L47-L77), [DECISIONS.md](/docs/DECISIONS.md#L1-L4)

## Getting Started Path

The fastest meaningful interaction with this repository requires no GPU and no large downloads — install five pinned packages, drop in the manuscript files, and run the audit:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
export ATLAS_BASE=$(pwd)
cp /path/to/MANUSCRIPT.md /path/to/SUPPLEMENTARY.md outputs/atlas/comparative/
python pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py      # 312 checks: paper, supplement, figures, site
python pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py   # rebuilds index.html from the result files
```

If you prefer to explore before running anything, open the live atlas directly — it is a static page with the feature maps fetched on demand, servable locally with `python -m http.server`.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L37-L45), [REPRODUCE.md](/docs/REPRODUCE.md#L19-L45)

# Quick Start



This page takes you from a fresh clone to a working, verifiable copy of the Comparative SAE Atlas on your own machine — without requiring a GPU, and in most paths without downloading anything. It covers the one-time environment setup, the shortest route to *seeing* the atlas, the audited route to *trusting* it, and the full route to *re-running* every published number. Deeper mechanics (how the SAE is trained, how the null models work, how the site is assembled) are deliberately out of scope here; each section points to the dedicated page that owns them.

The repository compares **ten single-cell foundation models** — run on the same 6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells, each opened with one sparse autoencoder per layer (172 in all) — and asks what each model encodes, what they share, and whether their features predict biology they were never shown. A live version runs at `https://avantipova.github.io/comparative-sae-atlas/`, and the same site is served from this repository's `index.html`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L9)

## The Repository at a Glance

Before running anything, it helps to know what is already on disk. The key beginner insight: **the final result files ship with the repository**. The 59 result files and 7 figures that every published number is read from live in `outputs/atlas/comparative/` — so verifying and re-serving the site needs no download at all. Only *re-running the analysis from raw feature catalogues* requires fetching a 1.2 GB release archive.

```
.
├── index.html, data/            the site: a 12 MB page plus feature maps fetched on demand
├── outputs/atlas/comparative/   the 59 result files and 7 figures every number is read from
├── pipeline/atlas_h100/         the GPU stage: adapters, SAE, extraction, per-model analyses
├── pipeline/scripts/            the local stage: matrices, controls, prediction tests, assembly, audit
├── pipeline/atlas_template.html the site's markup; index.html is built from it
├── docs/REPRODUCE.md            how to check, rebuild, re-run, re-extract (canonical runbook)
├── docs/RESULTS.md              every result file: written by, read by, what it holds
└── requirements.txt             the local analysis environment (Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3.4)
```

Not in the repository, by design: the manuscript and supplement (the audit needs you to drop them in), the per-run feature catalogues and external inputs (1.2 GB, published as release assets fetched by `pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh`), and the SAE weights and activations (about 17 GB, which stay on the GPU host).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L30), [figures/](outputs/atlas/comparative/figures)

## How the Pieces Fit Together

Every Quick Start command below touches one of three layers. The GPU stage is the only part that needs special hardware — and you can skip it entirely, because its outputs (the feature catalogues) were already published as release archives, and their *downstream* results already sit in the repository.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph GPU["GPU stage — pipeline/atlas_h100/ (optional)"]
        A["10 model checkpoints"] --> B["adapters/ extract<br/>activations per layer"]
        B --> C["TopK SAE per layer<br/>(172 total)"]
        C --> D["feature_catalog_L*.json<br/>per model"]
    end
    subgraph REL["Release archives — fetch_runs.sh"]
        D --> E["1.2 GB catalogues<br/>+ gene-set vocabulary"]
    end
    subgraph LOCAL["Local stage — pipeline/scripts/ (CPU, your laptop)"]
        E --> F["matrices, nulls,<br/>prediction tests"]
        F --> G["atlas_assemble<br/>→ controls.json"]
    end
    H["outputs/atlas/comparative/<br/>59 result files — shipped in repo"] --> I["inject_atlas.py"]
    G --> I
    I --> J["index.html + data/explorer.json<br/>→ open in browser"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L24), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L1-L13), [pipeline/scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L1-L5)

## Step 0: Set Up the Environment (Once)

Clone the repository, create a virtual environment, install the pinned dependencies, and set the one environment variable every script depends on:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Biodyn-AI/atlas-comparison && cd atlas-comparison
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
export ATLAS_BASE=$(pwd)    # every script reads and writes under $ATLAS_BASE/outputs/atlas/
```

`ATLAS_BASE` is the single most important setting: every local script resolves its data root from it, defaulting to the authors' own path if unset — so always export it. The pins in `requirements.txt` (Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3.4, SciPy, h5py, anndata, matplotlib) are exactly the versions the published nulls, figures and audits were computed under.

> [!TIP]
> There are **two separate environments** and they must never be mixed. The local analysis runs on Python 3.13 with NumPy 2.3.4 (`requirements.txt`); the GPU extraction ran on Python 3.12 with PyTorch 2.13 and NumPy **1.26.4** (`pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml`). The NumPy major versions differ on purpose. If you never touch the GPU folder, only `requirements.txt` matters to you.

| | Local analysis (all you need today) | GPU extraction (optional, advanced) |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.13 | 3.12 |
| NumPy | 2.3.4 | 1.26.4 |
| Deep learning stack | none | PyTorch 2.13 + CUDA 13 |
| Hardware | laptop CPU | NVIDIA H100 |
| Defined by | `requirements.txt` | `pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml` |

Sources: [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L6-L17), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L18), [pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml](pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml#L1-L9), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L87-L89)

## Which Path Do You Take?

The reproduction runbook defines three stages; this page arranges them as four escalating paths, ordered by how much you want to do. Each path is self-contained — stop after any of them.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Step 0 done: venv + requirements.txt + ATLAS_BASE"] --> Q{"What do you want?"}
    Q -->|"Just look"| P1["Path 1 — open the live site<br/>or serve index.html locally"]
    Q -->|"Trust but verify"| P2["Path 2 — audit_all.py<br/>312 checks, six modules, all PASS"]
    Q -->|"Re-run the science"| P3["Path 3 — fetch_runs.sh (1.2 GB)<br/>then the local stage in documented order"]
    Q -->|"Re-extract from scratch"| P4["Path 4 — H100 + checkpoints<br/>environment.yml + run_full_fixed.sh"]
    P3 --> F["figures + tables + audit_all"]
    P4 --> P3
```

Sources: [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L3-L4), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L19-L134)

## Path 1: See the Atlas (No Downloads)

Open the hosted site in a browser, or serve the repository's own copy locally with any static server:

```bash
python -m http.server 8765      # from the repository root, then open http://localhost:8765/
```

The page is a 12 MB HTML document; the heavier feature maps for the Layer Explorer are fetched on demand, so a local serve stays lightweight. This is the entire "install" for a first look — no Python execution, no audit, no data files.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L8-L9), [README.md](README.md#L14), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L32-L35)

## Path 2: Verify the Published Numbers (No Downloads)

This is the repository's signature workflow: an audit that **re-derives every number** in the paper, supplement, figures and site from the result files already on disk.

```bash
cp /path/to/MANUSCRIPT.md /path/to/SUPPLEMENTARY.md outputs/atlas/comparative/
python pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py
```

Expected output: **six modules, all PASS, 312 checks**. The one prerequisite is the manuscript itself: `MANUSCRIPT.md` and `SUPPLEMENTARY.md` are not in the repository (they are shared separately), and the audit needs them dropped next to the results in `outputs/atlas/comparative/`. The audit is split into focused checkers — manuscript numbers for Results 3.1–3.3 and Methods, Results 3.4–3.5 and Discussion, derived numbers, hand-written supplementary tables, and figure-vs-input hashes — and `audit_all.py` runs them all, telling you whether the state is safe to trust.

> [!TIP]
> If you only ever run one command from this page, run `audit_all.py`. It is the machine-checked guarantee that the numbers you are reading match the result files that produced them — the same guarantee the authors used across eight reviewer passes.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L37-L45), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L19-L30), [pipeline/scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L84-L88)

## Path 3: Rebuild the Site from the Result Files

Still no downloads. `inject_atlas.py` embeds the data blocks from the shipped result files into the site template and writes both `index.html` and `data/explorer.json`:

```bash
python pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py   # writes index.html and data/explorer.json
python -m http.server 8765                # then open http://localhost:8765/
```

This is the same command that produced the committed site, so after running it you can diff your rebuilt `index.html` against the committed one — a concrete, checkable artifact. To go one step further and re-render the seven figures and generated supplementary tables, the runbook chains the figure scripts and re-stamps the figure manifest before regenerating Tables S2–S12 — the full sequence is in `[docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md)` step 1.

Sources: [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L30-L45), [README.md](README.md#L44), [pipeline/scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L80-L82)

## Path 4: Re-Run the Full Local Analysis

Everything so far read pre-computed results. To recompute them from the raw feature catalogues, first fetch the release archives — 1.2 GB unpacked — which the fetch script downloads, checksum-verifies, and unpacks into `outputs/atlas/`:

```bash
bash pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh     # add --legacy only for the superseded first run
```

The default is `runs-v2`, the **corrected extraction** (every model reads all 6,000 cells; the earlier `runs-v1` had a position cap that let AIDO.Cell see 32 cells while tGPT saw all 6,000, plus filler genes and an unseeded SAE). Do not reach for `--legacy` unless you specifically want the superseded catalogues.

| archive | size | holds |
|---|---|---|
| `runs-ts3_out.tar.gz` | 70 MB | feature catalogues on the shared corpus: five depth-matched layers for seven models, every layer for GeneCompass, scFoundation, Tahoe-x1 |
| `runs-alllayer_cat.tar.gz` | 57 MB | every-layer catalogues for seven models (AIDO.Cell … tGPT) |
| `runs-heldout_cat.tar.gz` | 23 MB | catalogues on the independent held-out draw (5,581 cells, none shared with the corpus), all ten models |
| `runs-seeds.tar.gz` | 24 MB | the SAE-seed control (three seeds), read by `controls_import.py` |
| `inputs-genesets.tar.gz` | 101 MB | GO_BP, KEGG, Reactome sets, STRING v12 edges, TRRUST edges, the 16,205-gene background |

Two inputs are **not** redistributed and must be fetched from their own sources: NCBI `gene2pubmed.gz` and `Homo_sapiens.gene_info.gz` into `outputs/atlas/pubmed/`, and the Replogle et al. 2022 Perturb-seq files (`K562_gwps_normalized_bulk_01.h5ad`, `rpe1_normalized_bulk_01.h5ad`) into `outputs/atlas/perturb/`. Without them, the literature- and perturbation-evidence scripts cannot run.

The local stage then runs in a documented order, grouped as: build matrices → controls (the nulls) → predictions → assembly → figures → tables → final `audit_all`. Order genuinely matters — `controls.py` reads matrices that `alllayer_matrix.py` writes, and `atlas_assemble.py` and the controls iterate to a fixed point (two passes in practice). Run that phase with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` so ties between equally ranked concepts resolve identically. Expect minutes to an hour per permutation-based script on a laptop (`controls.py` about 3 minutes); all seeds are fixed, so your numbers should reproduce exactly.

Sources: [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L47-L59), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L61-L68), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L79-L88), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L90-L132), [README.md](README.md#L27-L35)

## Path 5 (Optional): Re-Extract on a GPU

Only for those who want to reproduce the extraction itself. You need the ten model checkpoints, an H100-class GPU, and the conda environment from `pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml`. Build the shared corpus twice (seed 0 = corpus, seed 1 = held-out draw), drop the 419 overlapping cells, then run the fixed shell scripts:

```bash
cd pipeline/atlas_h100
python build_ts_corpus.py --per-tissue 2000 --seed 0 --out external/perturb/tabula_3tissue_6k.h5ad
python build_ts_corpus.py --per-tissue 2000 --seed 1 --out external/perturb/tabula_3tissue_6k_heldout.h5ad
python make_heldout_disjoint.py          # drop the 419 cells the two draws share
bash run_full_fixed.sh                   # every layer, every model, all 6,000 cells
bash run_heldout_fixed.sh                # the held-out draw, five depth-matched layers
bash run_seeds_fixed.sh                  # the SAE-seed control
bash run_downstream_fixed.sh             # cell embeddings, CKA, probes, SVD, explorer
```

The extraction scripts are **resumable** — a model with a `DONE` marker is skipped — so interrupted runs restart cheaply. Note Tahoe-x1 needs its own virtual environment (`torch 2.6.0` with `flash-attn`), pointed at via `ATLAS_TAHOE_VENV`. The critical flag is `--per-cell 168`: every model reads all 6,000 cells and keeps at most 168 gene-token positions per cell (≈1M positions per layer), which is precisely the correction that produced `runs-v2` — omitting it silently recreates the superseded v1 behaviour. The SAE weights (~17 GB) stay on the GPU host and are never archived; only the per-layer catalogues are.

Sources: [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L134-L158), [pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh#L1-L24), [pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml](pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml#L11-L37)

## Command Summary

| command | what it does | what it needs | works offline? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `python -m http.server 8765` | serves the site | nothing | yes |
| `python pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py` | 312 checks across paper, supplement, figures, site | manuscript files dropped in | yes |
| `python pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py` | rebuilds `index.html` + `data/explorer.json` | shipped result files | yes |
| `bash pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh` | downloads, checksum-verifies, unpacks 1.2 GB of catalogues | internet | no |
| `bash pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh` | all-layer SAE extraction, resumable per model | H100, ten checkpoints, GPU env | no |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L37-L45), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L25-L35), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L53-L55), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L139-L150)

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | cause | fix |
|---|---|---|
| `audit_all.py` cannot start | `MANUSCRIPT.md` / `SUPPLEMENTARY.md` missing | copy both into `outputs/atlas/comparative/` |
| scripts write to, or look in, the wrong place | `ATLAS_BASE` unset (defaults to the authors' path) | `export ATLAS_BASE=$(pwd)` before running anything |
| numbers differ from the paper after re-running | you fetched `--legacy` (v1) catalogues | re-run `fetch_runs.sh` without the flag (default `runs-v2`) |
| `pip install` conflicts around NumPy 1.x | GPU environment mixed into the local venv | keep the two environments separate; local uses only `requirements.txt` |
| prediction scripts return stale pair graphs after re-fetching catalogues | cached co-firing graph | delete `outputs/atlas/comparative/.cofire_cache.pkl` |
| figure checks fail after re-rendering | figure manifest stale | `python pipeline/scripts/audit_figures.py --update` |
| `run_full_fixed.sh` fails only on Tahoe-x1 | Tahoe needs its own venv (torch 2.6 + flash-attn) | set `ATLAS_TAHOE_VENV` to a dedicated environment |

Sources: [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L21-L23), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L12-L17), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L54-L59), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L119-L120), [docs/REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L43-L45), [pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh#L7-L10), [pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml](pipeline/atlas_h100/environment.yml#L5-L6)

## What You Just Built

If you followed Path 3, you rebuilt a 12 MB interactive atlas whose analysis backbone looks like this — Figure 1 of the paper, regenerated entirely from the files already in your clone:

![Fig1 overview](https://github.com/Biodyn-AI/atlas-comparison/blob/main/outputs/atlas/comparative/figures/Fig1_overview.png?raw=true)

The audited headline behind it: the naive "universal core" of 1,977 concepts shared by all ten models does **not** survive a random-gene null (random genes score higher, z = −24.2), but a calibrated backbone of 96 concepts shared by at least 8 of 10 models is real — 27.5× a uniform null and 51.2× a degree-matched one, and it replicates on an independent draw of cells. Reading the results first, before the machinery, is the recommended order for beginners.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L61-L73), [figures/](outputs/atlas/comparative/figures)

# Ten Foundation Models Compared



This page introduces the ten single-cell foundation models behind the Comparative SAE Atlas: who they are, how they differ, and — most importantly — what the project does to make their differences *measurable* rather than confounded. A **foundation model** here is a large neural network pretrained on millions of single-cell transcriptomes, which you can then reuse for many tasks. The core engineering idea of this repository is that all ten models are run through one identical pipeline (same cells, same sparse autoencoder, same annotator), so any difference in the output can be attributed to the model itself and not to the data it saw. This page stays at the level of the models and the comparison machinery; deeper mechanics live in the Deep Dive pages.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L6), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L5-L14)

## The Ten Models at a Glance

The ten models were chosen to span three orders of magnitude in size (10 million to 3 billion parameters) and four different ways of "reading" a cell. All ten are gene-token transformer models: they represent a cell as a sequence of gene tokens and process it with stacked transformer layers. The table below is the project's canonical registry, defined once in `pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml` and mirrored in the manuscript's Table S1.

| model | params | d_model | layers | reads a cell as | objective | prior | species | checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIDO.Cell | 10M | 256 | 8 | expression, all 19,264 genes | MLM | none | human | `genbio-ai/AIDO.Cell-10M` |
| scGPT | ~50M | 512 | 12 | binned expression | MLM | none | human | `bowang-lab/scGPT` whole-human |
| tGPT | ~120M | 1024 | 8 | rank order | autoregressive | none | human | `lixiangchun/transcriptome-gpt-1024-8-16-64` |
| scFoundation | 100M | 768 | 12 | expression, read-depth aware | MAE | none | human | `biomap-research/scFoundation` |
| GeneCompass | 104M | 768 | 12 | rank order + value | MLM (ID and value) | knowledge (GRN, family, promoter, co-expression) | human+mouse | `xCompass-AI/GeneCompass` base |
| MaxToki | 217M | 1232 | 11 | rank order (corpus-scaled) | autoregressive | none | human | `theodoris-lab/MaxToki` 217M |
| Geneformer-V2 | 316M | 1152 | 18 | rank order | MLM | none | human | `ctheodoris/Geneformer` Geneformer-V2-316M |
| UCE | 650M | 1280 | 33 | ESM2 protein tokens sampled by expression | masked | ESM | multi-species | `snap-stanford/UCE` 33-layer |
| C2S-Scale | 2B | 2304 | 26 | rank-ordered gene names as text | autoregressive | text (Gemma-2-2B) | human+mouse | `vandijklab/C2S-Scale-Gemma-2-2B` |
| Tahoe-x1 | 3B | 2560 | 32 | binned expression | MLM | none | human | `tahoebio/Tahoe-x1` 3B |

Two columns deserve a beginner's note. **d_model** is the width of the vector each token is represented by — it ranges from 256 (AIDO.Cell) to 2,560 (Tahoe-x1) and directly determines how large the per-model sparse autoencoder must be. **Layers** is the number of transformer blocks whose internal states the pipeline extracts; summed across all ten models, the pipeline trains **172 SAEs in total** (8+12+8+12+12+11+18+33+26+32).

Sources: [configs/models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L1-L25), [README.md](README.md#L43-L57), [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L12-L15)

## Three Axes of Difference

Reading the table column by column, the models differ along three conceptual axes, and each axis is a hypothesis about what information matters in a cell.

**Input encoding** — how a raw count matrix becomes tokens. Four schemes appear. *Expression* models (AIDO.Cell, scFoundation) feed continuous values, with scFoundation additionally scaling by each cell's read depth. *Binned expression* (scGPT, Tahoe-x1) discretizes values into bins. *Rank order* (tGPT, MaxToki, Geneformer-V2, GeneCompass) feeds only the ordering of genes within a cell, discarding magnitudes entirely. Two outliers go further: UCE converts genes to **ESM2 protein-language tokens** (so the model reads protein embeddings informed by protein structure), and C2S-Scale treats **ranked gene names as literal text** for a language model that started life as Gemma-2.

**Objective** — the pretraining task. *Masked language modeling* (MLM) hides some tokens and predicts them from context; *autoregressive* models predict the next token in sequence, GPT-style; *MAE* (masked autoencoder, scFoundation) reconstructs masked inputs. This distinction decides what "understanding a cell" means for each model before the atlas even starts.

**Prior** — outside knowledge carried into the weights. Seven models are tabula rasa (prior: none). GeneCompass injects a knowledge graph of regulatory networks, gene families, promoters and co-expression; UCE inherits knowledge from ESM2's protein pretraining; C2S-Scale inherits general text knowledge from Gemma-2. The atlas can therefore ask: does a prior help, hurt, or not matter?

Sources: [configs/models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L10-L25), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L203-L218), [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L12-L15)

## What Makes the Comparison Fair: One Corpus, One SAE

The comparison is only meaningful if every model processes identical inputs through identical downstream machinery. Three invariants hold for all ten models:

**One corpus.** All models read the same 6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells — 2,000 each from immune, kidney and lung tissue — drawn from cellxgene-census v1.18.0 with seed 0. A second draw with seed 1 (minus the 419 cells it accidentally shares with the corpus, leaving 5,581) serves as a fully held-out replication set. Before this project, earlier single-model atlases used different corpora (Geneformer on K562, scGPT on Tabula Sapiens), so any model difference could have been a data difference; here that confound is removed by construction.

**One sparse autoencoder configuration.** After extraction, each model's residual stream at each layer is compressed by a **TopK SAE** — a small network that learns a wider dictionary of interpretable features, keeping only the k=32 most active per token. The configuration is fixed and identical: dictionary of 4× d_model features, MSE loss, Adam at 3e-4, 4 epochs, seeded (seed 0) for both NumPy and torch. Training data is balanced identically too: every model sees at most 168 gene-token positions from *every one* of the 6,000 cells, about 1M positions per layer.

**One annotation standard.** Feature catalogues are annotated by one calibrated method (top-10 genes, ≥3 of them in one curated pathway set), fixed on the discovery corpus before the held-out corpus was ever touched — details belong to [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation).

Sources: [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L4-L24), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L5-L14), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L26-L41)

The flow from raw checkpoints to the numbers on the site looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph GPU["GPU stage — pipeline/atlas_h100/ (H100 host)"]
        CKPT["10 model checkpoints<br/>downloaded from Hugging Face"]
        CORPUS["Shared corpus<br/>6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells (seed 0)<br/>+ held-out draw (seed 1, 5,581 cells)"]
        ADAPTERS["10 adapters<br/>one file per model"]
        RESID["Residual stream activations<br/>every layer, gene-token positions only"]
        SAE["One TopK SAE per layer<br/>k = 32, dict 4×d_model, seed 0<br/>172 SAEs across ten models"]
        CKPT --> ADAPTERS
        CORPUS --> ADAPTERS
        ADAPTERS --> RESID --> SAE
    end
    subgraph LOCAL["Local stage — pipeline/scripts/ (no GPU needed)"]
        CAT["Feature catalogues<br/>top-20 genes per feature, per layer"]
        ANN["Calibrated annotator<br/>+ null models"]
        RESULTS["59 result files<br/>outputs/atlas/comparative/"]
        SITE["Interactive atlas site<br/>index.html + audit_all.py"]
        SAE --> CAT --> ANN --> RESULTS --> SITE
    end
```

Sources: [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L1-L24), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L48-L66)

## The Adapter Contract: How Model Differences Are Isolated

Ten very different checkpoints (one needs `flash-attn` in its own conda environment, one needs a revived `torchtext` shim) must all emit the same data format, or nothing downstream could be shared. That is the job of the **adapter contract** in `pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py`. Each of the ten adapters implements a single method, `iter_activations(adata, batch_size)`, which per batch of cells yields three things: a dict mapping each extracted layer to a float32 array of shape `[n_positions, d_model]`, the HGNC gene symbol (upper-cased) of every position, and the global cell index of every position. Only *gene* token positions are yielded — CLS tokens, padding, and depth/special tokens are dropped inside the adapter, so downstream code never knows they existed. Everything after the adapter — SAE training, catalogues, annotation — is written model-agnostically against this one interface.

> [!TIP]
> The adapter contract is the load-bearing design decision of the whole comparison: because the interface yields `(layer → activations, gene symbols, cell ids)`, adding an eleventh model would require writing exactly one new file in `adapters/` and zero changes anywhere else. This is why "the rest of the pipeline is model-agnostic" is stated as a contract, not an aspiration.

Sources: [adapters/base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L1-L40), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L70-L75), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L78-L82)

A concrete example makes the pattern clear. The AIDO adapter's `load()` reads the checkpoint's config to learn how many layers it has and applies the depth-matching rule; its `iter_activations()` aligns the input matrix to the model's 19,264-gene vocabulary, runs the forward pass under `torch.no_grad()`, pulls the `hidden_states` tuple, reshapes each requested layer to `[n_positions, 256]`, and tiles the gene-symbol array to match. All ten adapters follow this load/iterate shape while hiding their wildly different preprocessing (binning, rank encoding, ESM tokenization) behind it.

Sources: [adapters/aido.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/aido.py#L1-L56)

## Comparing Different Depths: the Depth-Matched Read-Out

A subtle problem: how do you compare "the same part of the network" between an 8-layer model and a 33-layer model? Absolute layer indices are meaningless across architectures. The project's answer is **relative depth**: all layers are extracted for every model, and wherever one comparable depth per model is needed, the five layers at **0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100%** of network depth form the depth-matched read-out. The rule is implemented in four lines: `depth_matched(n_layers)` takes the indices `round(f × (n_layers − 1))` for those five fractions, deduplicates (small models can collapse some), and sorts them. UCE's 33 layers map to a clean 0, 8, 16, 24, 32; AIDO's 8 layers collapse to a coarser set of five (with two adjacent indices landing close together).

One discipline rule follows from this and matters for reading any result: **feature counts are never summed across layers**, and features from different layers are never read as concepts coexisting in one representation — each layer is its own representational space with its own dictionary. The per-layer story (mid-network peaks, late collapse of annotation rate) is exactly what the all-layer extraction was designed to reveal, and it feeds [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd).

Sources: [common/layers.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/layers.py#L1-L20), [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L26-L29), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L16-L24)

## What the Comparison Found

The payoff of the fair setup is a set of model-level verdicts, each audited against its result file. For a beginner, the headline is that model identity clearly matters for some tasks and clearly does not for others:

| question | verdict across the ten models | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Do features predict unseen biology? | **Only 4 of 10 pass.** Gene pairs that co-fire recover held-out TRRUST regulatory edges above a degree-preserving null: UCE 10.2×, Tahoe-x1 9.4×, C2S-Scale 5.5×, Geneformer-V2 2.5× (p ≤ 0.005); the other six do not | `hypothesis_final.json` |
| Do models agree on a shared backbone? | A calibrated backbone of **96 concepts** is shared by ≥8 of 10 models (27.5× the uniform random-gene null), but **no concept is in all ten** | `backbone_terms.json`, `stats_final.json` |
| Does model size track concept count? | Yes, descriptively: concepts against parameters **r = 0.855** (bootstrap CI 0.68–0.984), on n = 10 models — reported as descriptive only | `controls.json` |
| Do SAE features add value over PCA? | **In all ten models**, the SAE explains more variance than the best rank-32 PCA subspace, by +0.02 (tGPT) to +0.55 (Geneformer-V2) | `svd_vs_sae` files, `cka_svd_null.json` |
| Is the shared structure just co-expression? | Largely: a model-free co-expression dictionary recovers 73–95 of the 96 backbone concepts; models' own middle layers recover 23–96 | `coexpr_core_baseline.json` |
| Is the SAE healthy in every model? | No: tGPT's dictionaries have the most dead features (21.3% on average, 58.6% at worst) — flagged as a confound for tGPT-specific results; near-duplicate feature blocks appear in every model except Geneformer-V2 and GeneCompass | `sae_health.json` |

Two cross-model findings sharpen the picture further. Agreement between independently trained models is a precision signal: gene pairs predicted by two models are 15.3× over the null versus 5.0× for pairs from one model — yet agreement beyond two adds nothing (none of the 918 pairs shared by five or more models is a known edge). And the geometry result is model-independent: linear CKA between every pair of models exceeds its cell-shuffle floor (worst pair 43×), meaning all ten models organize this corpus into recognizably similar representation spaces despite their different encodings, objectives and priors.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L59-L120), [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L10-L78), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L26-L41), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L219-L223)

> [!TIP]
> When reading any per-model number in this project, check whether it came from the depth-matched five layers or from all layers — the two views differ (the mid-depth slice gives 97 backbone concepts where the standard mid layer gives 96, because rounding lands one layer apart for even-depth models). The rule "never sum features across layers" exists precisely so these two views are never conflated.

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L234-L238)

## The Corrected Extraction: Why "As Extracted" Matters

One caution for interpreting every number above: the published catalogues come from a **corrected re-run** (`runs-v2`), not the first release. The first extraction had a position cap that took training positions in corpus order, so models that read every gene saw very few cells — AIDO.Cell saw 32 cells, scFoundation about 160, while tGPT (64 tokens per cell) saw all 6,000. That meant the v1 comparison was, in effect, comparing models trained on *different data* — exactly the confound the shared corpus was built to eliminate. Three further faults (arbitrary filler genes in top-gene lists, an unseeded torch SAE, a stale UCE preprocessing cache) were fixed at the same time. After the re-run, the backbone grew from 78 to 96 concepts, held-out replication now covers all ten models, and TRRUST prediction holds in four models instead of five (scGPT drops out). The full fault-by-fault account belongs to [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run); the takeaway for this page is simply that every number quoted here is from the run where all ten models genuinely saw the same cells with the same budget.

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L264-L299), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L48-L68), [README.md](README.md#L29-L32)

## Where to Go Next

The natural reading path from here, following the catalog:

- To see the consequences of these comparisons for scientific claims — including which headline claims failed their own nulls — read [Key Findings and Retracted Claims](4-key-findings-and-retracted-claims).
- To understand how a checkpoint becomes a feature catalogue step by step, start with the extraction stage: [Model Adapter Contract](6-model-adapter-contract), then [TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training) and [Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw).
- To go deeper on the evaluation machinery behind the table above: [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test) explains the four-of-ten verdict, [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd) explains the all-pairs agreement result, and [Co-Expression Baseline Comparisons](15-co-expression-baseline-comparisons) explains why the shared backbone is attributed to the data.
- To see the models side by side interactively, open the live atlas (`index.html` in the repository root), where every displayed number is read at page-load from the result files in `outputs/atlas/comparative/`.


# Key Findings and Retracted Claims



This page is the scoreboard of the comparative SAE atlas: the findings about ten single-cell foundation models that **survived** their null-model tests, and the claims that were **retracted** when those same nulls killed them. Every number below is audited against the result file that produced it, and every retracted claim is kept as a reproducible negative result rather than deleted — this repository treats a failed control with the same care as a success.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L64-L68), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L1-L4)

## How a Claim Earns Its Place Here

The core discipline of this project is simple to state: **no claim is made unless a null model built to reproduce it by chance fails to do so**. Each result is stated against a null matched to the failure mode it guards against — random genes for annotation claims, degree-matched genes so popularity cannot win, rewired co-firing graphs so study bias cannot win, shuffled cells for geometry claims. The result is an empirical p-value, and a verdict.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["172 feature catalogues<br/>one SAE per model layer"] --> B["A cross-model claim<br/>e.g. concepts shared by many models"]
    B --> C["Matched null model<br/>random genes / degree-matched / rewired graph"]
    C --> D["Permutation testing<br/>empirical p from N draws"]
    D --> E{"Does the real result<br/>beat its null?"}
    E -- "yes" --> F["Survives: reported with fold-over-null<br/>stored in a result JSON"]
    E -- "no" --> G["Retracted: kept as a<br/>reproducible negative result"]
    F --> H["audit_all.py re-derives<br/>every number: 312 checks"]
    G --> H
```

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L99), [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L48-L55)

The permutation counts differ by computational cost and are stated wherever a derived number appears. Two statistical hygiene rules follow for beginners. First, with N permutations the smallest possible p-value is 1/(N+1), so most "significant" results in this project sit at that floor — that is expected, not suspicious. Second, results near the threshold are labelled marginal rather than promoted: MaxToki at equal budget sits at p = 0.04, and the corroboration gain in one robustness variant sits at p = 0.055.

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L101-L107)

| Claim | Null built to defeat it | Permutations |
|---|---|---|
| Shared backbone (concepts in 8+ of 10 models) | Uniform random genes; degree-matched random genes | 250 each |
| Backbone across depth | Uniform random genes at each of five depths | 250 |
| Held-out replication of backbone | Random-gene backbones on both cell draws | 150 |
| Naive core (**retracted**) | Uniform random genes, mid layer and all-layer union | 100; 20 |
| CKA between models | Shuffle the cells of one embedding | per pair |
| Held-out regulatory recovery per model | Rewire co-firing graph, keep every gene's degree | 500 |
| Literature co-mention | Publication-count-preserving shuffle | 200 |
| Perturbation support | Responsiveness-matched gene | 200 |

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L89-L99)

## What Survived: The Findings

Eight findings passed their nulls. The most important structural lesson is finding 3: much of what the models appear to contribute is already **the co-expression structure of the data**, which is why the project keeps reporting the model-free baseline next to every model result.

| # | Finding | Headline numbers | Evidence file |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A calibrated backbone is real and modest | 96 concepts in 8+ of 10 models; 27.5× uniform null, 51.2× degree-matched, p < 0.004 | `backbone_terms.json` |
| 2 | The backbone replicates on unseen cells | Jaccard 0.52 vs 0.035 null, p = 0.02, all ten models | `heldout_calibrated.json` |
| 3 | Co-expression alone recovers most of the backbone | 73–95 of 96 concepts from model-free dictionaries | `coexpr_core_baseline.json` |
| 4 | Geometry agrees without any annotator | Worst CKA pair 43× above its shuffle floor; SAE beats rank-32 PCA in 10/10 models | `cka_svd_null.json` |
| 5 | Four of ten models predict held-out regulation | UCE 10.2×, Tahoe-x1 9.4×, C2S-Scale 5.5×, Geneformer-V2 2.5×, p ≤ 0.005 | `hypothesis_final.json` |
| 6 | Two-model agreement sharpens precision | 15.3× vs 5.0× for one model; precision 0.23% | `agreement_curve.json` |
| 7 | Literature and perturbation give small support | Co-mention 2.3×; perturbation 1.24× (K562), 1.33× (RPE1) | `hypothesis_pubmed.json`, `hypothesis_perturb.json` |
| 8 | No new biology — and the cause is the evidence | Only 98 of 4,272 pairs unverifiable; models feature 5,953 thinly-studied genes | `study_bias_coverage.json` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L69-L113), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L127-L145)

The backbone finding deserves its own unpacking because it is the project's positive centrepiece. Under the calibrated annotator (a feature's top-10 genes, at least 3 in one curated pathway of at most 200 genes), 96 concepts are shared by at least 8 of the 10 models. By the genes behind each match, 42 of them form one protein-synthesis block, 12 are other housekeeping, and 42 are specific programmes such as antigen presentation and cytokine signalling — 37 distinct programmes in all. It is present at every depth (55 to 133 concepts) and replicates on an independent cell draw sharing no cell with the corpus. **No concept is found in all ten models** — the all-ten intersection is brittle by construction, which is exactly why the naive version was retracted.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L73-L80), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L129-L136)

The held-out prediction test is the second centrepiece. For each model, gene pairs that co-fire in the same features (recurrence in at least five features) are scored against TRRUST, a regulatory database no step of the pipeline ever touched. Four of ten models beat a null that rewires the co-firing graph while preserving every gene's degree. Two design points matter for interpreting the numbers: an equal-budget re-scoring at 50,707 pairs keeps all four passing models significant (only dictionary size, not quality, limits how many pairs a model can offer), and pairs predicted by **two models independently** jump to 15.3× over the null — while agreement among five or more models adds nothing, since none of the 918 such pairs is a known edge.

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L147-L173), [README.md](README.md#L92-L103), [pipeline/scripts/agreement_curve.py](pipeline/scripts/agreement_curve.py#L1-L14)

> [!TIP]
> Notice what finding 3 does to interpretation: when a model-free dictionary of a seed gene plus its nine most correlated genes recovers 73–95 of the 96 backbone concepts, the honest claim is not "models encode housekeeping" but "the data's co-expression structure is recoverable, and models rediscover it". Every robustness analysis in this repo runs this baseline first.

## What Was Retracted, and Why the Negatives Are Kept

Four claims failed their nulls and were retracted. The repository's convention is unusual and worth internalising: **the scripts and result files for all four are kept**, so any future reader can reproduce the retraction, not just the headline findings.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph R["Retracted claims"]
        R1["Naive universal core<br/>1,977 concepts in all ten"]
        R2["Annotation rate as<br/>an interpretability score"]
        R3["'100% of SAE features<br/>invisible to SVD'"]
        R4["'New biology' shortlist"]
    end
    subgraph S["What replaced them"]
        S1["Calibrated backbone:<br/>96 concepts, 8 of 10 models"]
        S2["Calibrated rate:<br/>1.0-29.3% per model, mid layer"]
        S3["SAE vs rank-32 PCA<br/>variance at matched sparsity"]
        S4["Study-bias analysis:<br/>the atlas ranks, it cannot confirm"]
    end
    R1 --> S1
    R2 --> S2
    R3 --> S3
    R4 --> S4
```

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L109-L125), [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L35-L58)

| Retracted claim | What killed it | Decisive numbers | Kept in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Universal core of ~2,000 concepts shared by all ten | Random-gene null + held-out check | Random genes share **3,570** vs real 1,977 (z = −24.2); mid layer 365 vs 582 (z = −4.9); held-out Jaccard 0.50 vs **0.51** between two random draws | `random_null.json`, `heldout.json` |
| Annotation rate as interpretability score | Same null — random genes annotate almost as often under the permissive annotator | Calibrated rate (1.0–29.3% at mid layer) is the only usable version | `recalibrate_final.json` |
| "About 100% of SAE features invisible to top SVD axes" | True of random directions at this dimensionality — a property of the dimension, not the features | The load-bearing test is variance at matched sparsity: SAE beats top-32 PCA in all ten models, +0.02 (tGPT) to +0.55 (Geneformer-V2) | `svd_projection_k.json` |
| "New biology" shortlist (genes topping unannotated features in 5+ models) | Two nulls show it is a *deficit*, not an excess | **0 of 207** candidates survive | `novel_null.json`, `novel_calibrated.json` |

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L111-L123), [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L35-L36)

The first retraction is the clearest teaching example. `random_null.py` re-runs the annotation on every model's mid-layer catalogue with **random background genes** in place of the real top genes, then builds the "core" the same way. If the real core were biology, it should exceed the random one; instead random genes produce a *larger* core (3,570 vs 1,977, z = −24.2), because the databases are large and overlapping. The apparent "reproducibility" of the core across two cell draws (Jaccard 0.50) was also a mirage — two independent *random* draws overlap at 0.51.

Sources: [pipeline/scripts/random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py#L1-L9), [pipeline/scripts/random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py#L131-L151), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L111-L113)

The fourth retraction is subtler and shows two different null designs. `novel_null.py` asks whether genes topping *unannotated* features beat an equal-size random subset of features; `novel_calibrated.py` goes further with a **degree-matched label permutation** — it permutes the annotated/unannotated label across features while keeping each gene's degree exactly constant, so popularity cannot pass and the only thing tested is whether a gene's consensus concentrates on unannotated features. Both nulls agree: the shortlist is a deficit. The mechanism, worked out in the study-bias analysis, is that consensus tracks database coverage rather than filling its gaps — only 98 of 4,272 predicted pairs were never co-mentioned, and the models feature 5,953 genes with fewer than five papers, on which the recurrence filter is 7.0× harsher.

Sources: [pipeline/scripts/novel_null.py](pipeline/scripts/novel_null.py#L1-L9), [pipeline/scripts/novel_calibrated.py](pipeline/scripts/novel_calibrated.py#L1-L13), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L120-L123), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L198-L206)

> [!TIP]
> The label-permutation null in `novel_calibrated.py` is the pattern to remember: instead of shuffling genes (which changes their popularity), it shuffles *labels* on the same features, holding every gene's degree exactly constant. Any "is this subset special?" question can be answered with this trick.

## The scGPT Lesson: Why a Verdict Changed After the Re-Run

One finding on this page changed verdict outright, and understanding why is the best introduction to the extraction faults. After the first release, an external read of the code found that `extract()` stopped after 500,000 gene-token positions in corpus order — so models reading every gene saw very few cells (AIDO.Cell saw 32, scFoundation about 160, Geneformer-V2 and MaxToki about 270, UCE 492) while tGPT saw all 6,000. Everything downstream compared models trained on different data, so all catalogues were re-extracted and every analysis re-run from scratch (release `runs-v2`; superseded `runs-v1` kept).

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L264-L296), [README.md](README.md#L32-L35)

| Quantity | Superseded catalogues (runs-v1) | Corrected catalogues (runs-v2) |
|---|---|---|
| scGPT held-out TRRUST fold | 11.9× — passed | 1.7×, p = 0.27 — **does not pass** |
| scGPT's training cells | ~420 (position cap) | All 6,000 |
| Models passing the prediction test | 5 | 4 |
| Backbone size | 78 concepts | 96 concepts, still far above nulls |
| Held-out replication | Held | Replicates on all ten models |

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L156-L161), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L290-L295)

Note the asymmetry in what changed: scGPT dropped out of the passing set, but the backbone *grew stronger* (78 → 96 concepts). This is what a well-designed null architecture buys you — when inputs are corrected, results move in whichever direction the truth lies, and the nulls tell you whether the movement matters. A related late correction touched three model-facts entries (MaxToki's input encoding, GeneCompass's rank-plus-value input, tGPT's ~120M parameter count); everything reading model size or input type was recomputed, no conclusion changed, and architecture-to-feature associations remain reported as descriptive only (n = 10 models, bootstrap CIs about ±1).

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L208-L223), [README.md](README.md#L115-L118)

## A Beginner's Glossary for the Numbers on This Page

| Term | What it means here |
|---|---|
| Null model | The same analysis with the biology removed by construction — if the real result matches it, the claim is dead |
| Fold over null | Observed value ÷ null mean; "27.5×" means the real backbone is 27.5 times larger than chance |
| z-score | (observed − null mean) ÷ null SD; z = −24.2 means the real result is 24 SDs *below* what randomness gives |
| Jaccard | Shared members ÷ total members of two sets; 0.52 vs a 0.035 null means strong overlap beyond chance |
| Empirical p | (null draws at or above observed + 1) ÷ (N + 1); smallest possible value is 1/(N+1) |
| Degree-matched | Each real gene is swapped for a random gene with the same gene-set membership count, so gene popularity cannot produce the effect |
| Configuration model | Rewire a graph randomly while preserving every node's degree — the null behind the TRRUST prediction claims |

Sources: [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L48-L55), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L107)

## Verify It Yourself, and Where to Go Next

Every number on this page is re-derived from its result file by `audit_all.py` (312 checks across paper, supplement, figures and site), and figures are stamped against the hashes of their inputs so a stale figure fails the audit. The audit deliberately does *not* check prose claims, architecture facts, or figure legibility — those were checked by hand over three passes, and two display-floor bugs that the audit could not catch are disclosed on the figures themselves. To run the audit you need the manuscript and supplement dropped into `outputs/atlas/comparative/`; the full procedure is on the Quick Start page.

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L256-L262), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L234-L241), [README.md](README.md#L37-L45)

Reading progression for this catalog:

- **Before this page**: [Ten Foundation Models Compared](3-ten-foundation-models-compared) — who the ten models are and how each reads a cell.
- **To understand the retraction machinery**: [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation), [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim), and [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test).
- **For the geometry findings**: [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd).
- **For findings 7–8 in depth**: [Literature and Perturbation Evidence](14-literature-and-perturbation-evidence) and [Co-Expression Baseline Comparisons](15-co-expression-baseline-comparisons).
- **To see how the scGPT verdict reversed**: [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run) and [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks).


# Architecture Overview



This page maps the architecture of the Comparative SAE Atlas: how ten single-cell foundation models are reduced to a comparable, auditable set of results, and where every component lives. The repository is not an application so much as a **pipeline with a strict phase boundary** — everything that needs a GPU and model weights runs on the extraction host, everything that needs only the published feature catalogues runs locally, and an audit layer closes the loop between the results and the four surfaces that cite them (manuscript, supplement, figures, website). Read this page before the stage-specific deep dives; it establishes the vocabulary and the data flow the rest of the catalog assumes.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L8), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L1-L7)

## The System in One Diagram

The architecture decomposes into three stages separated by one artifact: the **feature catalogue** (`feature_catalog_L<NN>.json`), which is the only thing that crosses the GPU/local boundary. Everything upstream of it requires model weights and activations; everything downstream requires nothing but JSON and NumPy.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph GPU["Stage 1 — GPU Extraction (H100 host, PyTorch 2.13)"]
        CORPUS["build_ts_corpus.py<br/>6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells<br/>seed 0 · held-out draw seed 1"]
        ADAPT["adapters/*.py — ten models<br/>10M → 3B params, one contract"]
        EXTRACT["common/pipeline.py — extract()<br/>streamed activations, fp16/fp32 memmaps"]
        SAE["common/sae.py — train_sae()<br/>TopK SAE per layer, k=32, 4×d_model"]
        CATALOG["feature_catalog_L*​.json<br/>top-20 genes per feature"]
        CORPUS --> ADAPT --> EXTRACT --> SAE --> CATALOG
    end

    subgraph LOCAL["Stage 2 — Local Analysis (Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3.4)"]
        ANN["annotation: permissive (GPU) +<br/>calibrated (local recalibrate*.py)"]
        NULLS["null models: random-gene,<br/>degree-matched, cell-shuffle"]
        HYP["held-out regulatory test:<br/>hypothesis_trrust*.py chain"]
        ASM["atlas_assemble.py →<br/>atlas_full_notf.json"]
        CATALOG2["catalogues fetched via<br/>fetch_runs.sh (release assets)"]
        CATALOG2 --> ANN --> ASM
        CATALOG2 --> NULLS --> ASM
        CATALOG2 --> HYP --> ASM
    end

    subgraph SITE["Stage 3 — Audited Surfaces"]
        INJ["inject_atlas.py<br/>index.html ← atlas_template.html"]
        AUD["audit_all.py — 312 checks:<br/>text · supplement · figures · site"]
        SURF["index.html (12 MB) +<br/>data/explorer.json (on demand)"]
        ASM --> INJ --> SURF
        ASM -.->|numbers read from<br/>result files| AUD
    end

    CATALOG -- "the only GPU→local artifact" --> CATALOG2
```

The boundary is deliberate and documented: *"Everything that only needs the catalogues runs locally and is in `../scripts/`"* [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L1-L7). This is the single most important architectural decision in the repository — it means reproducing all published numbers requires no GPU at all.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L25), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L9-L22), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L82-L89)

## Stage 1 — GPU Extraction: Contract-First Decoupling

The extraction stage must handle ten models that differ in everything — parameter count (10M to 3B), depth (8 to 33 layers), input representation (raw expression, binned values, rank order, even protein tokens via ESM2), and training objective (MLM, autoregressive, MAE). The architecture solves this with a **single adapter contract**: each model implements `Adapter.iter_activations(adata, batch_size)`, which yields, per batch, a dict `{layer_index: float32 array [n_positions, d_model]}`, the HGNC symbols of those positions, and their cell ids. Only gene-token positions are yielded — CLS, padding and other special tokens are dropped — so everything downstream is model-agnostic [pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L1-L40).

> [!TIP]
> The adapter contract also carries a subtler requirement: any adapter that preprocesses or filters cells must expose `self.processed_obs`, so downstream perturbation tests can align per-cell labels to `cell_ids` even when the adapter reorders or drops cells internally. This is why the contract lives in `base.py` rather than in each adapter — it is an interface guarantee, not a convenience.

`run_model.py` is the end-to-end orchestrator for one model: it resolves the adapter from a registry, loads the corpus, and calls `pipeline.extract()` followed by `pipeline.build_catalog()`. Mode flags (`--all-layers`, `--per-cell 168`, `--seed`) control extraction scope and determinism [pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L14-L86). Inside `extract()`, per-layer activations are **streamed to disk while the model runs** — raw float32 rows are written incrementally, then converted to a memory-mapped `.npy` in float16 when values fit (float32 only when a model's outliers exceed the float16 range, as tGPT's do). This is what lets all layers of a 3B model be extracted without holding tensors in memory [pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L17-L75).

The SAE that consumes these activations is a fixed, shared configuration — TopK (k=32), dictionary at 4×d_model, MSE loss with no L1 penalty, unit-normalized decoder columns, Adam at 3e-4 for 4 epochs, fully seeded. It deliberately mirrors the bio-sae schema "for join-compatibility with the prior Geneformer/scGPT atlases," which is what lets all ten models be annotated against one vocabulary and compared [pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L1-L25). Per layer, `build_catalog()` trains the SAE, saves its weights as `sae_L<NN>.pt`, and writes the catalogue: the top-20 genes per feature by mean activation, with a stable descending sort and zero-activation genes excluded so no feature list ever contains filler [pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L83-L127).

Sources: [pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L14-L86), [pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L17-L127), [pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L1-L25)

## The Model Registry as Configuration

The ten models are declared declaratively in one YAML file that serves as the registry for both the adapters and the paper's Table S1. Each entry records the adapter module, parameter count, depth, how the model reads a cell, its objective, external priors it carries, and its checkpoint — the "inductive axis" along which the comparison is later analyzed [pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L1-L9). Depth heterogeneity is handled by `common/layers.py`, which maps each model's layer stack onto five depth-matched read-outs (0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100 % of depth), so a 8-layer AIDO.Cell and a 33-layer UCE can be compared at equivalent relative positions [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L9-L22).

| Model | Params | Layers | Reads a cell as | Objective | Prior |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIDO.Cell | 10M | 8 | expression, all genes | MLM | none |
| scGPT | ~50M | 12 | binned expression | MLM | none |
| tGPT | ~120M | 8 | rank order | autoregressive | none |
| scFoundation | 100M | 12 | expression, read-depth aware | MAE | none |
| GeneCompass | 104M | 12 | rank order + value | MLM | knowledge graph |
| MaxToki | 217M | 11 | rank order | autoregressive (Llama) | none |
| Geneformer-V2 | 316M | 18 | rank order | MLM | none |
| UCE | 650M | 33 | ESM2 protein tokens | masked | ESM |
| C2S-Scale | 2B | 26 | rank-ordered gene names as text | autoregressive | text (Gemma-2) |
| Tahoe-x1 | 3B | 32 | binned expression | MLM | none |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L40-L52), [pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L11-L25)

## Stage 2 — Local Analysis: Results as the Single Source of Truth

The local stage in `pipeline/scripts/` consumes catalogues and external gene-set databases, and produces **59 result files** in `outputs/atlas/comparative/` plus seven figures. Its internal architecture is a directed data flow that `docs/RESULTS.md` documents exhaustively: every file lists its writer and its readers [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L1-L8). Three sub-systems matter at the architecture level:

**Matrices and calibration.** Per-model feature catalogues are re-annotated into concept × model matrices (`reannotate_string.py`, `alllayer_matrix.py`), and `recalibrate*.py` scripts derive the calibrated annotator from grid searches against null models — the calibration analysis lives here precisely because it needs no GPU [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L38-L41).

**Nulls and hypothesis tests.** Every claim is paired with a null: random-gene and degree-matched nulls for the backbone (`random_null.py`, `degree_null.py`), the cell-shuffle null for CKA (`cka_svd_null.py` on the GPU side), and a chain of `hypothesis_*.py` scripts that implement the held-out TRRUST regulatory-prediction test with progressively hardened variants (robustness, size-matching, study-bias strata) [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L31-L37).

**Assembly.** `atlas_assemble.py` merges the component JSONs into `atlas_full_notf.json` — the 356 KB aggregate that the site embeds and the audit reads — and is written to be robust to missing pieces, keeping a block absent rather than crashing [pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L1-L16). The site itself is then rebuilt by `inject_atlas.py` from `atlas_template.html`, so `index.html` is a **build product, never edited by hand** [README.md](README.md#L10-L25).

> [!TIP]
> Note the two-environment split, which is architectural rather than incidental: extraction ran on Python 3.12 / PyTorch 2.13 / NumPy 1.26.4 on an H100, while local analysis runs on Python 3.13 / NumPy 2.3.4 (the major NumPy version differs). The repository states this explicitly so a reproducer knows they need *only* the local `requirements.txt` — the 17 GB of SAE weights and raw activations stay on the GPU host and are never archived.

Sources: [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L1-L60), [pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L1-L16), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L82-L89)

## Stage 3 — The Audit Layer: Closing the Loop

The outermost architectural component is `audit_all.py`, which exists because three things can drift apart and each has bitten the project: text vs results, supplement vs results, and figures vs results. It runs six check modules — manuscript core, derived numbers, supplement tables, figures, and the public site — and exits non-zero on any mismatch, with the discipline stated plainly: *"Fix the source of the disagreement, not the check"* [pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py](pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L1-L50). Architecturally this makes the result files the **sole authority**: the manuscript, supplement, figures and site are all treated as downstream projections that must be provably consistent with them.

The same philosophy governs data acquisition. The per-run feature catalogues and external inputs (1.2 GB) are published as release assets and fetched with checksummed scripts (`fetch_runs.sh`), so the local stage never depends on the GPU host being reachable [README.md](README.md#L10-L25). A `pipeline/legacy/` directory holds superseded builders kept purely for provenance and "used by nothing" — the active pipeline never imports from it.

Sources: [pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py](pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L1-L50), [README.md](README.md#L10-L25)

## How a Correction Propagates

The architecture was stress-tested when three faults in the first extraction release were found — a position cap that let some models see 32 cells and others all 6,000, filler genes in top-gene lists, and an unseeded SAE. Each fault traces to a specific architectural location: the corpus-order position cap in `extract()`'s non-streaming path (fixed by the seeded `--per-cell` mode), the unstable sort in `build_catalog()` (fixed by the stable sort dropping zero-activation genes), and the SAE seed in `train_sae()`. The corrected re-run (`runs-v2`) is the source of every published number, with the change history recorded as decision 16 in `docs/DECISIONS.md` [README.md](README.md#L62-L74). This episode defines the repository's release discipline: catalogues are versioned as release archives, superseded outputs are preserved but isolated, and the audit re-verifies every surface against the new files.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L62-L74), [pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L68-L80), [pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L17-L75)

## Reading Progression

This page gave you the map. The catalog's deep dives follow the data flow, and the natural order mirrors the pipeline's own stages:

1. **[Model Adapter Contract](6-model-adapter-contract)** — the `iter_activations` interface and per-model quirks in full detail, the first architectural boundary you encountered above.
2. **[TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training)** — inside `common/sae.py`: the TopK mechanism, hyperparameters, and seeding.
3. **[Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw)** — how `build_ts_corpus.py` constructs the comparison substrate both stages depend on.
4. For the statistics, continue to **[Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation)** and **[Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim)**.
5. For the engineering guarantee that results stay trustworthy, see **[Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map)** and **[Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks)**.
6. To see where the pipeline ends, **[Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files)** covers how `atlas_full_notf.json` becomes the interactive atlas.

# Model Adapter Contract



The adapter contract is the single seam that lets ten architecturally unrelated single-cell foundation models flow into one shared analysis pipeline. Every model plugs in by implementing `iter_activations`, which yields per-layer residual-stream activation rows plus the HGNC gene symbol and a global cell index for every row; everything downstream — SAE training, feature catalogs, annotation — is model-agnostic and consumes only that tuple. This page documents the contract surface, the yield protocol, the layer-selection rules, and how ten very different token universes are normalized onto it.

Sources: [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L1-L7), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L1-L4), [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L2-L4)

## Why the Contract Exists

The atlas compares models spanning 10M–3B parameters, 8–33 layers, and five different ways of reading a cell (rank order, rank plus value, expression value, ESM2 protein tokens, gene names as text). Any claim of *equal treatment* across such heterogeneity requires that the comparison never depend on model internals — hence a deliberately narrow interface: forward hooks on each transformer block's post-residual output, unfolded to one row per (cell, gene) token position, mirroring the bio-sae "Phase 0" extraction design this pipeline was derived from. The runner (`run_model.py`) resolves a model name to an adapter module via a registry, instantiates it, loads weights, and hands the object to the model-agnostic `pipeline.extract`/`build_catalog` pair.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph HET["Ten heterogeneous models"]
        M1["AIDO — all-gene expression"]
        M2["Geneformer / MaxToki — rank-value Ensembl"]
        M3["UCE — ESM2 protein tokens"]
        M4["C2S — gene names as text"]
        M5["scGPT, tGPT, scFoundation,<br/>GeneCompass, Tahoe"]
    end
    subgraph CONTRACT["The contract: adapters/base.py"]
        L["load(device)"]
        IA["iter_activations(adata)<br/>yields (acts, syms, cell_ids)"]
```
