```mermaid
    end
    subgraph DOWN["Model-agnostic downstream"]
        EX["pipeline.extract<br/>memmaps + symbols + cell ids"]
        SAE["TopK SAE + feature catalog"]
        ANN["annotation"]
    end
    HET --> CONTRACT
    IA --> EX
    EX --> SAE
    SAE --> ANN
```

Sources: [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L12-L18), [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L6-L7), [models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L1-L5), [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L50-L56)

## The Contract Surface: `adapters.base.Adapter`

`Adapter` is a small abstract class whose members divide into three kinds: identity metadata consumed by downstream catalogs, configuration written by `load()`, and the one mandatory generator. The base implementations raise `NotImplementedError`, so the contract is *structural by convention* — only the yield tuple is ever checked at runtime by the consumer.

| Member | Kind | Obligation |
|---|---|---|
| `name: str` | class attribute | Display/catalog identity; becomes the `"model"` field in every `feature_catalog_L*.json` |
| `layers: Sequence[int]` | class attribute | Residual layer indices to extract; `0` = input embedding; set at load time from depth |
| `d_model: int` | class attribute | Activation row width; sizes the downstream SAE dictionary |
| `n_layers` | instance attribute (convention) | Total block count, consulted by `--all-layers` / `--mid-only` overrides |
| `load(device)` | method | Load weights + vocab in eval mode onto the device |
| `iter_activations(adata, batch_size)` | generator | The yield protocol (next section) |
| `processed_obs` | attribute, default `None` | Required for perturbation tests when the adapter preprocesses/filters cells |
| `meta: dict` | class attribute | Free-form provenance slot |

Sources: [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L14-L39), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L91-L127)

## The Yield Protocol

`iter_activations` is a generator walked once by `pipeline.extract`. Per batch of cells it yields a three-element tuple whose columns are *position-aligned*: element *i* of `syms` and `cell_ids` describes the same row as row *i* of every array in `acts`.

| Element | Shape | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `acts` | `{layer: float32 [n_positions, d_model]}` | Post-residual hidden states, one row per gene-token position |
| `syms` | `str [n_positions]` | Uppercase HGNC symbol per position — the join key to annotation vocabularies |
| `cell_ids` | `int [n_positions]` | Global 0-based cell index in processing order |

Two invariants do the heavy lifting. First, `n_positions` is the sum of each cell's *gene-token* count — CLS, pad, depth, and other special tokens must be dropped, so a batch yields only interpretable (cell, gene) pairs. Second, `cell_ids` are global across the whole corpus pass, which is what enables downstream per-cell operations such as split-half controls and the seeded per-cell subsampling described below.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as run_model.py
    participant A as Adapter instance
    participant P as pipeline.extract
    R->>A: resolve registry entry, instantiate
    R->>A: load(device) — weights + vocab, eval mode
    R->>R: override adapter.layers (--all-layers / --mid-only)
    R->>P: extract(adapter, adata, out_dir, per_cell, seed)
    loop per batch of cells
        P->>A: iter_activations(adata, batch_size)
        A-->>P: (acts, syms, cell_ids) — position-aligned
        P->>P: seeded per-cell subsampling (per_cell > 0)
        P->>P: stream layer rows to layer_XX.f32
    end
    P->>P: write gene_symbols.npy, cell_ids.npy, extraction.json
```

> [!TIP]
> The consumer unpacks the tuple defensively as `acts, syms, *rest` and treats a missing `cell_ids` as `None` — tolerated only in the legacy corpus-order mode (`per_cell=0`). In per-cell stream mode the missing third element is the contract's single runtime-enforced clause: extraction aborts with `ValueError: "<adapter name>: per-cell sampling needs per-position cell ids"`. When writing an adapter, always yield all three elements.

Sources: [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L23-L36), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L11-L12), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L32-L57)

## Layer Selection: `layers`, `n_layers`, and Depth Matching

Each adapter sets `self.layers` inside `load()` from its configured block count via `depth_matched(n_layers)` — the agreed spec of relative depths 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100 %, rounded, deduplicated (small models can collapse picks), and sorted. This removes the layer confound: a 6-layer model and a 26-layer model are read at the same *relative* depths, and UCE's 33 blocks map to `(0, 8, 16, 24, 32)`. The runner can override this at dispatch time: `--all-layers` replaces `layers` with `range(n_layers)` for the full depth profile, and `--mid-only` reduces it to the middle block — the layer the cross-model statistics are read at. The `layers` count recorded in `configs/models.yaml` is exactly what `--all-layers` extracted.

A per-model subtlety the contract absorbs: hidden-state tuple indexing differs by framework convention. AIDO indexes `hidden_states[L]` directly (embedding layer included in the tuple, then slicing off non-gene prefix positions), while the Geneformer family indexes `hidden_states[Ly + 1]` because `hidden_states[0]` is the embedding output. Downstream never sees these corrections.

Sources: [layers.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/layers.py#L1-L14), [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L58-L65), [models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L3-L5), [aido.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/aido.py#L49-L52), [geneformer.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/geneformer.py#L104-L109)

## The `processed_obs` Clause

Some adapters cannot pass cells through untouched: AIDO re-aligns the AnnData object against its gene ordering, others filter to in-vocab genes or subsample. Any adapter that changes which cells are processed — or their order — **must** set `self.processed_obs` to a pandas DataFrame of the cells actually processed, in yield order, so callers can recover per-cell labels aligned to `cell_ids`. This exists specifically for the CRISPRi perturbation test, which joins responses back to cell metadata; a silently misaligned join would invalidate responsiveness statistics. The pattern is uniform: AIDO assigns it from the re-aligned object's `.obs` before the batch loop, scGPT and Geneformer assign it from `adata.obs` at the top of `iter_activations`.

Sources: [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L32-L38), [aido.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/aido.py#L33-L37), [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L157-L160), [c2s.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/c2s.py#L48-L51)

## One Contract, Ten Token Universes

The registry in `run_model.py` maps model names to adapter modules; it is a superset of the canonical ten recorded in `configs/models.yaml` (entries such as scPRINT, scBERT, and a CellPLM stub exist as recipes, not atlas members). What the ten extracted models share is the contract; what differs is the definition of "one position" — and each adapter owns that translation.

| Model | d_model | Layers | Reads a cell as | Position definition (code-verified) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIDO | 256 | 8 | expression, all 19,264 genes | Every HGNC gene, fixed order from `aido_genes.tsv`, `syms = np.tile(genes, batch)` |
| scGPT | 512 | 12 | binned expression | Nonzero, in-vocab genes sorted by expression, capped at `max_seq_len` 1200 |
| tGPT | 1024 | 8 | rank order | rank-order tokens |
| scFoundation | 768 | 12 | expression (read-depth aware) | — |
| GeneCompass | 768 | 12 | rank order + value | — |
| MaxToki | 1232 | 11 | rank order (corpus-scaled) | Inherits Geneformer's rank-value tokenization wholesale |
| Geneformer | 1152 | 18 | rank order | Genes with token + positive corpus median; rank key `count / gene-median`; top `max_len` 2048; empty-symbol rows filtered from the yield |
| UCE | 1280 | 33 | ESM2 protein tokens | Gene = token index inverted through the species protein-embedding order + offsets; special/chrom/CLS skipped |
| C2S | 2304 | 26 | rank-ordered gene names as text | Gene = **last subword** position of its BPE span, recovered via tokenizer offset mapping |
| Tahoe | 2560 | 32 | binned expression | — |

Geneformer's rank-value design illustrates why per-adapter care matters: it normalizes each count by the gene's corpus median, but since total-count scaling is a per-cell constant, only `count / gene_median` affects the token *order* — so the adapter reproduces ranking without replicating the full normalization. C2S is the extreme case: a Gemma-2 decoder-only LM where the "gene token" doesn't exist at all, so the adapter fabricates gene-anchored positions by attributing each gene's residual to the last subword it attended through.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Adapter {
        <<abstract>>
        +str name
        +Sequence layers
        +int d_model
        +dict meta
        +DataFrame processed_obs
        +load(device)
        +iter_activations(adata, batch_size)*
    }
    class AIDOAdapter
    class ScGPTAdapter
    class GeneformerAdapter {
        +str hf_auto = "masked"
    }
    class MaxTokiAdapter {
        +str hf_auto = "causal"
    }
    class C2SAdapter
    class UCEAdapter
    Adapter <|-- AIDOAdapter
    Adapter <|-- ScGPTAdapter
    Adapter <|-- GeneformerAdapter
    GeneformerAdapter <|-- MaxTokiAdapter
    Adapter <|-- C2SAdapter
    Adapter <|-- UCEAdapter
```

The class diagram also shows the codebase's one inheritance shortcut: `MaxTokiAdapter` subclasses `GeneformerAdapter` and flips a single class attribute (`hf_auto = "causal"`, selecting `AutoModelForCausalLM` over `AutoModelForMaskedLM`) because both theodoris-lab models share the same rank-value Ensembl vocabulary — including defaulting `token_dict_dir` back to the Geneformer-V2 checkpoint.

Sources: [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L14-L28), [models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L14-L24), [aido.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/aido.py#L29-L31), [aido.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/aido.py#L51-L55), [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L133-L155), [geneformer.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/geneformer.py#L6-L8), [geneformer.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/geneformer.py#L82-L95), [geneformer.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/geneformer.py#L112-L114), [maxtoki.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/maxtoki.py#L13-L24), [c2s.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/c2s.py#L1-L5), [c2s.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/c2s.py#L37-L74), [uce.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/uce.py#L1-L7)

## Dependency Isolation Inside Adapters

Because each adapter wraps an upstream codebase on a shared H100 host, most of their engineering effort goes into making imports and hook points *reliable* rather than reimplementing model logic — the scGPT and UCE docstrings both state the policy explicitly: wrap the upstream model and tokenization, do not reimplement. Five recurring patterns:

| Pattern | Where | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Module stubbing | scGPT `_stub_optional_deps` | Injects inert `sys.modules` entries for `datasets`, `wandb`, `seaborn`, `networkx`, `torch_geometric` so `scgpt.__init__` imports without pulling conflicting transitive versions; `_stub_attr` keeps dunders missing so `inspect`/torch module walks don't trip |
| Vendored shim | `adapters/_shims/torchtext/vocab.py` | A minimal `Vocab` implementing exactly the API scGPT's `GeneVocab` calls, swapped in when torchtext's C++ extension is incompatible with the host's torch |
| Standard-encoder forcing | scGPT `use_fast_transformer=False` | Loads flash-trained weights into a standard `nn.TransformerEncoder` (upstream remaps `Wqkv.` → `in_proj_`), making `.layers[L]` hookable without flash-attn |
| NestedTensor disabling | scGPT `enable_nested_tensor = False` | Stops eval-mode + padding-mask from converting layer I/O to NestedTensor, which breaks per-layer hooks |
| Content-addressed cache | UCE work dir keyed on `sha1(obs_names + var_names)` | Prevents UCE's `AnndataProcessor` from silently reusing a previous corpus's preprocessing when its output files already exist |

> [!TIP]
> The hookability traps are the subtlest part of the contract: both the flash-attention fast path and TransformerEncoder's NestedTensor optimization hide per-layer I/O from `register_forward_hook`. Any new adapter whose upstream uses such fast paths must force the standard implementation before hooks will fire — this is why scGPT's adapter is loaded with `use_fast_transformer=False` even though the checkpoint was trained with flash attention.

Sources: [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L1-L9), [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L29-L34), [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L58-L72), [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L79-L85), [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L115-L127), [vocab.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/_shims/torchtext/vocab.py#L1-L2), [uce.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/uce.py#L77-L90)

## The Consumer Side and Output Artifacts

`pipeline.extract` is the contract's only consumer, and it responds to the tuple in one of two modes. In legacy corpus-order mode (`per_cell=0`) it buffers rows until `max_positions` is reached — a mode kept for reproducing published runs, with the documented caveat that because models emit very different token counts per cell, it caps cells unequally (AIDO contributes 32 cells, tGPT all 6,000). In per-cell stream mode (`per_cell>0`) every corpus cell is read and at most `per_cell` of its positions are kept, drawn uniformly without replacement under the run seed — equal cell weighting across models — while rows stream straight to disk so all layers of a 3B model fit in memory. Per layer it then finalizes `layer_XX_activations.npy` memmaps (float16 when `|max_abs| < 65,000`, else float32; tGPT has outliers above 150,000) plus `gene_symbols.npy`, `cell_ids.npy`, and an `extraction.json` provenance record (positions, cells, per_cell, seed, per-layer dtype and max-abs, layer list). Those files, not the adapter objects, are what the rest of the repository consumes.

Sources: [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L15-L31), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L62-L88), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L75-L86)

## Adding or Verifying an Adapter

The codebase carries an explicit verification protocol. `aido.py` is annotated "VERIFIED forward path (used in our audit)"; several registry entries carry "(VERIFY on H100)" comments with expected-tweak notes, and each written-from-repo adapter ends its docstring with a concrete checklist of what to confirm on the GPU host (vocab APIs, preprocessing details, prompt prefixes). `models.yaml` adds that how each model reads a cell and what prior it carries was verified against the model papers and configs (decision log item 11), mirroring supplement Table S1.

| Step | Requirement | Where enforced |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Subclass `Adapter`; set `name`, `d_model` | Catalog identity; SAE width | [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L15-L17) |
| 2. `load(device)`: weights + vocab, eval mode; set `n_layers` and `layers` | Depth-matched default via `depth_matched` | [aido.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/aido.py#L19-L31) |
| 3. Yield the 3-tuple, position-aligned | `ValueError` in stream mode if `cell_ids` missing | [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L34-L36) |
| 4. Emit gene-token positions only | Drop CLS/pad/depth/special tokens | [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L30) |
| 5. Uppercase HGNC symbols per row | Join key for annotation | [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L27) |
| 6. Set `processed_obs` if filtering/preprocessing | Perturbation-test label alignment | [base.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/base.py#L32-L38) |
| 7. Smoke test: `--model X --smoke` (32 cells) | End-to-end sanity before full extraction | [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L39) |
| 8. Record verification state in the docstring | "VERIFIED" vs "VERIFY on H100" convention | [aido.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/aido.py#L1-L3), [scgpt.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/scgpt.py#L17-L21) |

Sources: [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L14-L28), [geneformer.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/geneformer.py#L10-L16), [c2s.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/c2s.py#L10-L12), [uce.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/uce.py#L14-L17), [models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L7-L9)

## Where to Go Next

The adapter contract ends where the SAE begins: the memmaps, `gene_symbols.npy`, and `cell_ids.npy` produced here are the training inputs for a TopK dictionary per layer, covered in [TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training). The corpus every adapter reads — and the seed-1 held-out draw — is specified in [Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw). The per-cell sampling mode and its migration from the original corpus-order cap are documented in [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run), and the whole stage sits within the stage map in [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview). For how the ten models' capabilities compare once extracted, start at [Ten Foundation Models Compared](3-ten-foundation-models-compared).

# TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training



This page explains the dictionary-learning core of the GPU extraction stage: how the pipeline turns raw transformer activations into interpretable gene-level features. It covers the TopK SAE architecture, the training loop and its seeding contract, the exact outputs produced per layer, the health controls that qualify those outputs, and how to reproduce the published runs. The SAE implementation lives in one small, model-agnostic file that every one of the ten models passes through.

## Role in the Extraction Stage

The extraction pipeline is a fixed chain: adapter → per-layer activations → one TopK SAE per layer → feature catalogue → annotation. Because every model is followed by the identical dictionary learner, a "feature" means the same thing across all ten models — an active direction in a k = 32-sparse dictionary over that layer's residual stream — and every downstream comparison joins on the same vocabulary. Across the atlas this means 172 trained dictionaries (8 to 33 layers per model, 172 in all). The configuration is deliberately inherited, not invented: it matches the bio-sae contract used by the earlier Geneformer/scGPT atlases (a Gao et al. 2024 TopK variant), so new features are join-compatible with prior results. It was not swept; only seed variance was measured (see [Seeds, Health, and Known Weaknesses](#seeds-health-and-known-weaknesses)).

Sources: [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L1-L9), [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L9-L22), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L21-L59)

## Dictionary Architecture: TopKSAE

`TopKSAE` is a two-layer autoencoder with a hard sparsity gate. The forward contract, stated in the module docstring and mirrored exactly in code: **encode** `h = TopK_k(W_enc(x − μ) + b_enc)` with ReLU applied to the kept top-k values scattered back into a zero vector; **decode** `x̂ = W_dec·h + b_dec`; **loss** is plain MSE — there is no L1 term, because TopK *enforces* sparsity structurally. Initialization is deterministic: Kaiming-uniform for the encoder weight, zeros for both biases, and decoder columns pre-normalized to unit length along the dictionary dimension at construction time. A `μ` buffer holds the per-dimension input mean (filled from data before training) so the model learns a centered representation without a normalization layer.

The diagram shows one activation row flowing through encode, the reconstruction, and the post-step decoder re-normalization:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    x["activation row x"] --> S["subtract μ (data mean buffer)"]
    S --> E["W_enc·x + b_enc"]
    E --> T["torch.topk, k = 32"]
    T --> R["ReLU on the kept values"]
    R --> SC["scatter into zero vector h"]
    SC --> D["x_hat = W_dec·h + b_dec"]
    D --> L["loss = MSE(x, x_hat)"]
    L --> U["after opt.step(): re-normalize decoder columns"]
```

Sources: [sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L1-L10), [sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L35-L65)

## The Training Loop

`train_sae(X, cfg)` receives the full activation matrix for one layer (`[n_positions, d_model]`) and trains a fresh dictionary. The procedure is: set `μ` from `X.mean(0)`; subsample without replacement down to `train_positions` (1M — the full ~1M-row layer pools fit, so nothing is dropped in practice); then run 4 epochs of Adam over shuffled mini-batches of 4,096 rows, minimizing MSE, calling `unit_norm_decoder()` after *every* optimizer step. The seeding contract is dual: NumPy's `default_rng(seed)` governs the position subsample, and `torch.manual_seed(seed)` governs weight init and the per-epoch shuffles. Because the layer arrays are memmaps, `np.asarray(A)` materializes one layer at a time — memory scales with a single layer, not the whole model.

| Hyperparameter | Default | Meaning | Set where |
|---|---|---|---|
| `k` | 32 | active features per position | `SAECfg`, models.yaml `sae` |
| `expansion` | 4 | dictionary width multiplier (`d_sae = 4 × d_model`) | `SAECfg`, models.yaml |
| `lr` | 3e-4 | Adam learning rate | `SAECfg`, models.yaml |
| `epochs` | 4 | passes over the ~1M-position pool | `SAECfg`, models.yaml |
| `batch` | 4096 | mini-batch rows | `SAECfg` |
| `train_positions` | 1,000,000 | subsample cap per layer | `SAECfg` |
| `seed` | 0 | NumPy rng **and** torch | `run_model.py --seed` → both extractors and SAE |

Sources: [sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L68-L89), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L97-L104), [models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L11-L12)

## Held-Out Evaluation Statistics

After training, the loop evaluates on a 100,000-row held-out split drawn from the same layer's pool and records five numbers that travel with the checkpoint: `fvu` (fraction of variance unexplained, i.e., residual variance over input variance), `var_explained` (1 − fvu), `dead_frac` (share of features that never fire on the split), `alive` (firing feature count), and `mean_abs_decoder_cos` (mean absolute off-diagonal cosine of the normalized decoder — a dictionary-overlap diagnostic). These land in the catalogue JSON, in `sae_L{L}.pt`, and in the log line. The standalone `sae_health.py` then aggregates `dead_frac` across *every* layer of every model against a 10% threshold — an all-layer quality control written specifically because the manuscript consumed all-layer features — flagging per model the mid/mean/max dead fractions and listing "clean" models with zero dead features anywhere.

| Statistic | Computation | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| `fvu` / `var_explained` | residual / input variance | reconstruction quality, comparable across models |
| `dead_frac` | `(freq == 0).mean()` on held-out activations | dictionary waste; tGPT is the known outlier (21.3% mean, 58.6% worst) |
| `alive` | features with frequency > 0 | effective dictionary size |
| `mean_abs_decoder_cos` | off-diagonal \|cos\| of unit decoder columns | near-duplicate direction pressure |

Sources: [sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L91-L107), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L125-L126), [sae_health.py](pipeline/scripts/sae_health.py#L1-L9), [sae_health.py](pipeline/scripts/sae_health.py#L23-L44), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L50-L59)

## From Weights to Feature Catalogue

`build_catalog()` runs the whole per-layer loop. For each layer it trains the SAE, saves `sae_L{L:02d}.pt` (state dict, config dict, stats), then encodes the *entire* layer pool with `feature_activations` (batched at 65,536 rows, float32 out). Feature semantics come from averaging: activation rows are accumulated into a per-gene mean matrix `G` (genes as rows, features as columns), and each feature's genes are ranked by that mean with a *stable* descending sort — genes with zero mean activation are dropped rather than padded in, so a feature firing on fewer than 20 genes simply gets a shorter list. The catalogue JSON records `model`, `layer`, `d_model`, `d_sae`, `k`, `n_alive`, `n_genes`, the five health stats, and the top-20 gene lists with `max_activation` and `activation_frequency` per feature.

| Artifact | Contents | Consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `layer_{L:02d}_activations.npy` | memmap, float16 (or float32 if \|a\| ≥ 65,000, e.g. tGPT) | SAE training, GPU-side analyses |
| `gene_symbols.npy` / `cell_ids.npy` | HGNC symbol per position; per-position cell id | gene ranking; cell-level splits |
| `extraction.json` | positions, cells, per_cell, seed, per-layer dtype, max_abs | provenance audit |
| `sae_L{L:02d}.pt` | weights + config + training stats (~17 GB total; stays on the GPU host, not archived) | re-training controls, explorer |
| `feature_catalog_L{L:02d}.json` | top-20 genes/feature + health stats | all local analysis, `sae_health.py`, the site |

Sources: [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L91-L127), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L59-L88), [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L60-L74)

## The Training Set: ≤168 Positions per Cell

What the SAE *eats* matters as much as how it trains. The corrected contract (`--per-cell 168`, seed 0) reads every one of the 6,000 corpus cells and keeps at most 168 gene-token positions per cell, drawn uniformly without replacement by the seeded rng — roughly 1M positions per layer, the dictionary's training budget. Every model therefore trains on the same cells with equal cell weighting, regardless of how many gene tokens each model reads per cell. Rows are streamed to disk while the model runs (one raw `.f32` per layer), then compacted to float16 when the observed range allows, which is how all 33 layers of a 3B model fit on one host. The superseded v1 behavior — a corpus-order cap at `max_positions` with no per-cell control — gave AIDO.Cell only 32 cells and tGPT all 6,000, so v1 compared dictionaries trained on different data.

| Aspect | v1 (superseded) | v2 (`runs-v2`, published) |
|---|---|---|
| Training-set composition | first 500,000 positions in corpus order; 32–6,000 cells depending on model | ≤168 positions × all 6,000 cells (~1M/layer), equal weight |
| Top-gene ordering | non-stable sort padded short lists with zero-activation genes | stable sort, zero-mean genes dropped |
| SAE seeding | NumPy seeded; **torch unseeded** (init + shuffles nondeterministic) | both NumPy and torch seeded |

> [!TIP]
> The v1 run seeded NumPy but not torch, so weight initialization and per-epoch shuffling varied between identical invocations; the seed-variance control escaped this only because its scripts seeded torch themselves. Any reproduction older than `runs-v2` must be retrained, not re-used — the full fault list is in [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run).

Sources: [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L11-L58), [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L60-L74), [run_full_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh#L1-L24), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L264-L289)

## Per-Model Dictionary Sizes

The dictionary width is derived, not tuned: `d_sae = expansion × d_model = 4 × d_model`, so dictionaries scale with each architecture while `k`, learning rate, epochs, and seed stay fixed. The layers column is the number of SAEs trained per model in all-layers mode; the atlas total is 172.

| Model | d_model | Layers | d_sae |
|---|---|---|---|
| AIDO | 256 | 8 | 1,024 |
| scGPT | 512 | 12 | 2,048 |
| scFoundation | 768 | 12 | 3,072 |
| GeneCompass | 768 | 12 | 3,072 |
| tGPT | 1,024 | 8 | 4,096 |
| Geneformer-V2 | 1,152 | 18 | 4,608 |
| MaxToki | 1,232 | 11 | 4,928 |
| UCE | 1,280 | 33 | 5,120 |
| C2S-Scale | 2,304 | 26 | 9,216 |
| Tahoe-x1 | 2,560 | 32 | 10,240 |

Sources: [models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L14-L24), [sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L30-L32), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L21-L34)

## Seeds, Health, and Known Weaknesses

Seed 0 is the contract everywhere: the same `--seed` value drives position sampling, corpus construction, and SAE training, so a catalogue's provenance is a single integer. Because the atlas rests on one stochastic dictionary per model-layer, `seed_variance.py` re-quantifies that risk: it reloads *saved activations* (no re-extraction), retrains the mid-layer SAE under seeds 0–2, rebuilds the top-5 catalogue, annotates, and records per-(model, seed) `n_alive`, annotation rate, and concept sets — checkpointing and resuming per pair because the shared pod OOM-cycles. The measured answer: the permissive mid-layer core varies by 12% (435–580 concepts) across seeds, the all-layer core by 4%. Two known costs are documented rather than hidden: with more dictionary slots than distinct signals, surplus features fill with near-copies of the strongest signal (every model except Geneformer-V2 and GeneCompass shows such a block), and tGPT's high dead fraction confounds tGPT-specific results. One standing rule follows from per-layer training: feature counts are never summed across layers, because each layer owns an independent dictionary space.

Sources: [seed_variance.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/seed_variance.py#L1-L12), [seed_variance.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/seed_variance.py#L91-L99), [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L43-L47), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L46-L59), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L21-L30)

## Running It Yourself

The published catalogues come from release `runs-v2`, produced on the pod by the scripted sequence: build both corpora, then `run_full_fixed.sh` (all ten models, `--all-layers --per-cell 168 --seed 0`), then the held-out and seed sweeps, then downstream analyses. For a single model the entry point is `run_model.py`; `--smoke` runs 32 cells end-to-end in minutes, `--skip-annotate` omits the permissive annotation pass (as the fixed runs do — calibration happens locally), and `--mid-only` trains just the depth-matched middle dictionary.

```bash
# end-to-end, one model, every layer (the published configuration)
python run_model.py --model AIDO --corpus data/corpus.h5ad \
    --all-layers --per-cell 168 --seed 0 --out out_fixed --skip-annotate

# 32-cell sanity check
python run_model.py --model AIDO --smoke
```

Operational notes worth knowing before you start: the driver script is resumable (a model with a `DONE` marker is skipped; failures leave a per-model log), Tahoe-x1 must run in its own venv (torch 2.6.0, flash-attn 2.7.4) while the other nine share the main one, and the extraction environment is Python 3.12 / PyTorch 2.13 (CUDA 13) / NumPy 1.26.4 on an H100 — downstream local analysis needs only `requirements.txt`. One disambiguation: `pipeline/scripts/aido_sae.py` also trains a TopK SAE, but through a different stack (`mechaudit`, d_sae 2048, k 32, 40 epochs, TRRUST-gene residual) as a one-off audit of AIDO's layer 4 — it is not part of the atlas pipeline and its hyperparameters should not be confused with `common/sae.py`.

| Ops concern | Handling |
|---|---|
| Interrupted multi-model run | `DONE` markers; rerun `run_full_fixed.sh`, completed models skipped |
| CUDA dependency split | main venv for nine models; `ATLAS_TAHOE_VENV` for Tahoe-x1 |
| OOM on seed re-training | `seed_variance.py` checkpoints per (model, seed) and resumes |
| Missing weights in repo | `sae_*.pt` (~17 GB) and activations stay on the GPU host; catalogues ship in release archives |

Sources: [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L31-L49), [run_full_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh#L6-L24), [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L46-L89), [aido_sae.py](pipeline/scripts/aido_sae.py#L1-L10), [aido_sae.py](pipeline/scripts/aido_sae.py#L81-L84)

## Where to Go Next

Read the stage in order: the adapter contract that feeds this SAE is [Model Adapter Contract](6-model-adapter-contract); the corpus that defines the training set is [Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw). To see what the catalogues feed, continue to [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation) and the robustness controls in [Reviewer Robustness Analyses](16-reviewer-robustness-analyses); the v1 faults summarized above are fully documented in [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run), and the per-feature maps built from these dictionaries appear in [Layer Explorer Feature Maps](23-layer-explorer-feature-maps).

# Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw



This page documents the data substrate of the GPU extraction stage: the single 6,000-cell Tabula Sapiens corpus that all ten foundation models read, how it is drawn from CZ CELLxGENE Census with a fixed seed, and the independently-drawn held-out corpus that shares zero cells with it. It sits between the adapter contract ([Model Adapter Contract](6-model-adapter-contract)) and the SAE trainer ([TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training)): everything downstream — annotation calibration, null models, cross-model geometry — consumes exactly these two cell sets, so their construction is where comparability is won or lost.

## Why a Single Corpus Exists

The design decision is stated bluntly in the decision log: the earlier single-model atlases were built on different corpora (Geneformer on K562, scGPT on Tabula Sapiens), so any difference between them could have been the data rather than the model. With one corpus, a difference between two models is a difference between the models. The cost is equally explicit — cross-species models (UCE, GeneCompass, C2S-Scale) are read on human cells only, and the atlas says nothing about other tissues or platforms.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L6-L20), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L6-L11)

The corpus is deliberately small and structured: 6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells, 2,000 each from immune, kidney and lung, raw counts, drawn from cellxgene-census v1.18.0 with seed 0. A second draw with seed 1 under the identical protocol is the held-out corpus. This is a controlled experiment substrate, not a pretraining corpus — every downstream statistical test (nulls, permutation counts, calibrated thresholds) assumes this scale.

Sources: [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L6-L11), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L9-L20)

## Corpus Construction from CELLxGENE Census

`build_ts_corpus.py` pulls only the needed cells from the Census rather than downloading full Tabula Sapiens releases: it queries `census_info["datasets"]` for every dataset whose `collection_name` contains "Tabula Sapiens", asserts the list is non-empty, and embeds those dataset IDs into the obs value filter of every pull. The filter additionally requires `is_primary_data == True` and requests raw counts (`X_name="raw"`), with both `cell_type`/`tissue`/`tissue_general`/`assay` on the obs axis and `feature_id`/`feature_name` on the var axis.

Sources: [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L37-L61)

Three compartments are drawn, two by tissue and one by lineage:

| Compartment | Census filter | Published size |
|---|---|---|
| kidney | `tissue_general == 'kidney'`, primary data, Tabula Sapiens datasets only | 2,000 cells |
| lung | `tissue_general == 'lung'` | 2,000 cells |
| immune | `cell_type` in an explicit 18-entry immune-lineage list (T cells, B cells, plasma, NK, macrophage, monocyte subsets, DCs, mast, neutrophil) | 2,000 cells |

Sources: [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L14-L21), [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L63-L68)

Seeding enters twice, and both entry points matter for the held-out story. A single `np.random.default_rng(args.seed)` drives (a) the within-compartment subsample — `rng.choice(a.n_obs, per_tissue, replace=False)` whenever a compartment yields more cells than requested — and (b) the final `rng.permutation` shuffle of the concatenated 6,000 cells. The shuffle originally served the v1 position cap ("cells shuffled so the 4M-position cap still sees all cell types"); in the corrected pipeline it remains as the reason a seed alone fully determines the cell set, making seed 0 and seed 1 genuinely independent draws from the same population.

Sources: [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L35-L45), [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L47-L68), [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L83-L84)

A final adapter-compatibility step makes one h5ad serve all ten models: gene symbols are uppercased into `var_names` (with `var_names_make_unique()`), while version-stripped Ensembl IDs land in `var["ensembl_id"]`. Symbol-based adapters (AIDO, scGPT, tGPT, UCE) and Ensembl-based adapters (Geneformer, MaxToki, Tahoe) therefore read the same file without per-model reprocessing, and a sanity check verifies the matrix holds integer counts.

Sources: [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L1-L10), [build_ts_corpus.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py#L70-L91)

## The Held-Out Draw: Same Protocol, Different Seed

Running the same script with `--seed 1` produces a statistically independent draw — and therefore, by collision arithmetic alone, cells that appear in both files. The measured overlap is **419 of 6,000 cells**. Because the held-out corpus exists to prove results on cells no SAE was trained on, those shared cells must be removed, which is the entire job of `make_heldout_disjoint.py`: load the main corpus's `obs_names` (cell barcodes) in backed mode, apply the boolean mask `~h.obs_names.isin(main_ids)`, print per-compartment kept counts, and write `tabula_3tissue_6k_heldout_disjoint.h5ad` — 5,581 cells with zero overlap.

Sources: [make_heldout_disjoint.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/make_heldout_disjoint.py#L1-L33), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L8-L11)

> [!TIP]
> The 419-cell overlap is not a bug — it is the expected consequence of two independent samplings from the same Census pool. Disjointness is enforced *post hoc* by barcode identity, not by partitioning the Census upfront, which is what keeps the two draws identically distributed.

The full data flow, from Census to per-model output directories:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CENSUS["CZ CELLxGENE Census v1.18.0<br/>Tabula Sapiens datasets, raw counts"] --> S0["build_ts_corpus.py --seed 0"]
    CENSUS --> S1["build_ts_corpus.py --seed 1"]
    S0 --> CORPUS["tabula_3tissue_6k.h5ad<br/>6,000 cells · 2,000 per compartment"]
    S1 --> HELD_RAW["tabula_3tissue_6k_heldout.h5ad<br/>6,000 cells"]
    CORPUS -. "419 shared barcodes" .-> DISJOINT["make_heldout_disjoint.py"]
    HELD_RAW --> DISJOINT
    DISJOINT --> HELDOUT["tabula_3tissue_6k_heldout_disjoint.h5ad<br/>5,581 cells · zero overlap"]
    CORPUS --> FULL["run_full_fixed.sh<br/>--all-layers --per-cell 168 --seed 0"]
    HELDOUT --> HELD["run_heldout_fixed.sh<br/>five depth-matched layers"]
    FULL --> OUT1["out_fixed/ · every layer, all ten models"]
    HELD --> OUT2["out_heldout_fixed/ · five depth-matched layers"]
```

Sources: [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L50-L58), [make_heldout_disjoint.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/make_heldout_disjoint.py#L17-L33)

`run_heldout_fixed.sh` closes the loop operationally: it checks `[ -f $CORP ] || python make_heldout_disjoint.py` before running any model, so the disjoint corpus is rebuilt if missing, and it writes to `out_heldout_fixed/` with the same resumable DONE-marker pattern as the full run.

Sources: [run_heldout_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_heldout_fixed.sh#L11-L18)

## How the Corpus Reaches Every Model: Per-Cell Position Sampling

Models read very different numbers of gene tokens per cell, so "the same corpus" needs one more guarantee: the same *cells* with equal weight, regardless of tokenization. This is enforced in `common/pipeline.extract()`. When `per_cell > 0` (streaming mode), the extractor requires the adapter to yield per-position cell IDs, then for each unique cell draws `rng.choice(pos, per_cell, replace=False)` positions — uniform, without replacement, seeded once per run from `--seed`. The `--per-cell` help text in `run_model.py` states the contract: *"read every cell, keep at most this many positions per cell (seeded); 0 = the original corpus-order cap on --max-positions"*.

Sources: [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L7-L24), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L25-L43), [run_model.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_model.py#L44-L53)

The published runs use `--per-cell 168 --seed 0`: every one of the 6,000 cells contributes at most 168 gene-token positions, about 1M positions per layer — the SAE's training budget. Activations are streamed to disk per batch as raw float32, then each layer is rewritten as an `.npy` memmap in float16 where values fit (`|a| < 65,000`) or float32 where they do not (tGPT has outliers above 150,000). Every run also persists `extraction.json` — positions, cell count, `per_cell`, seed, per-layer dtype, max absolute values — which is the provenance record that lets any downstream consumer verify *which* sampling produced a catalogue.

Sources: [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L60-L65), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L54-L80)

> [!TIP]
> Before trusting any cross-model or held-out comparison, read the `extraction.json` in the run directory: it records `positions`, `cells`, `per_cell` and `seed`, so a catalogue built under the v1 corpus-order cap cannot masquerade as a v2 one.

The v1 fallback is kept deliberately for reproducibility of the superseded catalogues, and it is the clearest illustration of why the per-cell mode exists:

| Property | v1: `--max-positions 500000`, no `--per-cell` | v2 (published): `--per-cell 168 --seed 0` |
|---|---|---|
| Selection | positions taken in corpus order until the cap | uniform without replacement, per cell |
| Cell coverage | unequal across models: AIDO.Cell 32, UCE 492, scFoundation ~160, tGPT all 6,000 | all 6,000 cells for every model |
| Cell weighting | models reading many genes/cell see few cells | every cell weighted equally |
| Held-out correctness | UCE's held-out catalogue was built on corpus cells (stale preprocessing cache) | adapter cache keyed on the cells it is given |

Sources: [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L67-L71), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L104-L111)

## Depth-Matched Read-Out on the Held-Out Run

The two extraction runners differ in exactly one consequential flag. `run_full_fixed.sh` passes `--all-layers` (every block of every model, 8 to 33 layers), while `run_heldout_fixed.sh` omits it, so `run_model.py` keeps the adapter's default five **depth-matched** layers: the block indices at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 % of depth, computed as `round(f * (n_layers - 1))` and deduplicated (small models may collapse some picks). This gives the held-out comparison one comparable depth per model without the cost of a full re-extraction, at ~1/6 the SAE training volume.

Sources: [layers.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/layers.py#L1-L20), [run_full_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh#L13-L17), [run_heldout_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_heldout_fixed.sh#L13-L17)

| Aspect | `run_full_fixed.sh` | `run_heldout_fixed.sh` |
|---|---|---|
| Corpus | `tabula_3tissue_6k.h5ad` (6,000 cells) | `..._heldout_disjoint.h5ad` (5,581 cells) |
| Layers | `--all-layers` (every block, 172 layers across ten models) | default: five depth-matched layers |
| Position sampling | `--per-cell 168 --seed 0` | identical |
| Output directory | `out_fixed/` | `out_heldout_fixed/` |
| Corpus guard | not needed (seed-0 file is the input) | rebuilds disjoint corpus if the file is missing |
| Resumability | DONE marker per model | same pattern |

Sources: [run_full_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh#L2-L24), [run_heldout_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_heldout_fixed.sh#L2-L24), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L22-L35)

## Provenance and Reproduction

The corpus contract is pinned in one place: `configs/models.yaml` records the corpus path (`external/perturb/tabula_3tissue_6k.h5ad`) and the extraction configuration (`per_cell: 168, seed: 0`) as a single comment-anchored block that all ten model entries share, alongside each model's layer count — the denominator for the depth-matched picks. The reproduce guide's GPU stage then spells out the exact command sequence: two `build_ts_corpus.py` invocations (seeds 0 and 1), `make_heldout_disjoint.py`, and the four runner scripts. The resulting held-out catalogues ship in the checksummed release archive `runs-heldout_cat.tar.gz` — "catalogues on the held-out draw (5,581 cells, none shared with the corpus), all ten models, five depth-matched layers" — so the held-out analysis never requires re-extraction.

Sources: [models.yaml](pipeline/atlas_h100/configs/models.yaml#L1-L13), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L90-L103), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L50-L60)

## Where the Held-Out Draw Is Consumed

The disjoint corpus is the control that separates "the model learned something" from "the SAE memorised its training cells": the calibrated annotator's configuration was fixed on the discovery corpus *before* the held-out corpus was touched, and the 96-concept backbone reproduced on the held-out draw — which shares no cell with the training corpus — on all ten models (Jaccard 0.52 against 0.035 for random backbones, p = 0.02). How those catalogues are turned into regulatory-prediction scores is the subject of the next methodology page; how the backbone itself is detected is covered in the local analysis stage.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L62-L84), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L132-L145)

**Suggested reading order**: continue with [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation) to see why annotation thresholds had to be locked before the held-out draw was used, then [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim), then [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test) for the main consumer of `out_heldout_fixed/`. For the local-stage detection that the held-out draw replicates, see [Concept Matrices and Backbone Detection](13-concept-matrices-and-backbone-detection).

# Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation



Every cross-model claim in this atlas rests on one methodological decision: which statistical procedure maps an SAE feature's top genes to biological concepts. The pipeline carries **two annotators side by side** — the *permissive* one inherited from the field's default practice, and the *calibrated* one derived in this repository by grid search against a random-gene null. This page explains what each annotator is, why the permissive variant was demoted to an illustrative role, how the calibrated configuration was found and frozen, and where each one now operates in the codebase.

Sources: [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L34-L41), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L57-L79)

## The Two Annotators

The permissive annotator is the join key of the comparative atlas: the same test run on every model's feature catalogue so features are comparable in a shared concept vocabulary. For each feature, the catalogue retains the top-20 genes ranked by mean activation; the annotator slices the top-5, intersects them with a 16,205-gene background, and tests Fisher's exact test (one-sided, `alternative="greater"`) against five databases — GO_BP, Reactome and KEGG fetched via Enrichr, plus the interaction databases STRING (score ≥ 700) and TRRUST — restricted to term sizes 5–500. All p-values across every feature × term × source combination are corrected jointly with Benjamini–Hochberg at q ≤ 0.05. The top-5 slice is deliberate: the inline comment records that it produced "empirically sharper/more specific concepts (higher odds-ratio, no saturation)" than wider slices.

Sources: [annotate.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/annotate.py#L1-L8), [annotate.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/annotate.py#L40-L57), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L23-L25), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L59-L60)

The calibrated annotator is a stricter construction that survived the same test applied to random noise: take the top-10 genes per feature, require at least 3 of them in a single **curated** pathway set (GO_BP, Reactome or KEGG only — no PPI or regulon sets), cap set size at 200 genes, and apply BH ≤ 0.05 on the hypergeometric upper tail against the same background. Its constants are declared once — `ALPHA, TOP, AMIN, MX, NPERM = 0.05, 10, 3, 200, 30` — and every downstream consumer re-declares the identical tuple, making the configuration auditable at each call site.

Sources: [recalibrate_final.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L2-L4), [recalibrate_final.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L17), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L39-L41), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L62-L63)

| Dimension | Permissive | Calibrated |
|---|---|---|
| Top genes per feature | 5 (of 20 kept in catalogue) | 10 |
| Test statistic | Fisher exact, one-sided greater | Hypergeometric upper tail `sf(A-1, BGN, TG, LG)` |
| Multiple testing | BH ≤ 0.05, one joint correction | BH ≤ 0.05, one joint correction |
| Databases | GO_BP, Reactome, KEGG, STRING ≥700, TRRUST | GO_BP, Reactome, KEGG only (curated pathways) |
| Term size window | 5–500 genes | 5–200 genes |
| Minimum overlap | 2 | 3 |
| Odds-ratio floor | none | none (swept in grids, dropped from winner) |
| Background | 16,205 genes | 16,205 genes |
| Canonical implementation | `atlas_h100/common/annotate.py` | `recalibrate_final.py` constants, re-declared in consumers |
| Sanctioned role | Per-model description; site labels marked illustrative | Every cross-model claim |

Sources: [annotate.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/annotate.py#L14-L14), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L35-L37), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L73-L79)

The two annotators sit at different points of the claim-dependency graph. The random-gene null is not a competing annotator but the *arbiter*: it is the instrument that convicted the permissive variant and the objective function against which the calibrated configuration was tuned.

```mermaid
graph TD
    CAT["feature_catalog_L*.json<br/>top-20 genes per SAE feature"] --> PERM["Permissive annotator<br/>top-5, Fisher exact, BH<br/>5 databases"]
    CAT --> CAL["Calibrated annotator<br/>top-10, overlap at least 3, hypergeom, BH<br/>curated pathways only"]
    RAND["Random-gene null<br/>random_null.py"] -- "convicts: random genes<br/>annotate almost as often" --> PERM
    RAND -- "objective function for<br/>grid search recalibrate*.py" --> CAL
    PERM -- "per-model description,<br/>site labels marked illustrative" --> SITE["Interactive Atlas site"]
    CAL --> BACKBONE["Shared backbone<br/>concepts in at least 8 of 10 models"]
    BACKBONE --> HO["Held-out replication<br/>heldout_calibrated.py"]
    BACKBONE --> DEPTH["Depth curves<br/>depth_calibrated.py"]
    BACKBONE --> CLAIMS["Every cross-model claim"]
```

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L65-L79), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L24-L37)

## Why the Permissive Annotator Fails Its Own Null

The decisive control asks a deliberately hostile question: if random genes annotate features at the same rate as real ones, is the "universal core" of shared concepts also just what noise produces? `random_null.py` implements this by replacing every feature's top genes with genes drawn uniformly from the background, re-annotating all ten models at the mid layer with the *unchanged permissive procedure*, rebuilding the random-gene core (the intersection across models), and comparing it to the real core with a z-score over 100 permutations. It also derives the mean pairwise Jaccard between models' concept sets, a deduplicated core, and — critically — a "reproducibility baseline" as the overlap of two independent random-gene cores.

Sources: [random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py#L1-L9), [random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py#L77-L110)

The result was unambiguous and inverted the expected sign. Under the permissive annotator the ten models appear to share 1,977 concepts, while random genes share 3,570 (z = −24.2): the real core is a *deficit* relative to noise, not an excess. At the mid layer the naive core was 365 real against 582 random, and its celebrated held-out "replication" (Jaccard 0.50) proved no better than two random draws (0.51). The failure mechanism is database structure, not model structure: because the databases are large and heavily overlapping, almost any gene quintet lands inside some sufficiently large set often enough to survive BH correction.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L65-L68), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L103-L105)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Draw random background genes<br/>in place of each feature's top genes"] --> B["Re-annotate all 10 models<br/>with the UNCHANGED annotator"]
    B --> C["Build random-gene concept sets<br/>and the intersection core"]
    C --> D["Compare real core vs null core<br/>z-score, fold, Jaccard baselines"]
    D -- "permissive: 1,977 real vs 3,570 random" --> E["Permissive annotator fails<br/>retracted as a claim instrument"]
    D -- "calibrated: 96 real vs 3.5 null at the<br/>shared-by-8 tier" --> F["Calibrated annotator passes<br/>adopted for cross-model claims"]
```

Sources: [random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py#L111-L129), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L65-L68)

> [!TIP]
> The permissive annotator was not modified in response to this failure — it was demoted. Keeping the original procedure intact, with all its outputs, preserves the negative result as a reproducible artifact (`random_null.json`, `heldout.json`) rather than erasing an embarrassing baseline. This is why the retraction is auditable by [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks).

## Deriving the Calibrated Annotator: Three Grid Rounds

The calibration was a search over annotator *configurations*, not a tuning of p-values. Each grid round evaluates a candidate configuration by running it on both real top-gene lists and random-gene lists, then scores it on two axes: does the random-gene annotation rate collapse to a controlled false-positive floor, and does the real cross-model core now beat the random core by a clear margin? Round one (`recalibrate.py`) swept the database subset (dropping STRING/TRRUST interaction sets), the maximum gene-set size (100 vs 200), the minimum overlap `a` (2 vs 3), and an odds-ratio floor (0, 5, 10) — with the top-5 slice held fixed. A configuration "won" if the random rate was controlled and the real core exceeded the random core beyond two standard deviations.

Sources: [recalibrate.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate.py#L1-L8), [recalibrate.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate.py#L100-L106)

Round two (`recalibrate2.py`) covered the two plausible rescues the first grid missed: keeping the loose overlap `a ≥ 2` but imposing a high odds-ratio floor (10 or 20) to retain only *specific* small-set hits, and conversely widening the gene slice to top-10 or top-20 while raising the overlap requirement to `a ≥ 3` or `a ≥ 4` — reasoning that real coherent features should be given the chance to land three genes in one set. Its acceptance test sharpened: a configuration must keep the real annotation rate *usable* (≥ 10 %) **and** drive the core z above 2. The top-10, `a ≥ 3`, size ≤ 200, no-PPI cell of this grid is the one that cleared both bars.

Sources: [recalibrate2.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate2.py#L1-L6), [recalibrate2.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate2.py#L74-L100)

| Round | Script | Knobs swept | Acceptance test | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `recalibrate.py` | DB subset (drop PPI), max set size 100/200, min overlap 2/3, OR floor 0/5/10; top-5 fixed | Random rate controlled AND real core > null mean + 2σ | `recalibrate.json` |
| 2 | `recalibrate2.py` | OR floor 10/20 at a ≥ 2; top-N 5/10/20 with a ≥ 3/4; set size 100/200/300 | Real rate ≥ 10 % AND core z > 2 | `recalibrate2.json` |
| Freeze | `recalibrate_final.py` | none — winner frozen: top-10, a ≥ 3, curated ≤ 200, no PPI | Shared-by-k spectrum vs null per tier, 30 permutations | `recalibrate_final.json` |
| Stress | `recalibrate_robust.py` | 5 neighbour configs × sharing tiers ≥ 7/8/9/10 | Fold over null per cell; housekeeping vs specific split | `recalibrate_robust.json` |

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L61-L64), [recalibrate_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_robust.py#L1-L6)

Two procedural disciplines matter as much as the winning numbers. First, the target of the search is a **false-positive rate, not an effect size**: the grid was run until random genes annotated about 3 % of features against about 9 % for real ones, so the annotator is validated by the same null machinery that every downstream claim must survive. Second, the configuration was **frozen on the discovery corpus before the held-out corpus was touched** — the round-three script computes the honest shared-by-k spectrum and the all-ten core under the frozen winner, and the held-out evaluation (`heldout_calibrated.py`) then applied the constants verbatim, with no reopening of the search.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L68-L71), [recalibrate_final.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L78-L101), [heldout_calibrated.py](pipeline/scripts/heldout_calibrated.py#L2-L7)

> [!TIP]
> Every calibrated script re-declares the winning tuple (`TOP=10, AMIN=3, MX=200`) rather than importing it. This looks like duplication but functions as a distributed contract: each consumer's docstring restates the annotator string, so any script that silently drifts from the frozen configuration is legible in a diff — the pattern the audit system relies on when re-deriving manuscript numbers.

## Implementation Anatomy

The two annotators share a statistical skeleton but differ in execution strategy. The permissive `annotate_catalog` walks every (feature, source, term) triple with a nested loop, builds the 2×2 contingency table by hand, and calls `scipy.stats.fisher_exact` per term — correct but O(features × terms) in Python-level calls. The calibrated `annotate()` inverts this: it builds a **gene-to-terms index** once (`idx[gene].append(term)`), counts term membership per feature with a `Counter`, prunes every candidate below `AMIN = 3` *before* testing, then evaluates the hypergeometric survival function as one vectorized array operation across all surviving (feature, term) pairs and applies BH jointly. The upper tail `hypergeom.sf(A - 1, BGN, TG, LG)` is the exact one-sided "at least A overlaps" probability, statistically equivalent to Fisher's `greater` but computed in bulk.

Sources: [annotate.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/annotate.py#L50-L68), [recalibrate_final.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L21-L57)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as feature catalog
    participant P as permissive annotate_catalog
    participant K as calibrated annotate
    participant S as gene-set JSONs
    C->>P: top_genes[:5] per feature
    C->>K: top_genes[:10] per feature
    S->>P: GO/KEGG/Reactome/STRING/TRRUST, size 5 to 500
    S->>K: GO/KEGG/Reactome only, size 5 to 200
    P->>P: per-term 2x2 table, fisher_exact call
    K->>K: index lookup, Counter, prune below 3
    P->>P: BH over all feature x term x source p-values
    K->>K: vectorized hypergeom.sf + BH
    P-->>C: annotation records with odds_ratio, q, overlap
    K-->>C: set of qualifying terms
```

Sources: [annotate.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/annotate.py#L40-L84), [recalibrate_final.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L40-L57)

Both annotators guard the same input edge cases: a feature contributing fewer than three genes to the background is skipped entirely, since no enrichment test on two drawable genes can be meaningful. Note also what the calibrated annotator deliberately *excludes* by dropping STRING and TRRUST: interaction databases were part of the permissive failure mode, because protein–protein and TF–target edges generate large, densely overlapping gene sets that random quintets hit by construction.

Sources: [recalibrate_final.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L42-L45), [recalibrate.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate.py#L2-L3)

## Stress-Testing the Chosen Configuration

A grid-search winner is only an argmax over one lucky cell unless the neighbourhood agrees with it. `recalibrate_robust.py` therefore sweeps five calibrated configurations — the winner plus perturbations to set size (150, 300), gene slice (top-12), and a restored odds-ratio floor (OR ≥ 5) — each crossed with four sharing thresholds (concepts in ≥ 7, 8, 9, or 10 of 10 models), and reports the real-vs-null fold at every cell of the grid. It then classifies the winner's ≥ 8 backbone against a keyword list of housekeeping machinery (translation, ribosome, splicing, proteasome, OXPHOS, cell cycle, chromatin, chaperone) versus specific programmes, so the surviving claim is quantified by *what kind* of biology it is, not just how many terms.

Sources: [recalibrate_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_robust.py#L1-L6), [recalibrate_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_robust.py#L96-L145)

Two further sensitivity checks close the remaining degrees of freedom. `topn_sweep.py` re-annotates every model's mid layer at top-5, 10, 15 and 20 genes under the permissive 5-database Fisher procedure, recording annotation rate, distinct concepts and median odds ratio — the evidence behind the original top-5 slice choice and the context for the calibrated annotator's top-10 choice. `kegg_robust.py` rebuilds the calibrated backbone with GO_BP and Reactome only: KEGG contributes 24 of the 96 backbone concepts, and without it the backbone is 72 concepts at 25.7× over the null, so no claim rests on that single database.

Sources: [topn_sweep.py](pipeline/scripts/topn_sweep.py#L1-L13), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L241-L247)

The calibrated annotator also faces a stronger null variant than uniform random genes: the degree-matched null replaces each gene with one of *equal gene-set membership degree*, so mere database hub-ness cannot manufacture the backbone. That null (250 permutations), alongside the full null taxonomy, is the subject of [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim); here it suffices that the backbone survives it at 51.2×.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L81-L99), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L127-L128)

## Where Each Annotator Lives Today

The division of labour is strict and documented. Every **cross-model** claim — the shared backbone, its depth profile, its held-out replication, the co-expression baseline — uses the calibrated annotator. The permissive annotator survives in two sanctioned niches: per-model description on the site (labelled *illustrative*) and the site's module theme labels (also permissive, labelled *hints*, since across all groups a label covers a median 20 % of a group's features). The per-layer concept matrices that feed the interactive explorer (`matrix_ts3_string.json`, `perlayer_concepts.json`) remain permissive because they serve browsing, not claims.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L73-L76), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L51-L58)

| Consumer | Annotator | Output file | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `recalibrate_final.py` | calibrated (frozen) | `recalibrate_final.json` | shared-by-k spectrum, all-ten core vs null |
| `heldout_calibrated.py` | calibrated | `heldout_calibrated.json` | backbone replication on seed-1 cells; Jaccard vs two-random-draw baseline |
| `depth_calibrated.py` | calibrated | `depth_calibrated.json` | per-layer annotation-rate curves, all 172 layers |
| `coexpr_core_baseline.py` | calibrated | `coexpr_core_baseline.json` | no-model co-expression dictionary baseline for the backbone |
| `random_null.py` | permissive | `random_null.json` | the control that retracts the naive core |
| `topn_sweep.py` | permissive (5 DB) | `topn_sweep.json` | top-N gene cutoff sensitivity |
| `reannotate_string.py`, `alllayer_matrix.py` | permissive | `matrix_ts3_string.json`, `perlayer_concepts.json` | site concept matrices and gene-search index |
| `kegg_robust.py` | calibrated minus KEGG | `kegg_robust.json` | database-sensitivity check |

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L24-L70), [depth_calibrated.py](pipeline/scripts/depth_calibrated.py#L1-L5)

One asymmetry deserves emphasis: annotation rate itself was retracted as an interpretability score under the permissive annotator, because random genes annotate almost as often. Under the calibrated annotator the rate becomes a usable per-model quantity — it spans 1.0 % to 29.3 % across the ten models at the mid layer — and `depth_calibrated.py` exists precisely to move the depth panel off the permissive variant, as its docstring puts it, "no more 'permissive illustrative'". Seed variance measurements were likewise taken under permissive (the mid-layer core varies by 12 %, 435 to 580 concepts; the all-layer core by 4 %), which contextualizes how much of that spread the stricter annotator had to absorb.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L106-L107), [depth_calibrated.py](pipeline/scripts/depth_calibrated.py#L1-L5), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L43-L46)

## What the Calibration Changed in the Results

The retraction ledger is the cleanest measure of the decision's impact. Four claims died under the random-gene null: the ~2,000-concept universal core (365 vs 582 random at mid layer; 1,977 vs 3,570 on the all-layer union); annotation rate as an interpretability score; the "100 % of SAE features invisible to SVD" observation (true of random directions too — see [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd)); and the "new biology" shortlist, whose degree-matched label permutation (`novel_calibrated.py`) showed 0 of 207 candidates surviving.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L101-L123)

What survived is correspondingly modest and specific. A backbone of **96 concepts** encoded by at least 8 of 10 models under the calibrated annotator — 27.5× the uniform null and 51.2× the degree-matched null — of which 42 concepts form one protein-synthesis block, 12 are other housekeeping, and 42 are specific programmes spanning 37 distinct themes; present at every depth (55 to 133 concepts) and reproduced on the held-out draw, which shares no cell with the corpus, on all ten models (Jaccard 0.52 against a 0.035 two-random-draw baseline, p = 0.02). Notably, no concept appears in all ten models — the all-ten intersection is brittle by construction, which is why the ≥ 8-of-10 tier, and not the intersection, is the calibrated backbone.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L125-L133), [heldout_calibrated.py](pipeline/scripts/heldout_calibrated.py#L89-L115)

This page's decision also pre-conditions the held-out regulatory test in an understated way: TRRUST qualifies as a clean evaluation target precisely because the calibrated annotator never used it, so the prediction stage scores against evidence no step of the pipeline consumed. That separation is developed in [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test).

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L148-L153)

## Reading Progression

The calibration story assumes the extraction and SAE machinery upstream: features are catalogued per layer by [TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training), and the discovery/held-out corpus split that disciplines the freeze order is defined in [Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw). The natural next pages are [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim), which generalizes the random-gene construction used here into the degree-matched, cell-shuffle and configuration-model nulls, and [Concept Matrices and Backbone Detection](13-concept-matrices-and-backbone-detection), which shows how the calibrated concept sets become the shared backbone and its programme composition. For the consequences of the retractions recorded above, see [Key Findings and Retracted Claims](4-key-findings-and-retracted-claims); for how these annotator choices are mechanically re-verified, see [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks).


# Null Models Behind Every Claim



Every quantitative claim in the atlas-comparison repository is paired with a null model constructed to produce that same claim by chance. This page documents the null family as an engineering system: the design principle that matches each null to the confound it excludes, the six distinct null implementations, the shared empirical-p convention, and the audit trail of what the nulls retracted versus what survived. This is the statistical core of the project — the layer that decides which claims a reviewer can act on and which are artefacts of database overlap, gene popularity, or study bias.

Sources: [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L48-L55), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L107), [pipeline/scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L20-L40)

## The Design Principle: Nulls Matched to the Claim

The repository's rule, stated in the decision log, is that **each result is stated against a null built to produce the same result by chance**. This is a stronger requirement than a generic permutation test. A generic null ("shuffle everything") answers only "is the number above zero?" — it cannot distinguish a genuine signal from a structural bias. The nulls here are *matched*: each one preserves every property of the data except the property the claim depends on. If a claim is about concepts shared across ten models, the null asks whether random genes annotate at the same rate. If a claim is about co-firing genes predicting regulatory edges, the null asks whether a degree-preserving rewiring of the co-firing graph recovers edges just as well — so gene abundance and study bias survive intact in the null and cannot explain the effect.

This matching discipline also inverts the usual role of a null: here, nulls were used **as calibration instruments during design**, not only as tests after the fact. The calibrated annotator was produced by a grid search (`recalibrate.py`, `recalibrate2.py`) over database, set size, minimum overlap and odds ratio, with the stopping criterion being the random-gene null itself — the search continued until random genes annotate roughly 3 % of features versus roughly 9 % for real ones. The chosen configuration was then frozen on the discovery corpus before the held-out corpus was ever touched.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Claims["Claim families"]
        A["Shared backbone<br/>(concepts in ≥ 8 of 10 models)"]
        B["Backbone across depth"]
        C["Held-out replication of backbone"]
        D["Cross-model CKA"]
        E["SAE vs PCA variance"]
        F["Regulatory prediction<br/>(co-firing → TRRUST)"]
        G["Literature co-mention"]
        H["Perturbation response"]
    end
    subgraph Nulls["Matched null models"]
        N1["Uniform random genes"]
        N2["Degree-matched genes<br/>(same gene-set membership)"]
        N3["Two-draw random backbones<br/>(Jaccard between them)"]
        N4["Cell shuffle of one embedding"]
        N5["Rank-k PCA + untrained dictionary"]
        N6["Configuration-model rewiring"]
        N7["Publication-count-preserving shuffle"]
        N8["Responsiveness-matched gene"]
    end
    A --> N1
    A --> N2
    B --> N1
    C --> N3
    D --> N4
    E --> N5
    F --> N6
    G --> N7
    H --> N8
```

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L107), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L69-L83), [pipeline/scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L20-L40)

## The Annotation Nulls: From Retraction to the Calibrated Backbone

Three nulls attack the annotation claims, forming a deliberate escalation ladder from weakest to strongest. The **random-gene null** ([random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py)) replaces every feature's top-5 genes with genes drawn uniformly from the 16,205-gene background and runs the identical permissive annotator (hypergeometric overlap ≥ 2, BH < 0.05, five databases) over the same per-model feature counts. Under this null, random genes annotate almost as often as real ones — and, decisively, the all-layer "universal core" of ~1,977 concepts shared by all ten models is *below* the random-gene core of 3,570 (z = −24.2). At the mid layer the naive core of 365 real concepts sits under a 582-concept random core. The script also computes two refinements: a deduplicated-core null (Jaccard ≥ 0.5 merging, to rule out ontology redundancy inflating counts) and a **held-out-style null** — the Jaccard overlap of two *independent* random-gene cores — which calibrates the "reproducibility" claim directly: the observed held-out core Jaccard of 0.50 is compared against a two-random-draw baseline of 0.51.

The **all-layer null** ([alllayer_null.py](pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py)) closes the reviewer-critical gap that the mid-layer null left: the retracted headline was an all-layer union, so the null must union per-layer concepts over every layer per model, intersect across the ten models, and compare against a random-gene null built the same way (random genes drawn per layer at each layer's real feature count). Because the null repeats the annotator per layer per permutation, the implementation swaps the per-feature Python loop for a sparse gene × term incidence matrix and a matrix product — roughly a 50× speedup with an annotator provably identical to `random_null.py`'s. It runs only 20 permutations, a budget set by cost.

The **degree-matched null** ([degree_null.py](pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py)) is the strongest test in the ladder. Instead of uniform draws, each real top-gene is replaced by a random gene from the *same degree bin* — the same gene-set membership degree across curated GO/Reactome/KEGG — computed over a background sorted with stable ordering, degree-0 genes in their own bin, and the rest split into 40 quantile bins. This controls for gene popularity: high-degree genes are "hittable" by chance under any uniform null, so if the calibrated backbone still beats *this* null, it is not a gene-abundance artefact. It evaluates the calibrated annotator (top-10, ≥ 3 in a set ≤ 200 genes, no PPI) at sharing tiers ≥ 7/8/9/10 of 10 models with 250 permutations per tier, reporting the uniform null alongside for contrast.

| Null | Script | Permutations | Scope | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Uniform random-gene | `random_null.py` | 100 | Mid layer, permissive annotator | Retracts the naive core |
| All-layer union | `alllayer_null.py` | 20 | Per-layer counts preserved, permissive annotator | Retracts the all-layer core |
| Degree-matched | `degree_null.py` | 250 | Calibrated annotator, 40 degree bins, tiers ≥ 7/8/9/10 | Backbone survives |
| Two-draw held-out | `stats_final.py`, `random_null.py` | 150 | Jaccard between independent backbones | Replication survives |

The final link in the chain is [stats_final.py](pipeline/scripts/stats_final.py), which re-runs the backbone claim at publication grade: 250 permutations of the uniform null against the calibrated backbone at the mid layer, plus a 150-draw held-out replication null where random-gene backbones are built on *both* the discovery and held-out draws and their Jaccard is compared to the observed one. What survives this ladder is a backbone of 96 concepts at the ≥ 8-of-10 tier — 27.5× the uniform null and 51.2× the degree-matched null — and held-out replication at Jaccard 0.52 against a null of 0.035. The two-annotator story these nulls forced is covered in depth in [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation).

Sources: [pipeline/scripts/random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py#L1-L8), [pipeline/scripts/random_null.py](pipeline/scripts/random_null.py#L115-L131), [pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py](pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py#L1-L7), [pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py](pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py#L42-L84), [pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py](pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py#L1-L9), [pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py](pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py#L39-L47), [pipeline/scripts/stats_final.py](pipeline/scripts/stats_final.py#L1-L7), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L109-L125)

## The Geometry Nulls: Cell Shuffle and the Matched-Sparsity Baseline

[cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py) applies the same rigour to the annotation-free survivors — the results that need no gene lists at all. For **linear CKA** between every one of the 45 model pairs (not a hand-picked subset, the docstring notes), the null is a **cell shuffle**: cells of one embedding are permuted, destroying the cell-to-cell correspondence while leaving each embedding's internal geometry intact. Twenty shuffles per pair give the shuffled-CKA baseline; a real similarity is meaningful only above this floor. The implementation is minimal by design — the CKA itself is eight lines (centering, then the squared norm of the cross-Gram matrix normalised by the two self-Gram norms).

For the **SAE-versus-PCA** claim, the script answers the sharpest possible objection: is the SAE's variance-explained edge just *overcompleteness*? Three quantities are compared at matched sparsity k = 32: the top-32 SVD subspace (analytic, deterministic), the trained SAE, and an **untrained random TopK dictionary of identical shape** (same d, same d_sae, same k, torch seed 0, encoded on the first 20,000 activation rows). The two baselines need no permutations — "none needed" in the null table — because they are deterministic or exact. This framing is what retired a prior claim that "about 100 % of SAE features are invisible to the top SVD axes": that is equally true of random directions at this dimensionality, a property of the dimension rather than the features. The claim that survives is the matched-sparsity one — the SAE beats top-32 PCA in all ten models. The CKA/SVD machinery itself is documented in [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd).

Sources: [pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py#L1-L8), [pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py#L35-L51), [pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py#L53-L85), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L109-L125)

## The Prediction Null: The Configuration Model

The held-out regulatory test (see [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test) for the full protocol) rests on one null: the **configuration model**. Each model's co-firing graph — genes as nodes, an edge where two genes co-occur in ≥ 5 SAE features — is rewired while preserving **every gene's degree exactly**. The implementation in [hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py) is a two-column stub-matching shuffle: degrees are split into stub arrays, shuffled, and re-paired, dropping self-loops and duplicates, with edges encoded as packed 64-bit integers for set operations. Because the rewired graph retains abundance and study bias by construction — a gene that co-fires with everyone still co-fires with everyone in the null — neither can produce the observed TRRUST enrichment.
