TRRUST itself is genuinely held out: the calibrated annotator saw only curated pathway sets, never interaction databases, so no pipeline step touched the truth.

The script is a three-stage design worth noting as a pattern. Stage (A) **validates the null**: an analytic configuration-model expectation ([hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py#L98-L100), `E[edge] ≈ 1 − exp(−dₐd_b/2m)`) is checked against 500 real degree-preserving permutations per model, and the reported p-values come from those permutations, not the analytic formula. Stage (B) applies the same independent-per-model null to the **cross-model corroboration curve** — precision as the number of models predicting a pair rises — and the equal-budget re-scoring. Stage (C) emits the hypothesis list from pairs absent from TRRUST, STRING, and every curated pathway, with precision estimated from stage (B). One design subtlety is stored explicitly in the output: the curve rewires *all ten graphs per draw* but runs a fifth as many permutations (100), because the per-model count (500) had been mis-attributed to it in the manuscript until the field `n_perm_curve` was recorded.

Sources: [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py#L1-L19), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trtrust.py#L39-L46), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L1-L12), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L60-L69), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L94-L108), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L164-L172)

## The Evidence Nulls: Literature Shuffle and Responsiveness Matching

Two further kinds of evidence each carry a null engineered for their specific confound. For **literature co-mention** ([hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py)), the risk is trivially circular: heavily studied genes are co-mentioned with everyone. The null is a **publication-count-preserving shuffle** of the gene→paper bipartite graph — each gene keeps its paper count exactly, papers are reassigned at random via paper-side stub matching, and the observed mega-paper cap (papers annotating > 60 genes are skipped, exactly as in the observed data, applied for a like-for-like comparison) is honoured in the null too. Without that cap, 96 % of all pairs would be "co-mentioned" and the measure would say nothing.

For **perturbation evidence** ([hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py)), two confounds are handled at exactly two layers. The read-out is the *within-row percentile* of gene B's response among all genes when A is knocked down — immune to how globally disruptive perturbation A is (essential genes move everything, but ranks do not care). The null replaces B with a random gene **matched on its own responsiveness** (mean |X| across all perturbations, 20 quantile bins) — so a gene that reacts to everything cannot score by reactivity alone. Row effects fall to the ranking; column effects fall to the matching. The same construction is re-run per corroboration subset (≥ k models), each subset getting its own responsiveness-matched null rather than inheriting the full-set null.

> [!TIP]
> The null in `hypothesis_pubmed.py` contains a subtle reproducibility fix: papers are indexed in **sorted PMID order**, not set-iteration order, because Python randomises string hashing across processes — under the same seed, set-iteration indexing permuted the null differently in every run, giving z = 40.5 on one run and 36.6 on the next. The conclusion never moved, but as the comment puts it, "a number nobody can reproduce is not a number we can report." Any null implementation that iterates an unordered Python collection should apply the same discipline.

Sources: [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L1-L18), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L85-L120), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L1-L17), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L60-L94), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L111-L134), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L187-L205)

## The Statistical Convention: Empirical p and Permutation Budgets

Every permutation null in the repository reports the same convention: **p_emp = (number of null draws at or above the observed value + 1) / (N + 1)**. The add-one correction in the numerator guarantees p is never zero, and the one in the denominator guarantees p is never one — at the cost of a floor: with N permutations the smallest reportable p is 1/(N + 1), and most of the significant results sit exactly at that floor (e.g. p = 0.004 at N = 250). Permutation counts differ by computational cost and are stated wherever a number derived from them appears; alongside each p, the scripts emit the null mean, standard deviation, z-score, and a fold-change over the null, so every reported enrichment is auditable against its own null distribution. All draws use `np.random.default_rng(0)` seeded identically.

Two results deliberately sit near the threshold instead of at the floor and are reported as **marginal**: MaxToki under equal-budget re-scoring (p = 0.04) and the corroboration gain in one robustness variant (p = 0.055). Declaring these marginal rather than significant is part of the same discipline — the Poisson whiskers on the prediction figure exist for the same reason: 60 and 79 recovered edges do not support a ranking between 10.2× and 9.4×.

| Claim | Null | Permutations |
|---|---|---|
| Shared backbone (≥ 8 of 10 models) | Uniform random genes; degree-matched random genes | 250 each |
| Backbone across depth | Uniform random genes at each of five depths | 250 |
| Held-out replication of the backbone | Random-gene backbones on both draws, Jaccard between them | 150 |
| Naive core (retracted) | Uniform random genes, mid layer and all-layer union | 100; 20 |
| CKA between models | Shuffle the cells of one embedding | Per pair (20 shuffles) |
| SAE against PCA | Top-k PCA at the same k; untrained random dictionary | None needed |
| Held-out regulatory recovery per model | Configuration model: rewire the co-firing graph, every gene's degree exact | 500 |
| Corroboration curve, equal-budget re-scoring | The same, all ten graphs per draw | 100 |
| Robustness, literature, perturbation, publication strata | As above; publication-count-preserving shuffle; responsiveness-matched gene | 200 |

Sources: [docs/METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L48-L55), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L107), [pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py](pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py#L130-L140), [pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L94-L108)

## What the Nulls Retracted, and What Survived

The nulls are not decoration — four published claims were retracted by them, and the scripts and result files are deliberately kept so the negatives are reproducible. Beyond the universal core and the SVD-invisibility claim covered above, the **annotation rate itself** was retired as an interpretability score: random genes annotate almost as often under the permissive annotator, so only the calibrated rate is usable. And the **"new biology" shortlist** — genes topping unannotated features in at least five models — was tested against a size-matched feature-subset null ([novel_null.py](pipeline/scripts/novel_null.py), 200 permutations: draw the same number of features uniformly from *all* features per model and count genes reaching the threshold) plus a degree-matched label permutation ([novel_calibrated.py](pipeline/scripts/novel_calibrated.py)). Against these, the shortlist turned out to be a *deficit*, not an excess: 0 of 207 candidates survive. Consensus across models tracks database coverage; it does not fill database gaps.

What survived is the positive result set: the 96-concept calibrated backbone (27.5× uniform, 51.2× degree-matched null), CKA above its cell-shuffle floor for every one of 45 pairs (worst pair 43×), the SAE beating top-32 PCA in all ten models, and four of ten models predicting held-out TRRUST edges above their configuration-model nulls. The complete narrative of wins and losses lives in [Key Findings and Retracted Claims](4-key-findings-and-retracted-claims); the reviewer-round controls that extend this null suite (size-weighted nulls, seed CIs, bootstrap CIs on the n = 10 correlations) are catalogued in [Reviewer Robustness Analyses](16-reviewer-robustness-analyses), and the audit scripts that check every published number against the result file that produced it in [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks).

> [!TIP]
> Notice the asymmetry in how results are archived: retracted claims keep their null scripts and output JSONs alongside the survivors. When reading `outputs/atlas/comparative/`, treat a `*_null.json` file as the interpretive key for its sibling result files — a result file without its null is, by this project's standard, an uninterpretable number.

Sources: [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L109-L125), [pipeline/scripts/novel_null.py](pipeline/scripts/novel_null.py#L1-L10), [pipeline/scripts/novel_null.py](pipeline/scripts/novel_null.py#L107-L126), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L127-L150)

## Where to Go Next

The nulls form one leg of the statistical methodology triad. Continue with [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation) for how the null-driven annotator grid search works, [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test) for the full prediction protocol the configuration model supports, and [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd) for the annotation-free comparisons. To see how the permutation budgets and p-values are enforced at publication time, proceed to [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks); for how the null verdicts reshaped the project's headline claims, read [Key Findings and Retracted Claims](4-key-findings-and-retracted-claims).

# Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test



This page documents the repository's central falsifiability claim: that TopK SAE features, learned without any regulatory database, recover transcription-factor → target edges from TRRUST — a database that no step of the pipeline ever consulted. It covers the isolation argument that makes TRRUST "held out," the co-firing graph construction that turns features into predictions, the degree-preserving configuration-model null, the three-stage validation pipeline, the published results, the equal-budget correction for dictionary-size confounds, and the robustness variants that guard the conclusion.

**Positioning in the catalog**: this page is the payoff of the statistical methodology track — [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim) establishes the null discipline this test applies, and the results feed the interactive site's hypothesis block ([Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files)) and the manuscript audits ([Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks)).

## What Is Held Out, and Why It Is Genuine

The test's validity rests on one structural fact: the **calibrated annotator** — the only annotator whose results enter cross-model claims — accepts just curated pathway sets (GO_BP, Reactome, KEGG, each ≤200 genes, at least 3 of a feature's top-10 genes in one set), explicitly excluding interaction databases. TRRUST is therefore never seen by annotation. The co-firing statistic itself consumes no annotation at all: it reads only each feature's ranked `top_genes` list. Two independent layers isolate TRRUST from every step that produces a prediction. The design was also fixed before evaluation — the calibrated annotator's grid search ran on the discovery corpus before any held-out evaluation.

Sources: [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L34-L48), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L64-L72), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L70-L96)

The scripts enforce the complement of this isolation when emitting the final hypothesis list: pairs are excluded not only from TRRUST (`TRUTH`) but from every pair a curated pathway co-membership could have "seen" (`SEEN`, built from the same ≤200-gene GO/Reactome/KEGG sets the calibrated annotator uses) and from all STRING edges. A released pair is therefore absent from every database the pipeline touched — the strongest novelty claim the data can support.

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py#L31-L46), [hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L26-L36)

> [!TIP]
> The held-out status of TRRUST is **conditional on the annotator's database whitelist**. The `SEEN` exclusion set in the prediction scripts is rebuilt from the exact gene-set files the calibrated annotator consumed — if STRING or any regulatory database were ever added to annotation, both the "never seen" premise and the novelty of the released list would collapse simultaneously. This coupling is why `audit_manuscript_derived.py` checks the prediction result files against the annotator configuration.

One terminological disambiguation: "held out" in this page means the **database** was withheld. A separate, earlier control holds out **cells** — re-extracting all ten models on a seed-1 Tabula Sapiens draw with the 419 cells shared with the seed-0 corpus removed, to replicate the calibrated backbone (`make_heldout_disjoint.py`, `run_heldout_fixed.sh`, 5,581 cells). That experiment belongs to the backbone replication story and is covered in [Concept Matrices and Backbone Detection](13-concept-matrices-and-backbone-detection).

Sources: [make_heldout_disjoint.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/make_heldout_disjoint.py#L1-L33), [run_heldout_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_heldout_fixed.sh#L1-L24), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L7-L11)

## From SAE Features to a Predicted Regulatory Graph

Per model, the construction pools features over **all layers** (8–33 per model), takes each feature's top-10 genes, drops Ensembl-ID artifacts (`ENSG*` prefixes), and emits every within-feature pair as an undirected, lexicographically-sorted edge. A pair's **weight** is the number of distinct features containing both genes; a pair is *predicted* when weight ≥ 5. The top-10 cutoff matches the calibrated annotator's gene budget deliberately, so the prediction and the annotation read the same feature definition.

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py#L53-L74), [hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L47-L58), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L64-L67)

Two implementation details matter at scale. First, genes are interned into integer indices and each edge is bit-packed as `a * (1<<21) + b` with `a < b`, so the entire per-model graph collapses to a sorted `int64` array and truth membership testing is a vectorized `np.isin` against the packed TRRUST key array. Second, the co-firing graphs are computed once and pickled to a shared cache (`.cofire_cache.pkl`), which the downstream stages and the size-matched re-scoring reuse.

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py#L53-L74), [hypothesis_trrust3.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust3.py#L55-L71), [hypothesis_sizematched.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_sizematched.py#L42-L46)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Feature catalogs — all layers, all 10 models<br/>(alllayer_cat / ts3_out)"] -->|"top-10 genes per feature,<br/>Ensembl IDs dropped"| B["Per-model co-firing graph<br/>undirected pairs, weight = #features"]
    B -->|"weight ≥ 5"| C["Predicted pair set PRED[m]"]
    B -->|"stub-matched rewiring,<br/>degree exact"| D["Configuration-model null"]
    C --> E["Observed TRRUST hits"]
    D --> F["Null TRRUST hits"]
    E --> G["Per-model test:<br/>fold, z, empirical p"]
    F --> G
    G -->|"p_emp < 0.05"| H["Passing models: UCE, Tahoe-x1,<br/>C2S-Scale, Geneformer-V2"]
    H --> I["Corroboration: pairs predicted<br/>by ≥ 2 independent models"]
    I --> J["Exclude TRRUST ∪ STRING ∪<br/>curated-pathway co-memberships"]
    J --> K["hypothesis_pairs_full.json<br/>released prediction list"]
```

The diagram's left branch is the observed pipeline; the right branch is the null that must be beaten. Both branches share the graph topology except for edge placement — this is the design that makes the comparison interpretable, as the next section explains.

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L104-L160)

## The Configuration-Model Null

The null is a **configuration model**: each gene keeps its *exact* co-firing degree while edges are rewired at random. Mechanically, all edge stubs (one per endpoint) are concatenated, shuffled, re-paired two-by-two, and self-loops and duplicates are dropped. Because a well-studied or highly-expressed gene that co-fires with many partners still co-fires with exactly that many partners under the null, neither gene abundance nor study bias can manufacture enrichment — the only thing the null destroys is *which* partners a gene co-fires with.

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L61-L70), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L83-L84)

Stage 1 additionally computes an analytic expectation — a Chung-Lu-style sum `Σ(1 − exp(−d_a·d_b / 2m))` over reachable TRRUST edges — giving fold values without waiting on permutations. Stage 2 then validates that analytic shortcut against 500 real rewirings per model, reporting the null mean ± sd, a z-score, and the empirical p-value with the repository-wide convention `p = (#{null ≥ obs} + 1) / (N + 1)`.

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py#L81-L86), [hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L104-L121), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L88)

## Three-Stage Validation Pipeline

The test evolved across three scripts, each writing its own result file and each answering a distinct question. Stage 2 reads nothing from stage 1; stage 3 is the only stage that consumes a predecessor's output — the passing-model list from stage 2.

| Stage | Script | Question answered | Null and permutations | Output artifact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `hypothesis_trrust.py` | Do co-firing pairs recover TRRUST edges at all, at confidence W ∈ {1,2,3,5,10}? | Analytic configuration-model expectation | `hypothesis_trrust.json` |
| 2 | `hypothesis_trrust2.py` | Does the analytic null survive 500 real rewirings? Does multi-model agreement raise precision? | Degree-preserving rewiring: per-model 500; all-ten-graph corroboration curve 100 (a fifth as many, stored explicitly) | `hypothesis_trrust2.json` |
| 3 | `hypothesis_trrust3.py` | Which multi-model pairs are in *no* database, and which models validate the generator? | Same null restricted to passing models, 200 rewirings | `hypothesis_final.json`, `hypothesis_pairs_full.json` |

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust.py#L3-L24), [hypothesis_trrust2.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust2.py#L3-L14), [hypothesis_trrust3.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust3.py#L3-L5), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L36-L41)

```mermaid
graph LR
    T1["hypothesis_trrust.py<br/>stage 1: analytic"] --> J1[("hypothesis_trrust.json")]
    T2["hypothesis_trrust2.py<br/>stage 2: permutations"] --> J2[("hypothesis_trrust2.json")]
    J2 -->|"PASSED = p_emp &lt; 0.05,<br/>sorted by fold"| T3["hypothesis_trrust3.py<br/>stage 3: deliverable"]
    T3 -->|"cofire cache"| SZ["hypothesis_sizematched.py"]
    T3 --> J3[("hypothesis_final.json")]
    T3 --> J4[("hypothesis_pairs_full.json")]
    RB["hypothesis_robust.py"] --> J5[("hypothesis_robust.json")]
    PR["pair_redundancy.py"] --> J6[("pair_redundancy.json")]
    SL["hypothesis_singlelayer.py"] --> J7[("hypothesis_singlelayer.json")]
    J2 & J3 & J4 & J5 & J6 --> AUD["audit_manuscript*.py"]
    J3 & J4 --> SITE["atlas_hypothesis_block.py<br/>→ atlas site"]
```

Stage 3 makes three changes beyond restriction. It flags **paralog families** with a naming rule — two symbols sharing a stem of ≥3 characters with suffixes ≤3 characters each (ACTB/ACTG2, S100A11/S100A4, HLA-A/HLA-B) — deliberately erring toward over-dropping (CDC42/CDC37 count as one family), the safe direction for a candidate list. It fixes degenerate reporting when a null permutation produces zero hits (fold printed as `inf*` with the zero-count stored). And it applies the release threshold **K = 2**: a pair enters the hypothesis list only when two *independently validated* models predict it.

Sources: [hypothesis_trrust3.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust3.py#L73-L118), [hypothesis_trrust3.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust3.py#L120-L146), [hypothesis_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_robust.py#L36-L47)

## Results: Four of Ten Models Pass

With the corrected feature catalogs, four of the ten models produce co-firing graphs that recover TRRUST edges significantly above their own degree-matched nulls:

| Model | Fold over null | Status |
|---|---|---|
| UCE | 10.2× | passes |
| Tahoe-x1 | 9.4× | passes |
| C2S-Scale | 5.5× | passes |
| Geneformer-V2 | 2.5× | passes |
| scGPT | 11.9× on superseded catalogs → 1.7×, p = 0.27 on corrected | retracted |
| remaining six | not significant at p < 0.05 | fail |

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L148-L172)

The scGPT entry is the test's most instructive negative: its apparent 11.9× enrichment was an artifact of catalogues trained on roughly 420 cells (the [extraction fault documented separately](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run)); on corrected catalogs the signal vanishes (1.7×, p = 0.27). The manuscript reports both numbers, which is precisely the kind of claim the audit system verifies against result files.

Cross-model corroboration is the second headline result: pairs predicted by **two** models independently are enriched **15.3×** over the configuration null versus **5.0×** for single-model pairs (2,000 rewirings via `agreement_curve.py`), a precision of 0.23%. Agreement beyond two models adds nothing. The 100-rewiring corroboration curve inside `hypothesis_trrust2.json` yields 11.5× for the ≥2 tier — a noisier estimate, retained and explained rather than silently replaced.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L166-L172), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L28-L28)

> [!TIP]
> The corroboration curve is computed over **all ten models**, never the four that passed — the four were *selected* on TRRUST, and re-scoring the selected subset against the same database would be circular. The selected-four numbers (5.4×, 15.4×) appear only as a direction check, and the selected set is read programmatically from `hypothesis_trrust2.json` (`p_emp < 0.05`) rather than typed in, so the selection criterion cannot drift from what was tested.

Because 60 and 79 recovered edges are too few to license fine-grained ranking, the figures add Poisson whiskers: the manuscript explicitly declines to claim UCE's 10.2× beats Tahoe-x1's 9.4×.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L184-L186)

## Capacity versus Quality: The Equal-Budget Re-Scoring

The per-model fold table has a structural confound the null cannot fix: how many pairs a model can *offer* is set by its dictionary width (4 × d_model) and layer count, spanning four orders of magnitude — AIDO.Cell contributes 2 predicted pairs, C2S-Scale 147,728 — and hit counts correlate with graph size at r = +0.90. Each model's fold is compared to a null built from its own graph, so the ratio is nominally protected, but a reader sees a league table and cannot distinguish capability from capacity.

Sources: [hypothesis_sizematched.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_sizematched.py#L3-L27)

The correction gives every model the **same prediction budget** — N = 50,707, the smallest graph among the passing models — under two regimes: `top-N` (the N highest-weight pairs, what a practitioner with a fixed budget would take) and `rand-N` (N random pairs, 20 draws, isolating size alone). All four passing models remain significant at equal budget:

| Model | Full-size fold | Equal-budget (50,707 pairs, top-N) |
|---|---|---|
| UCE | 10.2× | 11.8× |
| Tahoe-x1 | 9.4× | 11.0× |
| C2S-Scale | 5.5× | 8.4× |
| Geneformer-V2 | 2.5× | 2.4× |

Sources: [hypothesis_sizematched.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_sizematched.py#L72-L115), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L174-L178)

Two reporting rules follow. Models whose graphs are smaller than the budget are recorded as **untestable at that budget** — not as failures — the distinction the manuscript previously elided for AIDO.Cell. And only the equal-budget version licenses a claim about *quality*; both versions are persisted (`ranking_full_size`, `ranking_size_matched`, `ranking_preserved`, plus a Spearman rank correlation between the two rankings).

Sources: [hypothesis_sizematched.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_sizematched.py#L89-L124), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L174-L178)

## Robustness Variants

Five controlled perturbations ask whether the enrichment survives when plausible artifacts are removed. All use the same configuration-model null restricted to passing models:

| Variant | Mechanism | Artifact it rules out |
|---|---|---|
| R1 — no same-family pairs | Naming-rule paralog pairs (shared stem ≥3 chars, short suffixes) dropped | Enrichment carried by gene families rather than regulation |
| R2 — firing features only | Only features with `activation_frequency` above the per-model median | Near-zero-expression genes clustering together |
| R3 — stricter evidence | Per-pair bar raised from ≥5 to ≥10 features | Result resting on weak recurrence |
| R2+R1 | Both combined | Interaction of the two artifacts |
| Deduplicated support (`pair_redundancy.py`) | Features in the same co-activation community at the same layer vote once | Near-duplicate feature blocks satisfying W ≥ 5 by themselves |

Sources: [hypothesis_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_robust.py#L3-L14), [hypothesis_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_robust.py#L100-L110)

The near-duplicate check deserves its own scrutiny because the atlas shows that most models contain a block of near-copy features (a known consequence of dictionary oversizing, documented in [TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training) and decision 3). For every model, `pair_redundancy.py` measures how much faster community features fire than the rest, what share of each predicted pair's support comes from community members, whether block-carried pairs hit TRRUST at a different rate, and what survives deduplication. Its conclusion — that the prediction result does not rest on the block — is what Table S12 reports. A sixth variant, `hypothesis_singlelayer.py`, rebuilds the co-firing graph from a single layer to test whether the result requires pooling across depth. Two auxiliary results sit near the significance threshold and are reported as marginal rather than clean: MaxToki at equal budget (p = 0.04) and one corroboration gain in a robustness variant (p = 0.055).

Sources: [pair_redundancy.py](pipeline/scripts/pair_redundancy.py#L3-L18), [pair_redundancy.py](pipeline/scripts/pair_redundancy.py#L56-L80), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L37-L39), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L88), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L37-L38)

## Result Files and Downstream Consumption

The test's artifacts are nine JSON files in `outputs/atlas/comparative/`, each with a declared writer and consumers:

| File | Writer | Consumed by | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hypothesis_trrust.json` | stage 1 | — (exploratory) | Per-model analytic folds over the W grid |
| `hypothesis_trrust2.json` | stage 2 | stage 3, size-matched, audits, figures | Per-model permutation results; all-ten corroboration curve |
| `hypothesis_final.json` | stage 3 | site assembly, supplement tables, Fig 5, audits | Validated models + released prediction list |
| `hypothesis_pairs_full.json` | stage 3, then literature enrichment in place | site, supplement, robustness checks | All released pairs with models, weight, co-mentions, family flag |
| `hypothesis_robust.json` | `hypothesis_robust.py` | audits, supplement | The five robustness variants |
| `hypothesis_sizematched.json` | `hypothesis_sizematched.py` | audits, Fig 5 | Equal-budget re-scoring and both rankings |
| `pair_redundancy.json` | `pair_redundancy.py` | audits, supplement | Near-duplicate-block decomposition (Table S12) |
| `agreement_curve.json` | `agreement_curve.py` | site hypothesis block | 2,000-rewiring precision at ≥1 and ≥2 models |
| `hypothesis_singlelayer.json` | `hypothesis_singlelayer.py` | audits | Single-layer control |

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L28-L41), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L63-L63)

Nothing downstream reads these files casually: the manuscript, supplement, and site data blocks are built from result files and nothing else, with `audit_all.py` and its manuscript checks enforcing the linkage — the full data flow is mapped in [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map). The released list itself (4,485 pairs) then feeds the two independent corroboration channels — literature co-mention and Perturb-seq responsiveness — which are covered in [Literature and Perturbation Evidence](14-literature-and-perturbation-evidence).

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L3-L6), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L31-L33)

## Where This Sits, and Where to Go Next

Within the methodology track, this test is the constructive endpoint: [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim) defines the null vocabulary (degree matching, permutation floors, marginal-result reporting) this page applies; the feature catalogs it consumes are produced by the GPU stage described in [Model Adapter Contract](6-model-adapter-contract) and [TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training), with the cell-level held-out draw in [Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw). Reading next: [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd) continues the annotation-free methodology, and [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks) shows how every number quoted here is machine-checked against its result file.

# Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD



This page documents the **annotation-free** layer of the atlas: every comparison that asks what a model's representation *looks like geometrically*, without consulting a single gene set. It covers two method families — **linear CKA** between per-cell embeddings (cross-model and within-model, each against a cell-shuffle null) and **SVD/PCA tests** that determine whether the TopK SAE dictionaries find structure that low-rank subspace methods cannot reach. Everything here runs on the shared 6,000-cell corpus described in [Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw), and every number is backed by a null in the spirit of [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim).

Sources: [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L59-L67), [cell_cka.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cell_cka.py#L1-L9), [cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py#L1-L8)

## Why Geometry Without Annotation

The annotation-based backbone (page 13) had to survive a random-gene null first, because gene-set databases are large and overlapping enough to annotate noise. Geometry sidesteps that fragility entirely: it compares **distributions of cell embeddings** directly, using statistics that are invariant to each model's dimensionality and rotation. The page answers two questions that the annotated analyses cannot: do different architectures place the *same cells* in the same relative arrangement, and is the SAE's sparse dictionary genuinely something a rank-32 PCA cannot represent — or just an artifact of overcompleteness?

The repo's own verdict, recorded in the decision log, is that both questions now have defensible answers: every cross-model CKA pair sits far above its shuffle floor (worst pair 43×), and the SAE beats top-32 PCA in all ten models — but a seductive earlier claim ("≈100% of SAE features are invisible to SVD") was **retracted** because random directions fail the same test at this dimensionality.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L96-L109), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L110-L128), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L48-L57)

## The Embedding Substrate: One Corpus, Cached Per-Cell Vectors

`cell_cka.py` is the producer of everything geometric. For each model it re-runs the forward pass (no SAE required for the residual side), takes the seed-0 subsample of **2,000 cells shared by all models**, and mean-pools each layer's residual stream over the cell's own gene tokens into a `[n_cells, d_model]` embedding. Crucially it caches both spaces — the raw **residual** (`res_<i>`) and the **SAE-feature** space (`sae_<i>`, mean-encoded activations) — into `cka/{model}_emb.npz`, so a crash mid-run or a new analysis never re-pays the forward pass. Per-position GPU accumulation uses `index_add_` rather than CPU scatter, and a per-model batch cap (`C2S: 2`, `UCE: 8`, `MaxToki: 8`) protects a shared 80 GB GPU from OOM on large LM heads.

The same cache also stores per-feature **firing frequency** vectors (`freq_<i>`), exported separately as `freq_ts3.json` for the annotated-vs-unannotated checks downstream.

Sources: [cell_cka.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cell_cka.py#L20-L90), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L17-L17)

## Cross-Model CKA at Matched Depth

The pairing statistic is **linear CKA** on mean-centered embeddings:

```
CKA(X, Y) = ||YᵀX||² / (||XᵀX|| · ||YᵀY|| + ε)
```

Because both Gram matrices are `d × d` regardless of each model's `d_model` (256 to 2,560+), the statistic is directly comparable across architectures — that is the entire reason CKA was chosen over Procrustes or plain correlation. The builder phase (`cell_cka.py --cka`) loads every cached `_emb.npz`, forms the 10×10 matrix at each of the five **relative depths** (0/25/50/75/100%), in *both* residual and SAE space, and writes `cka_ts3.json` with a `layer_at_depth` map so readers know exactly which absolute layer each depth slot corresponds to.

> [!TIP]
> The depth-to-block mapping is the one genuinely subtle indexing decision here. For a five-layer (depth-matched) run, cache key `res_<r>` *is* relative depth `r`. But an `--all-layers` run saves every block, so relative depth `r` must be read at block `depth_matched(n_layers)[r]` — reading key `r` directly would silently compare blocks 0–4. This exact mislabeling shipped once: the site's CKA heatmap originally called blocks 0–4 "0–100% depth" until the fix (decision 16); the paper's CKA numbers were computed from a different file and were always correct.

`depth_matched(n)` itself is three lines: pick `round(f · (n−1))` for f ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}, deduplicate (small models can collapse slots), sort — the agreed spec that removes the layer confound between an 8-layer and a 33-layer model.

Sources: [cell_cka.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cell_cka.py#L93-L130), [layers.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/layers.py#L1-L19), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L262-L296), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L31-L36)

## Within-Model Depth Structure: the Layer×Layer Matrix

A companion script, `cka_layers.py`, turns CKA inward: for each model it loads the saved position-level activations from every layer (`layer_XX_activations.npy`, memory-mapped, position-aligned because they came from one forward pass), subsamples 30,000 shared positions, and produces an `[n_layers × n_layers]` CKA matrix per model in `cka_layers.json`. Unlike the cross-model analysis this is descriptive — no null — but it is diagnostic: **block structure** means stages where the representation is stable, and the sharpest adjacent-layer drop (the minimum consecutive CKA) marks where the model reorganizes. The script prints that sharpest transition per model directly to stdout.

Sources: [cka_layers.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_layers.py#L1-L6), [cka_layers.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_layers.py#L40-L52), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L15-L15)

## The Nulls: Cell Shuffle and the Random Dictionary

`cka_svd_null.py` is the rigor pass that the geometry claims must survive. **Part (A)** asks whether cross-model CKA is meaningful or just what any two 2,000-cell embeddings give: for each of all 45 model pairs (the ten-model list, explicitly "not a hand-picked four"), it computes the real CKA at mid-depth, then recomputes it 20 times with the rows of one embedding permuted — a permutation that destroys cell-to-cell correspondence while preserving each embedding's marginal structure. **Part (B)** asks whether the SAE's variance-explained edge is real or mere overcompleteness, comparing at matched sparsity `k = 32`: top-32 SVD variance, the *trained* SAE's stored `var_explained`, and an **untrained random-init TopK dictionary** of identical shape (seed 0) encoding and decoding 20,000 positions.

| Claim | Null / control | Permutations | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-model CKA is cell-aligned | shuffle rows of one embedding (per pair) | 20 draws each | every pair above floor; worst pair **43×** |
| SAE beats PCA | top-k SVD at the same k; untrained random dictionary | "none needed" | SAE > top-32 PCA in **all ten** models, +0.02 (tGPT) to +0.55 (Geneformer-V2) |

Both blocks land in one `cka_svd_null.json`, which `audit_manuscript_derived.py` re-checks against the manuscript. The decision log formalizes this as its per-claim null table: CKA gets the cell shuffle; SAE-vs-PCA needs no permutation count because its comparator *is* the null.

Sources: [cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py#L17-L49), [cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py#L51-L81), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L74-L95), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L16-L16)

## The SVD Side: Three Escalating Tests of the SAE

The SVD analyses form a deliberate escalation, each closing the loophole of the previous one:

1. **Alignment (`svd_vs_sae.py`)** — SVD of the centered residual on a 150k-position subsample; each SAE decoder direction (unit-norm column of `W_dec`) is called *novel* if its max |cos| against the top SVD axes is < 0.7. This reproduces the prior literature's "X% invisible" framing.
2. **Random-dictionary control (`cka_svd_null.py` part B)** — an untrained dictionary of the same shape provides the "what would a random direction do" counterfactual, exposing test 1's flaw.
3. **Capacity-matched projection sweep (`svd_projection_k.py`)** — written for reviewer R2-Major-2: for every k ∈ {1…256}, the mean projected energy `||B_k v||²` of each SAE direction onto the top-k PCA subspace, plotted against the **isotropic random baseline k/d** (a random unit direction has exactly k/d energy in any k-dimensional subspace). Rising above k/d at every k means SAE directions preferentially concentrate on high-variance axes; the curve reaching 1 as k → d means SVD *can* span them given enough axes.

Implementation note on scaling: test 3 estimates the top-k basis via the `d × d` covariance **eigendecomposition** (`np.linalg.eigh`) rather than full SVD, avoiding the tall `U` factor — on 100,000 rows of a 2,560-dimensional residual this is the difference between feasible and not. `make_figS1.py` renders the result as supplementary Fig S1, whose own title states the conclusion: *"SAE directions are reachable by SVD given enough axes, not invisible to it"* — the SAE's edge is sparse allocation at fixed k.

| Test | Output | Consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `svd_vs_sae.py` (per model, mid layer) | `svd/{model}_L{NN}_svd.json` — pct_novel, mean_maxcos, svd_var_at_k, sae_var | atlas assembly |
| `svd_projection_k.py` (all ten models) | `svd_projection_k.json` — sae_proj, k/d baseline, svd_var_at_k per k | `make_figS1.py` → Fig S1 |

> [!TIP]
> Docstring drift is a real hazard when reading these files: `cell_cka.py`'s docstring still says "between the seven models" and "7x7-per-depth", while its `MODELS` constant and the null script carry all ten (45 pairs). Trust the `MODELS` list and the null script's `ALL`/`PAIRS` constants — the seven-model wording is a relic of the original 3-tissue run before the catalogues were extended.

Sources: [svd_vs_sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/svd_vs_sae.py#L16-L59), [svd_projection_k.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/svd_projection_k.py#L1-L14), [svd_projection_k.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/svd_projection_k.py#L21-L60), [make_figS1.py](pipeline/scripts/make_figS1.py#L1-L4), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L96-L109), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L67-L67)

## Geometry the Data Already Has: the Raw-Expression Anchor

The sharpest finding in this family is a deflationary one. `raw_expression_baseline.py` computes linear CKA between the **2,000-HVG raw expression matrix** (log1p CP10k, no model) and every layer of every model's residual stream, each against a 20-draw cell-shuffle floor. The models' geometry agrees with the raw data's (CKA 0.18–0.63), and PCA-50 of the raw expression decodes tissue (0.94) and cell type (0.83–0.85) about as well as the models' middle layers. The decision log's reading: this is **geometry the data already has** — the models largely preserve an arrangement that a plain PCA recovers, rather than inventing a new one. The full decodability side of this comparison belongs to [Co-Expression Baseline Comparisons](15-co-expression-baseline-comparisons); here it matters as the anchor that keeps CKA claims honest.

Sources: [raw_expression_baseline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/raw_expression_baseline.py#L1-L11), [raw_expression_baseline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/raw_expression_baseline.py#L53-L76), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L110-L128)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
```

The published file inventory for this page, from the result-files map:

| File | KB | Written by | Read by | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cka_ts3.json` | 6 | `cell_cka.py` | `atlas_assemble.py` | 10×10 residual + SAE-space CKA at five relative depths, `layer_at_depth` map |
| `cka_layers.json` | 26 | `cka_layers.py` | `atlas_assemble.py` | per-model layer×layer CKA matrix |

Everything the site and manuscript use flows through `atlas_assemble.py` into `atlas_full_notf.json` — the geometry blocks are embedded there like every other panel, and the audit re-derives them from these files and nothing else.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L10-L17), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L67-L67), [cell_cka.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cell_cka.py#L100-L130)

## Running It Yourself

These are GPU-stage analyses except for the plotting. After the standard corpus build ([Quick Start](2-quick-start), [Model Adapter Contract](6-model-adapter-contract)), the documented sequence is:

```bash
cd pipeline/atlas_h100
bash run_downstream_fixed.sh          # cell embeddings, CKA, probes, SVD, explorer
# then svd_vs_sae.py (mid layer of each model); copy outputs to
# outputs/atlas/comparative/svd/  and  outputs/atlas/comparative/gsea_annot.json
```

`svd_projection_k.py`, `cka_svd_null.py` and `cka_layers.py` read only saved artifacts — feature catalogs, `sae_L{NN}.pt` checkpoints, memory-mapped activations, cached embeddings — and root themselves via `ATLAS_OUT` (the corrected re-run used `ATLAS_OUT=out_fixed`; see [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run)). On the laptop side, `make_figS1.py` needs only `ATLAS_BASE` and `outputs/atlas/comparative/svd_projection_k.json`, and `audit_all.py` re-derives every published geometry number from the shipped result files — no GPU required.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L107-L127), [svd_projection_k.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/svd_projection_k.py#L10-L14), [cka_svd_null.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/cka_svd_null.py#L17-L22), [make_figS1.py](pipeline/scripts/make_figS1.py#L8-L10)

# Concept Matrices and Backbone Detection



This page covers the **local analysis stage** that runs after GPU extraction completes: pure-CPU scripts that turn SAE feature catalogs into concept matrices — a concept × model view of what each foundation model encodes — and then detect the *backbone*: the set of biological concepts shared across models, validated against nulls. The deeper statistical philosophy behind the annotators and nulls lives in [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation) and [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim); here we walk the concrete implementation.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L48-L50), [METHODS.md](/docs/METHODS.md#L38-L46)

## Inputs and the Shared Annotator Core

Every script in this stage consumes the same two inputs. The first is per-layer **feature catalogs** (`feature_catalog_L*.json`), one per model-layer, each holding per-feature `top_genes` lists (the catalog keeps the top 20 genes ranked by mean activation), the alive-feature count `n_alive`, dictionary width `d_sae`, and the layer index. The second is the **gene-set library**: GO_BP, Reactome and KEGG sets (Enrichr via gseapy), TRRUST edges, STRING v12 PPIs (score ≥ 700), and a 16,205-gene background.

Sources: [METHODS.md](/docs/METHODS.md#L23-L28), [METHODS.md](/docs/METHODS.md#L38-L42)

Two annotators dominate everything downstream, and the scripts in this stage implement them with a common skeleton: build a gene → term inverted index, count overlaps between each feature's top genes and each candidate term, then test with a one-sided statistic and Benjamini-Hochberg correction at α = 0.05.

| | Permissive annotator | Calibrated annotator |
|---|---|---|
| Top genes used | 5 | 10 |
| Minimum overlap | ≥ 2 | ≥ 3 |
| Statistic | Fisher exact (greater) | Hypergeometric survival |
| Databases | GO_BP, Reactome, KEGG, **STRING, TRRUST** | GO_BP, Reactome, KEGG only (**no PPI/TF sets**) |
| Set-size filter | 5–500 genes | 5–200 genes (curated sets) |
| Output per feature | list of qualifying terms | set of qualifying terms |
| Implementations | `alllayer_matrix.py`, `alllayer_concepts.py`, `topn_sweep.py` | `recalibrate_final.py`, `degree_null.py`, `depth_backbone.py` |

A recurring catalog-resolution rule appears in nearly every script: prefer the all-layers directory (`outputs/atlas/alllayer_cat/<model>/`) and fall back to the depth-matched five-layer run (`outputs/atlas/ts3_out/<model>/`) if the all-layer catalogs are absent. The "mid layer" is always the **median element** of the layer-sorted catalog list, so models with different depths (8–33 layers) compare at a consistent relative position.

Sources: [recalibrate_final.py](/pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L59-L64), [alllayer_matrix.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_matrix.py#L73-L77), [METHODS.md](/docs/METHODS.md#L32-L36)

## Building the Concept Matrices

The stage produces three matrix artifacts with distinct scopes, all derived from the permissive annotator:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CAT["feature_catalog_L*.json<br/>alllayer_cat / ts3_out"] --> PERM["Permissive annotator<br/>top-5 · Fisher+BH · 5 DBs"]
    PERM --> MID["matrix_ts3_string.json<br/>mid-layer concept × model"]
    PERM --> ALL["matrix_alllayer.json<br/>union over EVERY layer"]
    PERM --> PL["perlayer_concepts.json<br/>concept set per model per layer"]
    ALL --> ASM["atlas_assemble.py<br/>(prefers matrix_alllayer)"]
    MID -- "carries axis/params/<br/>var_explained forward" --> ALL
    ASM --> SITE["atlas_full_notf.json"]
```

`alllayer_matrix.py` answers "what is a model's *full* concept repertoire across depth?" It runs the identical top-5 Fisher+BH annotator on **every** layer, then unions the per-layer term sets. Its output schema is deliberately compatible with the mid-layer matrix: `term_count` maps each term to total feature-hits summed across layers (the keys *are* the all-layer concept set), `annot_rate` back-solves `n_annot` from the **mean** of per-layer rates (keeping `n_feat` at the mid-layer `d_sae` so totals don't balloon), and axis/params/var-explained fields are copied from the mid matrix for continuity. It also writes `perlayer_concepts.json`, the full per-model, per-layer concept sets.

Sources: [alllayer_matrix.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_matrix.py#L2-L10), [alllayer_matrix.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_matrix.py#L86-L110), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L48-L50)

`alllayer_concepts.py` is the depth-parity variant: it annotates only the **five depth-matched layers** (0/25/50/75/100% of depth), selecting them by index with `round(x·(len−1)/4)` whenever a model has more than six catalogs, and reports per-layer counts, mid-layer counts, and the union. Finally, `atlas_assemble.py` — the assembler for the site's embedded data — **prefers `matrix_alllayer.json` over the mid-layer matrix** when present, deriving coverage, the universality spectrum (concepts by how many models encode them), and the universal core from the chosen matrix.

Sources: [alllayer_concepts.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_concepts.py#L1-L6), [alllayer_concepts.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_concepts.py#L68-L83), [atlas_assemble.py](/pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L63-L98)

> [!TIP]
> `alllayer_matrix.py` unions term *keys* across layers but keeps `feat_terms` (per-feature term assignments) from the mid matrix only — firing-rate and richness statistics stay per-feature-at-mid-layer while coverage becomes depth-wide. Reading the docstring before the schema prevents a common misreading of `n_feat`/`n_annot` in this file.

## Detecting the Shared Backbone

Backbone detection runs exclusively under the **calibrated annotator** at the mid layer. The chain that converged on it is recorded as three result files: `recalibrate.json` and `recalibrate2.json` (two grid searches over annotator settings against the random-gene null), then `recalibrate_final.py`, which computes the honest universality picture — per-model concept sets, the shared-by-k spectrum for k = 1…10, the all-10 core identities, and the ≥8-of-10 backbone, each compared to a random-gene null spectrum (30 permutations).

Sources: [recalibrate_final.py](/pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L1-L4), [recalibrate_final.py](/pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L17), [recalibrate_final.py](/pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_final.py#L68-L93), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L60-L62)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load mid-layer catalogs<br/>(median of layer-sorted list)"] --> B["Annotate each feature:<br/>top-10 genes ∩ background,<br/>≥3 in one curated set ≤200 genes"]
    B --> C["Hypergeometric sf → BH < 0.05<br/>= one concept set per model"]
    C --> D["Count in how many of the 10<br/>models each concept appears"]
    D --> E["Sharing tiers ≥7 / ≥8 / ≥9 / =10"]
    E --> F{"Beats nulls?"}
    F -- "yes" --> G["backbone_terms.json<br/>fold · z · empirical p"]
    F -- "no" --> H["claim retracted"]
    RN["random-gene null ×250"] --> F
    DN["degree-matched null ×250"] --> F
```

Two robustness scripts harden the result. `recalibrate_robust.py` sweeps five calibrated configurations (varying top-N, overlap minimum, max set size, and an odds-ratio floor) × four sharing thresholds (≥7/8/9/10), reporting real-vs-null fold per cell — showing the backbone is not an argmax over one lucky configuration — and additionally classifies every ≥8 backbone concept as **housekeeping** (translation, splicing, proteasome, OXPHOS, cell cycle, … matched by keyword) versus **specific** (immune, signalling, tissue). `backbone_terms.py` then fixes a presentation bug: the site's `shared_ge8_terms` list had been truncated to 40 entries when written, so a page titled "78 shared concepts" could only display 40; this script recomputes and stores *every* backbone concept at each tier with its source database, deliberately running **no null itself** — folds and p-values come from `stats_final.py` / `degree_null.py`, which share the same annotator.

Sources: [recalibrate_robust.py](/pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_robust.py#L1-L7), [recalibrate_robust.py](/pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_robust.py#L84-L91), [backbone_terms.py](/pipeline/scripts/backbone_terms.py#L2-L10), [backbone_terms.py](/pipeline/scripts/backbone_terms.py#L74-L80)

A separate composition analysis (`paper_draft/analysis/backbone_composition/`) classes the ~96 backbone concepts by the genes behind each match — protein synthesis, other housekeeping, or specific — grouped into biological programmes. The composition and housekeeping split together temper the headline: most of the backbone is ubiquitous cellular machinery, which is exactly why the nulls matter.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L11), [recalibrate_robust.py](/pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_robust.py#L122-L130)

## Nulls and Depth Robustness for the Backbone

Every backbone claim is paired with a null in `outputs/atlas/comparative/`:

| Null | Script | Permutations | What it controls for | Result file |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Uniform random-gene (tiers) | `stats_final.py` | 250 | chance annotation of random top-10 lists | `stats_final.json` |
| **Degree-matched** random-gene | `degree_null.py` | 250 | gene "popularity" (gene-set membership degree, 40 quantile bins) | `degree_null.json` |
| Random-gene configuration sweep | `recalibrate_robust.py` | 20 per config | annotator-parameter luck | `recalibrate_robust.json` |
| All-layer core null | `alllayer_null.py` | 20 (arg) | the retracted all-layer union claim | `alllayer_null.json` |
| Backbone × depth null | `depth_backbone.py` → `depth_backbone_fast.py` | 20 → 250 | mid-layer artefact accusation | `depth_backbone.json` |

Sources: [stats_final.py](/pipeline/scripts/stats_final.py#L1-L7), [stats_final.py](/pipeline/scripts/stats_final.py#L24), [degree_null.py](/pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py#L1-L8), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L20)

The degree-matched null is the strongest of these: instead of drawing uniformly from the background, each real top-gene is replaced by a random gene in the **same membership-degree bin**, so high-degree genes that are trivially "hittable" cannot inflate the backbone. If the calibrated backbone still beats this null, it is not a gene-abundance artifact.

Sources: [degree_null.py](/pipeline/scripts/degree_null.py#L39-L47), [METHODS.md](/docs/METHODS.md#L48-L55)

Two historical claims about the concept matrices were retracted by nulls from this stage, and the scripts keep the evidence: `random_null.py` showed the naive mid-layer "shared by all ten models" core does not survive random-gene annotation, and `alllayer_null.py` targeted the retracted headline of "~2,000 concepts shared by all ten models" — an **all-layer union** built by intersecting per-model unions across every layer. That script mirrors the real procedure exactly on the null side: random genes are annotated per layer with each model's per-layer feature counts, unioned per model, then intersected across all ten models, yielding a z-score and fold-over-null for the real core.

Sources: [alllayer_null.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py#L1-L8), [alllayer_null.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py#L110-L133), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L58)

`depth_backbone.py` pre-empts the reviewer question "is the ~78-concept ≥8/10 backbone a mid-layer artefact?" by recomputing backbone tiers at five depth fractions (layer chosen by index `round(f·(n−1))`), with `ge8_terms` membership tracked per depth and Jaccard stability computed against the mid-layer backbone. Its replacement, `depth_backbone_fast.py`, raises the null to 250 permutations and adds a safeguard worth studying: it first reproduces the stored run's observed counts exactly and **refuses to write the output file if any count differs** — the speedup must provably change nothing about the science.

Sources: [depth_backbone.py](/pipeline/scripts/depth_backbone.py#L1-L7), [depth_backbone.py](/pipeline/scripts/depth_backbone.py#L107-L115), [depth_backbone_fast.py](/pipeline/scripts/depth_backbone_fast.py#L1-L13), [depth_backbone_fast.py](/pipeline/scripts/depth_backbone_fast.py#L100-L140)

Finally, two sensitivity sweeps close the loop on annotator choices: `topn_sweep.py` re-annotates every mid layer at top-5/10/15/20 genes, recording annotation rate, distinct concept count, and median odds ratio, while `kegg_robust.json` re-runs the backbone with GO_BP and Reactome only.

Sources: [topn_sweep.py](/pipeline/scripts/topn_sweep.py#L1-L5), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L47), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L69)

## The Sparse Annotator: One Optimization, Adopted Everywhere

Permutation testing is the computational bottleneck — 250 permutations × 10 models × thousands of features — and the naive per-feature Python loop with `fisher_exact`/`hypergeom` calls per candidate term dominated runtime. The stage's shared fix is a **sparse incidence-matrix product**: build a genes × terms CSR matrix `M` from the gene-set library, encode each batch of features as a features × genes matrix `F`, then compute `F @ M` once — overlap counts for every feature-term pair materialize in a single sparse multiplication (~50× faster than the loop, verified to produce identical sets). The same trick underlies `alllayer_null.py` and `depth_backbone_fast.py`, and the latter adds one more optimization: sorting catalogs by the layer index parsed from the *filename* instead of opening each ~file to read its `"layer"` field, avoiding ~700 MB of JSON parsing before any real work.

Sources: [alllayer_null.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py#L42-L55), [alllayer_null.py](/pipeline/scripts/alllayer_null.py#L63-L84), [depth_backbone_fast.py](/pipeline/scripts/depth_backbone_fast.py#L56-L78)

> [!TIP]
> When porting these scripts, preserve the equality guard pattern from `depth_backbone_fast.py`: any performance rewrite of a statistical pipeline should first *reproduce stored observed values* and abort on mismatch. This repo's credibility argument ("nulls must be reported properly") extends to its own refactors.

## Where These Artifacts Flow

The matrices and backbone files are consumed downstream by the site assembler, figure makers, supplement tables, and the audit system: `matrix_alllayer.json` feeds `atlas_assemble.py` plus the controls scripts; `backbone_terms.json` feeds the atlas hypothesis block and figure generation; `depth_backbone.json`, `recalibrate_robust.json` and `alllayer_null.json` are checked by `audit_manuscript_core.py`, `audit_supplement.py` and `audit_manuscript_derived.py`, which assert manuscript numbers match these files. The backbone's strongest external validation — replication on the held-out corpus under the calibrated annotator (passes, unlike the permissive core) — is detailed in [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test).

Sources: [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L12), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L22), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L35-L36), [RESULTS.md](/docs/RESULTS.md#L48-L48)

Suggested next steps in the catalog: see how the two annotators were chosen and why, in [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation); how the null machinery generalizes beyond the backbone, in [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim); and how every result file connects to the manuscript, in [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map).

# Literature and Perturbation Evidence



This page documents the stage of the comparative-atlas pipeline that tests the released gene-pair predictions against evidence the models never saw during annotation: published literature and causal perturbation data. Where the held-out TRRUST test (see [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test)) establishes that the predictor is *calibrated*, this stage asks two strictly independent questions of the same prediction list — do the pairs show up in the literature more than chance, and does perturbing one gene actually move the other? It also governs the *novelty* claim: which confident pairs have never been co-mentioned anywhere, and therefore constitute genuine candidate discoveries.

Sources: [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L1-L19), [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L1-L18)

## Position in the Evidence Chain

Everything on this page consumes one artifact: `hypothesis_pairs_full.json`, the 4,485-pair released prediction list produced by `hypothesis_trrust3.py` (the final stage of the TRRUST chain). Three analysis scripts read that list, each against a different external dataset, and write compact JSON results into `outputs/atlas/comparative/`. Those result files then feed two consumers: `atlas_hypothesis_block.py`, which regenerates the site's prediction panels, and `make_fig5.py`, which renders panel C ("Independent evidence") of the manuscript figure. The diagram below traces this flow; the dashed edge marks the one *in-place mutation* in the chain — the PubMed script writes co-mention counts back into the released pair list.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["External evidence — dated bulk files, no live queries"]
        PM["NCBI gene2pubmed<br/>+ Homo_sapiens.gene_info<br/>(2026-09-11)"]
        PS["Replogle 2022 CRISPRi<br/>Perturb-seq: K562 + RPE1"]
    end
    PF["hypothesis_pairs_full.json<br/>4,485 released pairs"] --> PUB["hypothesis_pubmed.py"]
    PF --> PT["hypothesis_perturb.py"]
    PF --> SB["hypothesis_studybias.py"]
    PM --> PUB
    PM --> SB
    PS --> PT
    PS --> SB
    PUB --> PB["hypothesis_pubmed.json"]
    PT --> PJ["hypothesis_perturb.json"]
    SB --> SJ["hypothesis_studybias.json"]
    PUB -. "adds co_mentions in place" .-> PF
    PB --> HB["atlas_hypothesis_block.py"]
    PJ --> HB
    HB --> AT["atlas_full_notf.json<br/>'hypothesis' block"]
    AT --> SITE["index.html panels"]
    PB --> F5["make_fig5.py — panel C"]
    PJ --> F5
```

The repository's result-file map confirms this wiring precisely: `hypothesis_pairs_full.json` is written by `hypothesis_trrust3.py` and then `hypothesis_pubmed.py`, and is read by the site assembler, the supplement tables, the study-bias coverage check and the perturbation script; `hypothesis_perturb.json` and `hypothesis_pubmed.json` are consumed by `atlas_hypothesis_block.py`, `make_supp_tables.py`, `make_fig5.py` and the manuscript audits.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L37-L46), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L24-L26), [make_fig5.py](pipeline/scripts/make_fig5.py#L19-L23)

## Independent Evidence I: Literature Co-Mention

### Data and identifier mapping

The literature test runs on NCBI's `gene2pubmed` bulk file together with `Homo_sapiens.gene_info.gz`, deliberately chosen over live PubMed queries so the analysis is reproducible from a *dated* file rather than from a moving API. Symbols are first mapped to NCBI GeneIDs — current symbols plus synonyms, so older literature referencing a gene's former name is not silently dropped — and only pairs whose genes both map are testable. The script builds a gene→papers adjacency, reports how many gene–paper links it recovered and the median papers per gene, then counts the observed co-mentions for every predicted pair.

Sources: [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L2-L3), [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L37-L65)

### The publication-count-preserving null

The question is not "are these pairs co-mentioned?" — famous gene pairs always are — but "are they co-mentioned more than chance *given how much each gene has been studied*?" The null answers this by construction: each gene keeps its publication count **exactly**, and the papers are reassigned at random via a degree-preserving shuffle of the gene→paper bipartite graph (stub matching on the paper side fixes paper sizes too). A pair therefore cannot score merely because both of its genes are heavily studied — the exact confound a naive enrichment test would absorb. The permutation loop recounts co-mentions per pair for `NPERM` (default 200) shuffles and reports fold, z and the empirical p-value `(count + 1) / (N + 1)`.

Sources: [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L7-L11), [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L84-L100)

> [!TIP]
> The null is made bitwise-reproducible by numbering papers in **sorted PMID order** rather than Python set-iteration order. Set iteration randomises string hashing per process, which silently permuted the null under a fixed seed: the same data produced z = 40.5 on one run and 36.6 on the next. The in-code comment records the team's standard verbatim: *"a number nobody can reproduce is not a number we can report."* Any new null you add to this pipeline must pass the same test — run it twice, in fresh processes, before trusting it.

### The mega-paper cap

Papers annotating more than 60 genes are excluded from the co-mention count, and the *observed* statistic is recomputed under the same cap for a like-for-like comparison. The rationale is documented at the point of use: without the cap, a handful of proteomic and GWAS papers annotate thousands of genes at once and almost every pair becomes nominally co-mentioned. Importantly, the uncapped figure is **stored in the result JSON rather than discarded** — it is part of the reported result, not a printed-and-forgotten diagnostic. The block below summarises what `hypothesis_pubmed.json` exposes:

| Field group | Contents | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| `source`, `null`, `n_perm`, `mega_paper_cap` | provenance of data, null design, permutation count, cap threshold | audit and reproduction |
| `n_pairs_testable`, `observed_pairs_comentioned`, `observed_total_comentions` | coverage of the pair list and observed signal | headline validation numbers |
| `null_pairs_comentioned_mean` / `null_sd`, `fold`, `z`, `p_emp` | null distribution and the three reported statistics | comparison against chance |
| `observed_pairs_comentioned_uncapped`, `observed_pct_comentioned_uncapped` | the same counts with no 60-gene cap | kept deliberately as part of the result |
| `n_never_comentioned`, `n_never_but_both_studied`, `never_*` lists | novelty counts and candidate lists (150 / 60 item caps) | the discovery output |

Sources: [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L131-L147), [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L138-L152)

## Independent Evidence II: Causal Perturbation Evidence

### Read-out and null design

The perturbation test is, in the words of its own header, "the only test here that is neither a database nor the literature": if a model places genes A and B in the same feature, knocking A down should move B. The data is Replogle et al. 2022 genome-wide CRISPRi pseudobulk — K562 with 11,258 perturbations × 8,248 measured genes, and RPE1 as a replication cell line — loaded as normalised expression changes relative to controls, with multi-construct perturbations of the same gene averaged into one row. The read-out is deliberately rank-based: for an ordered pair (A perturbed, B measured), the statistic is the percentile of |ΔB| *within row A* — among all measured genes, how strongly did B respond? Because it is a within-row rank, the statistic is immune to how globally disruptive perturbation A is (essential genes move everything). A pair counts as a hit when B lands in the top 5% most-moved genes (`TOPQ = 0.05`).

Sources: [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L2-L18), [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L30-L31)

The null handles the two confound axes symmetrically — row effects by ranking, column effects by matching: the measured gene B is replaced by a random gene matched on its own *responsiveness* (its mean |Δ| across all perturbations, binned into 20 quantiles), so a gene cannot score merely by being reactive to everything. Both observed and null statistics are reported as top-5% hit rates, yielding `top5pct_fold`, `z_top5` and `p_top5` per cell line. The two nulls on this page eliminate complementary confounds, which is exactly why the pipeline runs both:

| Design decision | Literature co-mention | Perturb-seq response |
|---|---|---|
| Held fixed per draw | each gene's paper count; paper sizes (≤ 60 genes) | perturbation row A's response profile (within-row rank) |
| Randomised | paper→gene assignment on the bipartite graph | measured gene B → responsiveness-matched replacement (20 bins) |
| Confound eliminated | both genes being heavily studied | B reactive to every perturbation; A globally disruptive |
| Headline statistic | co-mentioned pairs vs null mean (fold, z, p_emp) | top-5% hit rate vs null rate (fold, z, p_emp) |

Sources: [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L13-L15), [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L48-L76), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L67-L70)

### Does model agreement raise the causal hit rate?

Beyond the aggregate test, the script repeats the analysis conditioned on the number of models that predicted each pair (`by_n_models`), testing whether agreement raises the causal hit rate as it does for TRRUST. Crucially, each k-models subset gets its **own** responsiveness-matched null built from its own genes — not a reuse of the global null — so each fold is internally valid. Subsets with fewer than 30 pairs are skipped rather than reported.

Sources: [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L16), [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L106-L137)

### The study-bias stratum analysis

The released pair list over-represents well-studied genes, so the pipeline asks whether that is a property of the models or of the filter. The motivation numbers are stated in the script header: the models feature 4,003 genes with fewer than 5 papers, but the pair list at W ≥ 5 retains only 141 of them (3.5%, against 16.8% of well-studied genes). Direct causal validation of understudied genes is blocked — 752 of the 793 protein-coding understudied genes the models feature are absent from the Replogle screen entirely (0.4% of the perturbed set, against 9.9% of all protein-coding genes). The strongest answerable question is therefore: *among testable pairs, does the causal signal decline as the responding gene becomes less studied?* To avoid pre-filtering low-abundance genes, the co-firing threshold drops from ≥ 5 to ≥ 2 features with a ≥ 2-model bar, and every pair carries its responding gene's publication count. Results are stratified as unmapped / <25 / 25–49 / 50–99 / 100–399 / ≥400 papers, each stratum against its own matched null; a flat profile licenses extrapolation to genes no external resource covers, a declining profile does not.

Sources: [hypothesis_studybias.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_studybias.py#L4-L15), [hypothesis_studybias.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_studybias.py#L35-L36), [hypothesis_studybias.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_studybias.py#L164-L168)

## Novelty: From Calibration to a Candidate List

The novelty half of `hypothesis_pubmed.py` is the payoff of the whole evidence chain, and its justification is worth reading carefully: among pairs the models predict confidently, those **never** co-mentioned anywhere are the candidates for genuinely unexplored biology — and this claim "is only meaningful because (1) and the TRRUST test establish that the predictor is calibrated: an uncorroborated pair from a validated predictor is a lead, whereas the same list from an unvalidated one is noise." The candidate lists are sorted by confidence (models, then weight), and a stricter `never_but_both_studied` subset keeps only pairs where both genes have ≥ 20 papers each — studied genes that have simply never been put together.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    P["Predicted pair (A, B)<br/>co-fires in SAE features"] --> T["TRRUST held-out test<br/>(page 11)"]
    T -->|"establishes calibration"| C["Predictor credibility:<br/>precision above degree-matched null"]
    P --> L["Literature co-mention<br/>(PubMed bipartite null)"]
    L --> V["Validation + novelty counts"]
    P --> Q["Causal Perturb-seq test<br/>(within-row percentile)"]
    Q --> W["K562 + RPE1 causal support"]
    C -.->|"licenses"| N["NEVER co-mentioned pairs<br/>= candidate new biology"]
    V -.->|"defines"| N
```

The released list itself is one flat JSON: 4,485 pairs, each with `[gene A, gene B, n_models, models, weight]` at generation time, augmented in place by the PubMed run with `co_mentions` and per-gene `papers` counts, and by the site assembler with a `same_family` flag. The concept relationships above are the mental model to keep: novelty is a *conditional* claim, downstream of both the calibration test and the literature scan.

Sources: [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L13-L16), [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L156-L168), [data/hypothesis_pairs_full.json](data/hypothesis_pairs_full.json#L1), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L38)

## Robustness of the Prediction Result

Each headline statistic on this page is bracketed by a variant that tries to break it. The variants re-use the same configuration-model null throughout and are summarised here; the reviewer-facing deep dive lives in [Reviewer Robustness Analyses](16-reviewer-robustness-analyses), and the TRRUST stages they modify belong to [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test).

| Variant | Script | What it changes | Guards against |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 no same-family pairs | `hypothesis_robust.py` | drops stem-suffix paralog pairs (ACTB/ACTG2, S100A11/S100A4) | result carried by gene families, not regulation |
| R2 firing features only | `hypothesis_robust.py` | keeps features above per-model median `activation_frequency` | near-zero-expression genes clustering together |
| R3 stricter evidence | `hypothesis_robust.py` | per-pair bar raised from ≥ 5 to ≥ 10 features | threshold choice driving the effect |
| R2+R1 combined | `hypothesis_robust.py` | both filters at once | interaction of the two artefacts |
| Equal budget | `hypothesis_sizematched.py` | every model scored on the same N = 50,707 top-weight pairs, plus rand-N draws | Fig 5A being a ranking of dictionary size, not quality |
| Single layer | `hypothesis_singlelayer.py` | co-firing graph from the mid-layer catalogue only, W ∈ {2, 5} | cross-layer aggregation inflating the result |
| Publication strata | `hypothesis_studybias.py` | perturbation test split by responding gene's fame | predictions working only for well-studied genes |

Two engineering details in this tier repay attention. First, the size-matched variant exists because graph sizes span four orders of magnitude (AIDO.Cell 2 pairs, C2S-Scale 147,728) and hit counts correlate with graph size at r = +0.90; models whose graphs are smaller than the budget are reported as *untestable*, not as failures. Second, the single-layer script is an act of provenance repair: the manuscript's "6.1× within a single layer" had been produced by a throwaway `/tmp` script that no longer existed, so this script was recovered from the session log and the two thresholds it silently used are now computed and stored explicitly.

Sources: [hypothesis_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_robust.py#L2-L10), [hypothesis_sizematched.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_sizematched.py#L2-L14), [hypothesis_singlelayer.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_singlelayer.py#L2-L16), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L62-L65)

## From Result Files to Site and Figure

The site never reads the analysis scripts' stdout — it reads a **derived block** regenerated from the canonical JSONs. `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` assembles the `hypothesis` key of `atlas_full_notf.json` from six result files, including the `independent` sub-block (literature and perturbation summaries), the full `pairs_all` matrix of every released pair with its `co_mentions` and `same_family` flag, and a `novelty` panel with example pairs. It edits only that one key, so re-running an analysis and re-injecting is sufficient to keep the public site true.

> [!TIP]
> The script exists because of a real incident: the site block was once hand-assembled, and after the literature null was made reproducible the page kept serving the old z = 40.48 while the manuscript said 34.7 — "the same class of drift the manuscript audit exists to catch, on the public half of the project." Note the two safety rails a maintainer should preserve: `--check` mode reports drift without writing (and exits non-zero, CI-friendly), and `diffs()` prints every changed leaf path so a rebuild says *what* moved, not just that it ran.

Two display guardrails in the assembly deserve emphasis for anyone extending the panels. When the corroboration null produced zero edges at some k, the stored fold would be astronomically meaningless, so `curve[k]["fold"]` is set to `None` rather than rendered — the figure prints "null = 0" instead of a number like "1.5e9×" that would be "the most confident claim on the page". And Figure 5 panel C places the three independent-evidence fold bars — literature co-mention, K562 and RPE1 perturbation — side by side against their own matched nulls, annotated "all p = 0.005", which is the empirical-p floor 1/(N+1) at NPERM = 200 described in the decision log's permutation policy.

Sources: [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L2-L11), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L54-L71), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L85-L112), [make_fig5.py](pipeline/scripts/make_fig5.py#L92-L114), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L102)

## Reproducing This Stage

All scripts resolve their base directory through the `ATLAS_BASE` environment variable (with a developer-specific default), so the stage runs anywhere the inputs are unpacked. Order matters: the TRRUST chain must run first because it produces both the released pair list and the five-model `PASSED` selection that the robustness and study-bias scripts consume; the PubMed run must precede the site-block rebuild because it annotates the pair list in place. The external inputs themselves are versioned release archives, not repository files — `gene2pubmed.gz` and the Replogle `.h5ad` files are fetched per the release procedure.

| Command | Key inputs (relative to `ATLAS_BASE`) | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `python scripts/hypothesis_trrust3.py [NPERM]` | feature catalogues (`alllayer_cat/` or `ts3_out/`), `genesets/` truth sets | `hypothesis_final.json`, `hypothesis_pairs_full.json` |
| `python scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py [NPERM]` | `outputs/atlas/pubmed/{gene2pubmed.gz, Homo_sapiens.gene_info.gz}` | `hypothesis_pubmed.json` + pairs file annotated in place |
| `python scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py [NPERM]` | `outputs/atlas/perturb/{K562_gwps_normalized_bulk_01.h5ad, rpe1_normalized_bulk_01.h5ad}` | `hypothesis_perturb.json` |
| `python scripts/hypothesis_studybias.py [NPERM]` | perturb + pubmed inputs + feature catalogues | `hypothesis_studybias.json` |
| `python scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py [--check]` | the `hypothesis_*.json` result files | drift report, or rewritten `atlas_full_notf.json` |
| `python scripts/make_fig5.py` | five hypothesis result JSONs | `figures/Fig5_hypothesis.png` |

Sources: [hypothesis_pubmed.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_pubmed.py#L22-L29), [hypothesis_perturb.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_perturb.py#L140-L145), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L74-L78)
