Permutation counts follow the project-wide policy recorded in the decision log: 500 rewirings for the per-model TRRUST test, 100 for the corroboration curve, and 200 for the robustness variants, literature, perturbation and publication-strata analyses; with N permutations the smallest attainable p is 1/(N+1), which is where most significant results sit. Once the stage is reproduced, the natural continuation is to see how much of this signal survives without any model at all in [Co-Expression Baseline Comparisons](15-co-expression-baseline-comparisons), then how the results are policed in [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks) and rendered into the public panels in [Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files).


# Co-Expression Baseline Comparisons



Every headline claim in this repository — the ≥8/10 shared concept backbone and the held-out TRRUST predictions from SAE co-firing graphs — has a paired no-model control: *what would the same statistic recover from gene–gene co-expression alone, computed on exactly the same cells?* This page documents that baseline subsystem: the backbone-level dictionary baseline (`coexpr_core_baseline.py`), the TRRUST-level comparison family (`coexpr_trrust.py`, `coexpr_degmatched.py`, `coexpr_rmatched.py`), the cell-level geometry counterpart (`raw_expression_baseline.py`), and the reviewer-hardening scripts in `review_10_coexpr/`. It sits in the **Local Analysis Stage** between literature evidence and the reviewer robustness suite, and it depends on the concepts from [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim) and [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test).

Sources: [coexpr_core_baseline.py](pipeline/scripts/coexpr_core_baseline.py#L1-L16), [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L2-L23)

## Why a No-Model Baseline Belongs Next to Every Claim

The repository enforces a strict discipline: a model earns credit only for signal that raw expression cannot produce. Co-expression is the natural adversary — neighboring genes in the same cell type correlate strongly, so top-correlated gene pairs or gene neighborhoods will trivially cluster into "concepts." The baselines therefore replicate the model pipeline's *read-out* (the calibrated annotator, the configuration-model null, the pair-key encoding) while swapping only the *data source* (Pearson correlation of log-normalized counts instead of SAE feature co-firing). All four baselines draw from the same 6,000-cell corpus (`tabula_3tissue_6k.h5ad`) and compare against the same ten-model co-firing cache, so every comparison is dimension-matched by construction.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CORPUS["6,000-cell corpus<br/>tabula_3tissue_6k.h5ad"] -->|"counts/10k → log1p → z-score"| CORR["Gene–gene Pearson r"]
    CORR --> BB["coexpr_core_baseline.py<br/>seed + 9 most correlated genes<br/>(backbone recall)"]
    CORR --> TR["coexpr_trrust.py<br/>global / node-matched top-N"]
    CORR --> DM["coexpr_degmatched.py<br/>greedy b-matching"]
    CORR --> RM["coexpr_rmatched.py<br/>per-bin TRRUST-rate null"]
    COFIRE["SAE co-firing graphs<br/>.cofire_cache.pkl<br/>(hypothesis_trrust3.py)"] --> BB
    COFIRE --> TR
    COFIRE --> DM
    COFIRE --> RM
    BB --> OUT1["outputs/atlas/comparative/<br/>coexpr_core_baseline.json"]
    TR --> OUT2["review JSON artifacts<br/>(paper_draft/analysis/…)"]
    DM --> OUT2
    RM --> OUT2
```

Sources: [coexpr_core_baseline.py](pipeline/scripts/coexpr_core_baseline.py#L30-L35), [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L8-L15), [coexpr_degmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_degmatched.py#L3-L15)

## Baseline One: Backbone Recovery Without a Model

`coexpr_core_baseline.py` asks the backbone question directly: does a dictionary built from gene–gene co-expression alone, with no model, recover the 78-concept backbone (the `>=8` tier of `backbone_terms.json`)? Each synthetic "feature" is a **seed gene plus its 9 most correlated genes** — Pearson correlation over the same 6,000 cells, on log1p CP10k-normalized counts, restricted to genes detected in ≥10 cells. The script then runs the *exact* calibrated annotator used by `stats_final.py`: top-10 genes per feature, requiring ≥3 genes in a curated GO/KEGG/Reactome set of ≤200 genes, hypergeometric test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction at α=0.05. Because the annotator code (constants `ALPHA=0.05, TOP=10, AMIN=3, MX=200`, the `bh()` and `annotate()` functions) is a line-for-line reuse, the only experimental variable is where the gene groups come from.

The script constructs two adversarial dictionaries per model and scores them alongside the real one. The **seed-matched** variant keeps each model's gene *choice* — one feature per live mid-layer feature, seeded with that feature's top gene — but replaces the model's grouping with co-expression neighbors. The **model-free** variant keeps only the count: the same number of features per model, seeded with genes drawn uniformly from detected genes. For each variant it records per-model backbone recall, and for each family of ten dictionaries it computes the ≥8/10 core (`K_CORE=8`) with size, overlap with the backbone, and **Jaccard similarity**. Results land in `outputs/atlas/comparative/coexpr_core_baseline.json` (72 KB, registered in `RESULTS.md` as "how much of the backbone needs no model"), including a per-backbone-term coverage counter across the seed-matched dictionaries.

> [!TIP]
> The annotator in this script is deliberately *not* reimplemented loosely — the docstring states "identical to stats_final.py", and the same `ALPHA/TOP/AMIN/MX` constants and hypergeometric+BH logic appear verbatim. This is what makes the comparison annotator-controlled: any difference in concept recovery is attributable to the dictionary source, never to a scoring discrepancy.

Sources: [coexpr_core_baseline.py](pipeline/scripts/coexpr_core_baseline.py#L1-L16), [coexpr_core_baseline.py](pipeline/scripts/coexpr_core_baseline.py#L33-L73), [coexpr_core_baseline.py](pipeline/scripts/coexpr_core_baseline.py#L93-L121), [coexpr_core_baseline.py](pipeline/scripts/coexpr_core_baseline.py#L126-L156), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L18)

## Baseline Two: Co-Expression Against TRRUST Under the Same Ruler

`coexpr_trrust.py` addresses gap "G1": do top co-expressed gene pairs recover held-out TRRUST edges as well as the SAE co-firing graphs, under the same configuration-model null? The script imports the repo's entire measurement apparatus — the docstring calls this the "same ruler" — with each element traced to its origin: co-firing graphs are the repo's own W≥5 graphs read from `.cofire_cache.pkl` (written by `hypothesis_trrust3.py`, sizes asserted equal to `hypothesis_sizematched.json:graph_sizes`); truth is TRRUST undirected with self-pairs dropped; pair keys pack unordered gene pairs as `i*2^21+j` int64 over the ten-model co-firing union; the null is `config_shuffle` copied **verbatim** from `hypothesis_trrust2.py:60-69` (degree-preserving stub matching, self-loops and duplicates removed); and the read-out is `p = (#null ≥ obs + 1)/(NPERM + 1)` with `fold = obs / null mean`.

Co-expression itself is computed three ways ("kinds") and the script supports selecting them: **pearson** (main), **spearman** (per-gene ranking with average ties), and **withincomp** (log-normalized values centered within each cell-type compartment, i.e. pooled within-compartment Pearson — controlling for the dominant compartment effect). Normalization is counts-per-10k over *all* genes, log1p, then restriction to the gene universe U (the co-firing union ∩ genes expressed in ≥10 cells); the 18,250-gene correlation matrix is built in row blocks of 512 in float32 with a 20,000-bin histogram over r to avoid materializing all pairs. Three matched comparisons are scored per kind: **(i) global top-N** at each model's published graph size and at the equal budget, **(ii) node-matched** — same genes, same N as each model's co-firing graph within U, with shared-pair counts and a Fisher exact test of cofire-vs-coexpr hit rates — and **(iii) overlap analyses** that split each co-firing graph by whether its pairs fall in the global top 1%/5% co-expressed, re-scoring each slice against a **masked null** (truth restricted to the same low-co-expression TRRUST edges), so the question becomes whether co-firing hits survive when co-expression is denied as an explanation.

> [!TIP]
> Every pair in this subsystem is keyed as `min(i,j)*2^21 + max(i,j)` — an unordered pair compressed into one int64. This makes TRRUST membership testing a single `np.isin` over sorted int64 arrays and lets the configuration null operate on packed keys without ever building Python pair objects. Any new baseline you add must reuse this encoding to stay comparable.

Sources: [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L7-L23), [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L74-L96), [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L177-L208), [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L273-L334), [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L335-L345)

## Baseline Three: Degree-Matched Graphs — the Strictest Like-for-Like

Global top-N comparisons can favor either side through size or degree effects, so `coexpr_degmatched.py` builds the strictest control: for each model, a co-expression graph on the **same genes** with **(nearly) the same degree sequence** and the **same number of pairs** as its co-firing graph. The mechanism is **greedy b-matching**: walk that gene set's candidate pairs in decreasing Pearson r and accept a pair only if both endpoints still have unused degree, where each gene's capacity equals its co-firing degree. Practically, a histogram over r (bins of 1e-4) selects a threshold yielding ~40× the target edge count (`CAND_MULT=40`); the greedy pass then runs, and if capacities remain unfilled, additional rounds re-correlate only among genes with free degree, descending below the first threshold (up to 12 rounds) — exact, because a pair touching a saturated gene can never be accepted later.

Each degree-matched graph and its co-firing twin are scored against TRRUST with 200 configuration-model rewirings under the shared read-out, and the script reports the pair overlap between the two graphs plus a Fisher exact test on their hit counts. Diagnostics in the output include the fill share (how many of the co-firing graph's edge slots co-expression could fill), the degree L1 unfilled share, and the minimum/median r of accepted pairs — so a reader can verify the baseline graph is genuinely high-quality co-expression, not a degenerate fallback.

Sources: [coexpr_degmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_degmatched.py#L1-L15), [coexpr_degmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_degmatched.py#L101-L170), [coexpr_degmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_degmatched.py#L131-L143)

## Baseline Four: The r-Matched Null

`coexpr_rmatched.py` inverts the question: instead of matching a baseline graph to the model, it asks how many TRRUST hits any graph would get **from its pairs' co-expression level alone**. All U pairs are binned by Pearson r (0.01-wide bins); within each bin the empirical TRRUST rate is `q_b = TRRUST edges in bin / all pairs in bin`. For any graph, the expected hit count from co-expression alone is `Σ q_{bin(r)}` over its pairs, and the null distribution is `Σ_b Binomial(n_b, q_b)` drawn 10,000 times with a fixed seed. This null **preserves each pair's co-expression level but not gene degree** — the exact complement of the configuration model, which preserves degree but destroys co-expression. It is applied to each model's co-firing graph within U, to its slice outside the top 5% co-expressed pairs, and, as a sanity check, to a co-expression top-N graph itself.

The two nulls form a 2×2 decomposition of "trivial" signal:

| Null | Preserves | Destroys | Question answered |
|---|---|---|---|
| Configuration model (`config_shuffle`) | Gene degree sequence | Pair-level co-expression | Are hits beyond what hub genes alone predict? |
| r-matched binomial sum (`coexpr_rmatched.py`) | Pair-level co-expression | Gene degree | Are hits beyond what correlation strength alone predicts? |
| Cell-shuffle floor (`raw_expression_baseline.py`) | Expression marginals | Cell-to-cell correspondence | Does geometry beat row-permuted expression? |

Sources: [coexpr_rmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_rmatched.py#L2-L14), [coexpr_rmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_rmatched.py#L82-L98), [raw_expression_baseline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/raw_expression_baseline.py#L70-L91)

## The Cell-Level Counterpart: Raw Expression Geometry

The co-expression baselines above target the *gene-pair* claims; `raw_expression_baseline.py` (GPU-side, under `pipeline/atlas_h100/`) is the analogous control for *cell-level geometry* results — CKA and tissue/cell-type decoding. Using the same 2,000-cell seed-0 subsample that `cell_cka.py` and `nonlinearity.py` use, it builds two raw representations with no model: PCA-50 of log1p CP10k over 2,000 Seurat-flavor highly variable genes, and the 2,000 HVGs themselves. It runs the same 5-fold stratified-CV probes (logistic and MLP, balanced accuracy) used for model embeddings, then computes **linear CKA between the raw HVG matrix and every layer of every model's residual stream**, with a floor from 20 cell-shuffle permutations. Its output, `raw_expression_baseline.json`, is registered in `RESULTS.md` alongside the co-expression backbone file — one artifact family, two levels of analysis.

Sources: [raw_expression_baseline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/raw_expression_baseline.py#L2-L14), [raw_expression_baseline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/raw_expression_baseline.py#L31-L45), [raw_expression_baseline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/raw_expression_baseline.py#L60-L95), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L59)

## Reviewer Hardening: The `review_10_coexpr` Suite

When the co-expression comparison itself came under hostile review, the `review_10_coexpr/` folder re-derived it under harsher conditions. `review_heavy.py` re-implements the shared ruler line-for-line (the baseline scripts run top-level code and cannot be imported) in a `Ruler` class, then executes three parts:

| Part | Test | Design |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | Independent recount at 6,000 cells | Global top-8,631 and top-41,952 by direct threshold-and-sort (no histogram); degree-matched graphs for the five passing models; a **leave-one-hub-out paired test** with an exact binomial test on discordant hits (which genes carry hits only one graph finds) |
| **P2** | Cell-prefix test | Co-expression recomputed on exactly the first K cells each model's SAE saw (from `prefix_estimate.json`: Tahoe-x1/Geneformer-V2 264, scGPT 424, UCE 496, C2S-Scale 984), with genes below a prefix detection floor zeroed; global, node-matched and degree-matched variants |
| **P3** | Unrestricted gene universe | All named (non-ENSG) genes with count > 0 in ≥10 of 6,000 cells — removing the co-firing union, itself a model-derived filter, from the gene universe |

`prefix_estimate.py` derives those cell counts from the extraction cap (500,000 gene positions, batches of 8, tokens per cell = min(#genes with count>0, per-model cap)); note the corrected `cells_seen()` simply returns the full cell count with the comment that per-cell sampling reads every cell and the position cap no longer applies — an example of the repo's retraction discipline. The comparison parameters themselves are no longer hard-coded: `_fixed_params.py` reads `PASSED` (models with per-model TRRUST p<0.05, strongest first), `BUDGET` (equal-budget edge count) and `GRAPH_SIZE` directly from the corrected result files. The folder also carries spot checks (`same_cells_check.py`, `salivary_check.py`, `residual_hits_prefix.py`, `lead_without_family.py`); the broader reviewer suite is covered in [Reviewer Robustness Analyses](16-reviewer-robustness-analyses).

Sources: [review_heavy.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_heavy.py#L2-L22), [review_heavy.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_heavy.py#L90-L103), [review_heavy.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_heavy.py#L184-L190), [prefix_estimate.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/prefix_estimate.py#L1-L29), [_fixed_params.py](paper_draft/analysis/_fixed_params.py#L1-L13)

## Artifact Map

| Artifact | Producer | Consumer / role |
|---|---|---|
| `outputs/atlas/comparative/coexpr_core_baseline.json` (72 KB) | `coexpr_core_baseline.py` | Registered in `RESULTS.md`; the backbone-without-model verdict |
| `out_alllayers/baselines/raw_expression_baseline.json` | `raw_expression_baseline.py` (GPU side, copied back) | Cell-level geometry floor for CKA and decoding claims |
| `coexpr_trrust.json` | `coexpr_trrust.py` | Per-kind co-expression vs co-firing, node-matched and masked-null slices |
| `coexpr_degmatched.json` | `coexpr_degmatched.py` | Degree-matched verdict with Fisher tests |
| `coexpr_rmatched.json` | `coexpr_rmatched.py` | Per-bin TRRUST rates and r-level-only expectations |
| `review_heavy.json`, `prefix_estimate.json` | `review_10_coexpr/` | Post-review recomputation under P1–P3 conditions |

The analysis-folder JSONs are written next to their scripts and incremental (each model/kind dumps as it completes), a pattern that matters for multi-hour correlation jobs.

Sources: [coexpr_trrust.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_trrust.py#L284-L384), [coexpr_degmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_degmatched.py#L131-L174), [coexpr_rmatched.py](paper_draft/analysis/coexpression_baseline/coexpr_rmatched.py#L89-L104), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L18-L19)

## Where to Go Next

The baselines here consume the calibrated annotator defined in [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation) and the configuration-model null formalized in [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim); the co-firing graphs they benchmark come from [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test). For how these checks were extended into the full reviewer response — including family-mask and input-encoding follow-ups — continue to [Reviewer Robustness Analyses](16-reviewer-robustness-analyses), and for where every output file flows next, see [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map).


# Reviewer Robustness Analyses



This page documents the repository's dedicated post-hoc verification layer: four numbered "hostile review" modules (`review_10_coexpr/` through `review_13_backbone/`) under `paper_draft/analysis/`, plus the pre-emptive robustness controls they sit alongside in `pipeline/scripts/`. Each module re-attacks one published claim family — the co-expression baseline, input-encoding artifacts, the TRRUST regulatory-direction test, and the backbone-composition contrast — using independently re-derived numbers, upgraded statistics, and re-implemented nulls. Understanding this layer requires familiarity with the co-firing graphs, the configuration-model null, and the calibrated annotation pipeline covered in [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim) and [Co-Expression Baseline Comparisons](15-co-expression-baseline-comparisons).

Sources: [README.md](paper_draft/analysis/README.md#L1-L16), [review_cheap.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_cheap.py#L1-L18)

## Two-Tier Robustness Architecture

The robustness apparatus is split deliberately. The **pipeline tier** (`pipeline/scripts/*robust*.py`, `hypothesis_sizematched.py`, `hypothesis_studybias.py`) runs during analysis and writes results into the release directory `outputs/atlas/comparative/`, so its conclusions are part of the shipped artifact. The **review tier** (`paper_draft/analysis/review_*/`) runs *afterward*: it reads the release outputs (including the shared `.cofire_cache.pkl` graph cache built by `hypothesis_trrust3.py`), treats the published numbers as claims to be attacked, and writes small checked-in JSONs next to its own scripts. Two shared modules bind the review tier together: `_fixed_params.py` derives the passing-model list, equal-size budget, and per-model graph sizes from the *corrected* runs-v2 outputs (never hard-coded from the superseded run), and `family_mask.py` centralizes the M1/M2 gene-family exclusion rules consumed by both `lead_without_family.py` and `trrust_robustness/s03b_family_masked.py`.

Sources: [README.md](paper_draft/analysis/README.md#L57-L91), [_fixed_params.py](paper_draft/analysis/_fixed_params.py#L1-L13), [family_mask.py](paper_draft/analysis/family_mask.py#L7-L19)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Release["Release artifacts: outputs/atlas/"]
        C["comparative/*.json<br/>hypothesis_trrust2 · sizematched"]
        CACHE[".cofire_cache.pkl<br/>from hypothesis_trrust3.py"]
        G["genesets/trrust_edges.json"]
    end
    COR["Rebuilt corpus<br/>6,000 cells · seed 0<br/>$ATLAS_CACHE/corpus6k.h5ad"]
    subgraph Pipeline["Pipeline tier: pipeline/scripts/"]
        R["hypothesis_robust · sizematched<br/>studybias · kegg_robust · recalibrate_robust"]
    end
    subgraph Review["Review tier: paper_draft/analysis/review_*/"]
        RV10["review_10_coexpr"]
        RV11["review_11_input_encoding"]
        RV12["review_12_trrust"]
        RV13["review_13_backbone"]
    end
    FIXED["_fixed_params.py<br/>PASSED · BUDGET · GRAPH_SIZE"]
    FM["family_mask.py<br/>M1 + M2 masks"]
    OUT["Checked-in review JSONs"]
    T3["Table 3 (make_table3.py)"]
    F5["Figure 5C (figures/fig5.py)"]
    C --> FIXED
    FIXED --> RV10
    FIXED --> RV12
    CACHE --> RV10
    CACHE --> RV11
    CACHE --> RV12
    G --> RV10
    G --> RV12
    COR --> RV10
    FM --> RV10
    R --> OUT
    RV10 --> OUT
    RV11 --> OUT
    RV12 --> OUT
    RV13 --> OUT
    OUT --> T3
    OUT --> F5
```

The diagram's key structural fact: review modules are *consumers* of release outputs, never producers of release claims — except through two sanctioned sinks. `make_table3.py` assembles Table 3 from the unmasked comparison JSONs (`hypothesis_trrust2.json`, `r1_stratified_direction.json`, `coexpr_trrust.json`, `coexpr_degmatched.json`, `review_cheap.json`), and Figure 5C additionally consumes `lead_without_family.json`. Everything else in the review tier is evidence that stays outside the manuscript tables.

Sources: [README.md](paper_draft/analysis/README.md#L93-L110), [README.md](paper_draft/analysis/README.md#L1-L16)

## The Hostile-Review Protocol

`review_cheap.py` establishes the protocol in six numbered checks. Check (1) re-derives roughly thirty numbers quoted in the analysis notes directly from the checked-in baseline JSONs, comparing each against a hard-coded expected value annotated with its source line (e.g. `("global top-4149 Pearson fold", 75.0, ..., "10:212")`), accepting matches within a 0.6% relative tolerance and printing any mismatch. The full check battery is gated on detecting the published run (`"8631" in pe["global"]`), so it silently skips rather than false-fails on corrected-run data. This converts prose claims into mechanically falsifiable assertions.

Sources: [review_cheap.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_cheap.py#L31-L76)

Check (2) performs the protocol's most important statistical upgrade. The published baseline compared co-firing against degree-matched co-expression graphs with a two-sided **Fisher test that treats the two graphs as independent samples** — but the graphs share pairs and shared pairs can both hit. The review conditions on *discordant* hits: among pairs found by only one graph, hits in the co-firing graph follow a binomial with success probability `n_cofire_only / (n_cofire_only + n_coexpr_only)` under equal precision, tested exactly. The Fisher p-value is still reported alongside for comparison. Checks (3)–(6) complete the battery: the pre-declared main kind (Pearson) re-scored at each passing model's *own* graph size with pooled leave-Tahoe-out binomial tests; a Monte Carlo spread of the Tahoe configuration null (5 seeds × 200 rewirings, versus the notes' single 3.93× and the published 4.44×); the TF–TF base rate computed *inside each model's node set* rather than the union-wide 22.6%; and enumeration of TRRUST edges touching the salivary-gene set used in the pair-quality check.

Sources: [review_cheap.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_cheap.py#L78-L126), [review_cheap.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_cheap.py#L128-L187)

A second protocol constraint shapes every review module: the baseline scripts run top-level code and cannot be imported, so their measurement functions are **re-implemented line for line** and then verified. `review_heavy.py` defines a `Ruler` class carrying the gene indexing, sorted truth keys (`i * 2^21 + j` after symbol uppercasing), and the stub-matching `config_shuffle` null copied verbatim from `hypothesis_trrust2.py`, and its docstring states the graphs were verified identical to the repo's cached pickle. `budget_tiebreak.py` goes further and asserts graph identity at runtime (`assert raw_alpha == pub`). Duplication here is a deliberate verification strategy, not an accident.

> [!TIP]
> When you see re-implemented "ruler" logic in this repo, check for the verification anchor: either an `assert` against the cached graph (`budget_tiebreak.py`) or an explicit identity statement in the docstring (`r1_stratified_direction.py`). A re-implementation without one is a red flag for silent divergence between the review and the published number.

Sources: [review_heavy.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_heavy.py#L42-L73), [budget_tiebreak.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/budget_tiebreak.py#L73-L78)

## Review 10: Co-Expression Baseline Re-Examination

The corpus-dependent half of the module, `review_heavy.py`, runs three parts. **P1** is an independent recount at 6,000 cells using a direct threshold-and-sort (no histogram binning) for the global top-N graphs, plus degree-matched graphs rebuilt with greedy b-matching that *retain the hit lists* — enabling leave-one-hub-out paired tests and asking which genes carry hits only one graph finds. **P2** is the cell-prefix test: since the extraction capped positions per batch, `prefix_estimate.py` reconstructs how many corpus cells each model's SAE actually saw (Tahoe-x1 and Geneformer-V2 at 264 cells, scGPT 424, UCE 496, C2S-Scale 984 — with the corrected per-cell-sampling extraction now reading every cell, making the cap moot), then recomputes co-expression on exactly those first K cells. **P3** removes a circularity: the published gene universe was the *co-firing union*, itself a model-derived filter, so the review rescoring against an unrestricted universe of all named genes expressed in ≥10 of 6,000 cells.

Sources: [review_heavy.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_heavy.py#L1-L17), [prefix_estimate.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/prefix_estimate.py#L1-L44), [review_heavy.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/review_heavy.py#L120-L168)

The synthesis script `lead_without_family.py` asks whether each model's degree-matched lead survives the two family masks — M1 (pairs sharing at least two leading symbol characters) and M2 (both genes in one curated DNA-binding-domain class) — applied via the shared `family_mask.py` helpers. The checked-in results show the answer is heterogeneous, which is precisely the value of running the check per model:

| Model | Cofire-only / Coexpr-only hits | p (unmasked) | After M1+M2 masking | p (masked) | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UCE | 51 / 40 | 0.294 | 21 / 39 | 0.027 | lead was family-pair padding; co-expression leads after masking |
| Tahoe | 62 / 36 | 0.011 | 53 / 34 | 0.053 | lead weakens to borderline (the Figure 5C headline case) |
| C2S | 77 / 46 | 0.007 | 43 / 45 | 0.915 | lead fully explained by family pairs |
| Geneformer | 12 / 38 | 0.00031 | 12 / 35 | 0.001 | co-expression leads both before and after masking |

Sources: [lead_without_family.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/lead_without_family.py#L1-L43), [lead_without_family.json](paper_draft/analysis/review_10_coexpr/lead_without_family.json#L1-L45), [README.md](paper_draft/analysis/README.md#L102-L110)

## Review 11: Input-Encoding Artifact Checks

This module stress-tests the lexical-artifact analysis — whether same-gene-prefix co-occurrence in SAE features reflects encoding artifacts — under harsher conditions. `prefix_robust.py` first lists, per model, which 3-letter prefixes compose *all* same-prefix within-feature pairs (purely descriptive), then re-tests the "same prefix, different HGNC group" excess after excluding the 20 prefixes with the most such pairs summed over all ten models. The exclusion set is chosen once, data-driven, before any testing — an anti-circularity discipline — and the surviving metric uses the same slot-permutation null as the published notes. `esm_allpairs.py` fixes a sampling-noise issue in the ESM2-cosine metric: `lexical.py` computed the observed mean cosine on a random 10,000-pair subsample, so the review recomputes it on *all* within-feature clean-list pairs and re-zs against the stored null SD — explicitly documented as conservative, since the stored SD still includes subsample noise.

Sources: [prefix_robust.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/prefix_robust.py#L1-L22), [esm_allpairs.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/esm_allpairs.py#L1-L10), [esm_allpairs.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/esm_allpairs.py#L27-L41)

Two checks target graph-construction fragility. `budget_tiebreak.py` quantifies how much the top-8,631 hit count depends on tie-breaking at the cutoff weight: pairs tied at the weight boundary enter or leave the budget depending on dict order versus alphabetical order, so the script reports hits under both orders, under 1,000 random tie orders, and the tie-free expectation (`hits_above + hits_at_cutoff × slots_left / n_at_cutoff`) per model. `residual_filler.py` defines filler genes mechanically — a gene whose appearances in detected tie-tail slots are ≥50% of its top-20 appearances *and* ≥20 in count — then recomputes the prefix signal on a "clean minus F" list with every filler gene blanked, a strictly stronger filter than the published clean lists, and additionally reports what share of the published top-8,631 pairs touch a filler gene.

Sources: [budget_tiebreak.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/budget_tiebreak.py#L1-L12), [budget_tiebreak.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/budget_tiebreak.py#L42-L62), [residual_filler.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/residual_filler.py#L1-L11), [residual_filler.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_11_input_encoding/residual_filler.py#L51-L84)

## Review 12: TRRUST Null Design — Finding and Fixing a Bias

This module documents the review process catching a genuine methodological flaw. `r1_stratified_direction.py` shows that `s03_hub_direction.py` compared the observed TF→non-TF hit count against a stub-matching null of the *whole* graph — but the observed graphs contain far more TF–TF pairs than their nulls (UCE: 738 observed versus 95.5 in the null), which leaves the null *more* TF–non-TF pairs to hit than the model actually had. The direction test was therefore biased against models (and the TF–TF test in their favor). The fix is a **block-stratified configuration null** that rewires each pair-type block separately so every gene keeps its exact numbers of TF and non-TF partners.

Sources: [r1_stratified_direction.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_12_trrust/r1_stratified_direction.py#L1-L23)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Split["Observed W>=5 graph, split by pair type"]
        TT["TF–TF block"]
        TN["TF–non-TF block<br/>(TF ends fixed in place)"]
        NN["non-TF–non-TF block<br/>(cannot contain a TRRUST edge)"]
    end
    TT -->|"stub-match among TF ends only:<br/>shuffle · re-pair · drop self-loops · collapse dupes"| S
    TN -->|"bipartite configuration model:<br/>permute non-TF ends"| S["Stratified null, NPERM draws<br/>seed 11"]
    NN -->|"never rewired"| X["excluded"]
    S --> BH["Per-model p_emp →<br/>BH correction across 7 models"]
    BH --> OUT["r1_stratified_direction.json"]
```

The script also reports a precision-matched version of the plain test (hits per TF–non-TF pair, observed versus null) so the old and new read-outs remain comparable, and it runs the stratified null with 1,000 draws (default 200, passed as `argv[1]`). The companion check `r2_curve_many_draws.py` addresses the *fold* estimate instead: note 12's ≥2-model fold of 14.06× (all ten) and 17.53× (five passing) on a single 100-draw stream sat far from the published 20.8×–28.43×, and the note called the fold "noisy" without quantifying it. Running the identical null for 2,000 draws (seed 2024), the script reports the null-precision mean with its Monte Carlo standard error, an approximate 95% CI for the fold, the fold's spread across independent blocks of 100 and 200 draws (what each prior run actually sampled), and — robust to all null choices — the null-free precision ratio at ≥2 models over ≥1 model.

> [!TIP]
> The block-stratified pattern generalizes: whenever a directional or type-conditional statistic is tested against a whole-graph null, check whether the null reallocates the *conditioning structure* (here, each gene's TF/non-TF partner counts). If it does not, the null is testing a different question than the observed statistic answers.

Sources: [r1_stratified_direction.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_12_trrust/r1_stratified_direction.py#L46-L106), [r2_curve_many_draws.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_12_trrust/r2_curve_many_draws.py#L1-L68)

## Review 13: Backbone Composition Sensitivity

`r1_checks.py` runs five hostile probes (a–e) against the backbone-composition analysis, all reusing `bb_common.py` and the s2 annotator caches so every number stays on the same ruler as the published notes. Probe (a) counts singleton programme classes under the primary clustering rule (`hit_weighted|complete|J>=0.3`); probe (b) reports the programme count across all 30 clustering rules, including the primary rule's rank; probe (c) replaces pooled raw hit counts with a **model-balanced** classification — each contributing model gets total weight 1, so feature-rich models like C2S and tGPT cannot dominate the gene-content fractions; probe (d) decomposes the published "all 7 of 7 agree: 127 concepts at 0% depth versus 15 at mid" contrast, recounting it excluding protein-synthesis and excluding MaxToki (the model that loses the translation block after input); probe (e) states an arithmetic floor: with 7 non-embedding models among 10, any ≥8-of-10 concept *must* include at least one of the three embedding-layer models, so "every deep concept has one or two embedding models" is half forced by combinatorics — only the 1-versus-2 split and "none has all three" are informative.

Sources: [r1_checks.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_13_backbone/r1_checks.py#L1-L13), [r1_checks.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_13_backbone/r1_checks.py#L19-L82)

The follow-ups push the two most consequential probes further. `r2_balanced_programmes.py` re-runs the primary programme clustering with model-balanced hit weights (each model's per-concept hit counts normalized to sum 1 before pooling — necessary because tGPT/C2S give the most hits for 78 of 78 concepts), sweeping complete/average/single linkage at J≥0.3 and J≥0.5. `r3_near_input_no_maxtoki.py` repeats the near-input excess count among only the six block-output models with MaxToki removed, at ≥5-of-6 and 6-of-6 thresholds per depth slice, observed counts only. Together these convert a single published clustering into a sensitivity surface, and they expose which parts of the depth narrative are structural (arithmetic floor) versus empirical (MaxToki's translation block).

Sources: [r2_balanced_programmes.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_13_backbone/r2_balanced_programmes.py#L1-L40), [r3_near_input_no_maxtoki.py](paper_draft/analysis/review_13_backbone/r3_near_input_no_maxtoki.py#L1-L23)

## Pipeline-Level Robustness Controls

The review tier did not appear from nothing — the pipeline already contains pre-emptive robustness analyses whose outputs live in the release itself, and which the review modules treat as claims to re-verify. `hypothesis_robust.py` perturbs the held-out TRRUST result three ways: R1 drops same-family paralog pairs, R2 keeps only features firing above the per-model median activation frequency (removing the near-zero-expression clustering artifact), and R3 raises the per-pair evidence bar from ≥5 to ≥10 features. Its `same_family` helper carries a cautionary docstring: the earlier regex-based rule "matched none of those three examples from its own docstring," so the replacement stem rule errs toward over-dropping — the safe direction for a negative control. `hypothesis_sizematched.py` separates capability from capacity: predicted-pair counts span four orders of magnitude (AIDO.Cell 2 pairs, C2S-Scale 147,728) and hit counts correlate with graph size at r = +0.90, so every model is re-scored at the *same* top-N budget, with a rand-N arm isolating pure size, and sub-budget models marked untestable rather than failed.

Sources: [hypothesis_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_robust.py#L1-L54), [hypothesis_sizematched.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_sizematched.py#L1-L20)

| Script | Concern attacked | Method | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hypothesis_robust.py` | family paralogs, dead features, weak evidence | R1/R2/R3 variants on same config null | `hypothesis_robust.json` |
| `hypothesis_sizematched.py` | dictionary size masquerading as quality | equal top-N budget + rand-N null | `hypothesis_sizematched.json` |
| `hypothesis_studybias.py` | result driven by well-studied genes | precision profile across PubMed-count strata; Replogle-screen coverage audit | `hypothesis_studybias.json` |
| `recalibrate_robust.py` | rescued backbone = one lucky config | sweep calibrated annotators × ≥7/8/9/10 thresholds; housekeeping-vs-specific split | `recalibrate_robust.json` |
| `kegg_robust.py` | KEGG licensing dependence | recompute backbone with KEGG dropped from {GO_BP, KEGG, Reactome} | `kegg_robust.json` |

Sources: [hypothesis_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_robust.py#L32-L54), [hypothesis_studybias.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_studybias.py#L1-L18), [recalibrate_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/recalibrate_robust.py#L1-L4), [kegg_robust.py](pipeline/scripts/kegg_robust.py#L1-L5)

`hypothesis_studybias.py` deserves emphasis as the deepest of these: the pair list retains only 141 of 4,003 understudied genes (3.5%, against 16.8% of well-studied genes), so the "no new biology" conclusion could be a filter property. Causal validation is blocked — 752 of the 793 featured understudied protein-coding genes are absent from the Replogle screen entirely — so the script asks the strongest answerable question: among *testable* pairs, does the causal signal decline as the responding gene's publication count drops? A flat profile licenses extrapolation to unstudied genes; a declining profile refutes it. It relaxes the co-firing threshold from ≥5 to ≥2 so low-abundance genes are not pre-filtered, and annotates every pair with the responding gene's publication count.

Sources: [hypothesis_studybias.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_studybias.py#L1-L18), [hypothesis_studybias.py](pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_studybias.py#L20-L45)

## Reproducing the Review Checks

All review modules run from the repository root after `bash pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh`, with `ATLAS_BASE` pointing at the unpacked releases, `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, and `PYTHONPATH` including `paper_draft/analysis` so `_fixed_params` imports resolve. Corpus-dependent scripts take the rebuilt 6,000-cell corpus path as `argv[1]`; null-heavy scripts take permutation counts as trailing arguments (e.g. `r1_stratified_direction.py 1000`, `r2_curve_many_draws.py 2000`). The `.cofire_cache.pkl` dependency is generated by `pipeline/scripts/hypothesis_trrust3.py` — the README warns to build it in a disposable copy, since that generator also rewrites the candidate list and summary.

| Variable | Input |
|---|---|
| `ATLAS_BASE` | repository root with release archives unpacked |
| `ATLAS_CACHE` | working cache (corpus, TRRUST TSV, HGNC, scGPT vocab, AIDO gene index) |
| `PYTHONPATH` | must include `paper_draft/analysis` for `_fixed_params` |
| `TRRUST_RAW` / `HGNC_PATH` / `SCGPT_VOCAB` / `AIDO_GENE_INDEX` | external reference inputs with cache defaults |

Sources: [README.md](paper_draft/analysis/README.md#L57-L91), [README.md](paper_draft/analysis/README.md#L93-L101)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["fetch_runs.sh + set ATLAS_BASE<br/>PYTHONHASHSEED=0 · ATLAS_CACHE · PYTHONPATH"] --> B["Build .cofire_cache.pkl<br/>(disposable copy recommended)"]
    B --> C["Build corpus6k.h5ad<br/>build_corpus_lowmem.py · same_cells_check.py"]
    C --> D1["review_10: prefix_estimate →<br/>review_heavy → review_cheap →<br/>lead_without_family"]
    C --> D2["review_12: r1_stratified_direction 1000 →<br/>r2_curve_many_draws 2000"]
    B --> D3["review_11: prefix_robust ·<br/>budget_tiebreak · residual_filler · esm_allpairs"]
    B --> D4["review_13: r1_checks →<br/>r2_balanced_programmes · r3_near_input"]
    D1 --> E["make_table3.py · figures/fig5.py<br/>(Table 3, Figure 5C)"]
```

## Where This Fits

The review tier is the adversarial complement to the constructive pages upstream: [Co-Expression Baseline Comparisons](15-co-expression-baseline-comparisons) defines the ruler these scripts re-implement, [Literature and Perturbation Evidence](14-literature-and-perturbation-evidence) defines the TRRUST/perturbation read-outs that `hypothesis_robust.py` and `hypothesis_studybias.py` perturb, and [Concept Matrices and Backbone Detection](13-concept-matrices-and-backbone-detection) defines the annotation machinery `review_13_backbone` re-sweeps. Downstream, the checked-in review JSONs are consumed by the Table 3 generator and audited alongside everything else in [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks); the corrected-run context that makes `_fixed_params.py` necessary is documented in [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run).


# Result Files and Data Flow Map



This page maps how data physically moves through the atlas-comparison repository: which files exist, which script writes each one, which scripts read it, and how ~70 component JSONs in a single directory become the manuscript numbers, the figures, and the public site. The repository enforces one architectural invariant — everything published is derived from `outputs/atlas/comparative/` and nothing else — and this page shows both the flow that populates that directory and the machinery that keeps it true. The canonical file-side reference is `docs/RESULTS.md`, and this page walks it from the data-flow side.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L1-L3), [scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L1-L5)

## The Single Data Root and the ATLAS_BASE Contract

Every local script locates its inputs and outputs through one environment variable rather than hard-coded paths: `ATLAS_BASE` points at a data root under which `outputs/atlas/comparative/` lives. The scripts carry the authors' local path only as a default fallback (`/Users/annaantipova/Desktop/biomech`), and the reproduction guide instructs you to override it with the repository checkout itself (`export ATLAS_BASE=$(pwd)`). This one-line contract is what makes the entire analysis stage portable — any machine that sets `ATLAS_BASE` can run every script unchanged.

The documentation is deliberately mirrored in two views. `pipeline/scripts/README.md` is the **script-side map** ("what does this script do"), while `docs/RESULTS.md` is the **file-side map** ("who writes this file, who reads it, what it holds") — the two cover the same ground from opposite directions. For this page the file side is authoritative: it inventories every JSON in the comparative directory with its KB size, writer, and readers.

Sources: [scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L1-L5), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L3), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L12-L13), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L12)

## Three Stages: GPU Extraction, Catalogue Handoff, Local Analysis

The flow crosses a hardware and environment boundary once, and the **feature catalogue JSON is the serialization boundary**. On the H100 host, `build_ts_corpus.py` produces the shared corpus (seed 0) and the held-out draw (seed 1); `run_model.py` then runs each model end-to-end — adapter → activations → TopK SAE per layer — and `build_catalog()` writes one catalogue per layer (`out_fixed/<M>/feature_catalog_L<NN>.json`, top-20 genes per feature) plus the SAE weights (`sae_L<NN>.pt`). The GPU folder also hosts the analyses that *cannot* run without activations or weights — CKA between models, SVD-versus-SAE comparisons, rank-based GSEA annotation, co-activation graphs, and the explorer feature maps — and each of these emits a result file that is later copied back into the comparative directory.

> [!TIP]
> The decision that "everything that only needs the catalogues runs locally" is what makes the whole project reproducible on a laptop: the ~17 GB of SAE weights and the raw activations never leave the GPU pod, and are not archived at all. The catalogue JSON — feature IDs, top genes, firing statistics — is a sufficient sufficient statistic for every published downstream claim.

The handoff between stages is the GitHub release: `fetch_runs.sh` downloads the per-run archives (`runs-ts3_out`, `runs-alllayer_cat`, `runs-heldout_cat`, `runs-seeds`, `inputs-genesets`), verifies each against `SHA256SUMS`, and unpacks them into `outputs/atlas/` so the local scripts can re-run with `ATLAS_BASE` pointing at the repository root. Extraction ran under Python 3.12 / PyTorch / NumPy 1.26 on the H100; local analysis runs under Python 3.13 / NumPy 2.3.4 — the catalogue files are the interface that lets two different environments cooperate without either seeing the other's dependencies.

Sources: [atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L1-L7), [atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L60-L65), [atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L73-L74), [atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L84-L88), [fetch_runs.sh](pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh#L17-L27), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L12-L13)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph GPU["Stage 1 - GPU host: pipeline/atlas_h100/"]
        CORPUS["build_ts_corpus.py<br/>seed 0 corpus + seed 1 held-out draw"]
        RUN["run_model.py<br/>adapter - activations - TopK SAE per layer"]
        CAT["feature_catalog_L-NN-.json<br/>+ sae_L-NN-.pt"]
        GS["GPU-only analyses<br/>cell_cka - svd_vs_sae - gsea_prerank<br/>explorer maps - coactivation"]
        CORPUS --> RUN
        RUN --> CAT
        RUN --> GS
    end
    subgraph HANDOFF["Bridge: GitHub release runs-v2"]
        FETCH["fetch_runs.sh<br/>download - SHA-256 verify - unpack to outputs/atlas/"]
    end
    subgraph LOCAL["Stage 2 - local CPU: pipeline/scripts/"]
        MATRIX["Matrix builders<br/>atlas_build_ts3 - reannotate_string<br/>alllayer_matrix - genes_search_ts3"]
        NULLS["Nulls and controls<br/>random_null - recalibrate_*<br/>stats_final - degree_null - controls*"]
        HYP["Hypothesis evidence<br/>hypothesis_trrust 1-3 - pubmed - perturb"]
        COMP["outputs/atlas/comparative/<br/>~70 result JSONs"]
        MATRIX --> COMP
        NULLS --> COMP
        HYP --> COMP
    end
    subgraph ASM["Stage 3 - assembly chain"]
        CHAIN["atlas_assemble.py - atlas_hypothesis_block.py<br/>- inject_atlas.py"]
        SITE["index.html + data/explorer.json"]
    end
    CAT -->|via release archives| FETCH
    GS -->|JSONs copied back| COMP
    FETCH --> MATRIX
    FETCH --> NULLS
    FETCH --> HYP
    COMP --> CHAIN
    CHAIN --> SITE
    AUD["audit_all.py"] -. "6 consistency checks" .-> COMP
    AUD -. "checks the public site too" .-> SITE
```

## The Result File Inventory

`docs/RESULTS.md` records every file with the discipline of a ledger: size in KB, the script that writes it, the scripts that read it, and one sentence on what it holds. Reading the "written by" column across all entries reveals exactly **three provenance classes**, and it is worth internalizing them because they tell you where a number comes from:

| Provenance class | Example files | Written by | Typical consumers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local analysis scripts | `matrix_alllayer.json` (19.2 MB), `matrix_ts3_string.json` (16.9 MB), `recalibrate_final.json`, `controls.json`, `hypothesis_final.json`, `hypothesis_pairs_full.json` (569 KB, all 4,485 released pairs) | `alllayer_matrix.py`, `reannotate_string.py`, `recalibrate_*.py`, `hypothesis_trrust3.py`, … | `atlas_assemble.py`, audits, figure/table builders |
| GPU-side, copied back | `cka_ts3.json`, `freq_ts3.json` (22.4 MB), `gsea_annot.json`, `nonlinearity_alllayers.json`, `raw_expression_baseline.json`, `explorer_slim_*.json`, `svd/<M>_L<NN>_svd.json` | `cell_cka.py`, `gsea_prerank.py`, `svd_vs_sae.py`, `build_explorer_slim.py` (all in `atlas_h100/`) | `atlas_assemble.py`, `inject_atlas.py`, figure scripts |
| Assembled artifacts | `atlas_full_notf.json` (356 KB) — and transitively `index.html`, `data/explorer.json` | `atlas_assemble.py`, then `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` (rewrites one key), `inject_atlas.py` | the site, downstream controls (`controls4.py`), audits |

The table is also honest about its own topology: rows with an empty "read by" column are endpoints — nulls and grids like `random_null.json`, `heldout.json` (the permissive replication that *fails*), or `depth_ts3.json` — kept because audits or history reference them, while the header notes that files no script reads were deliberately left out of the repository. The `figures/` subdirectory carries the seven manuscript figures plus `.sources.json`, a hash-stamped manifest of each plotting script's inputs.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L5-L69), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L71-L77), [scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L9-L18), [scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L42-L55)

## The Assembly Chain: Component Files to Site Payload

Three scripts in `pipeline/scripts/` turn the component JSONs into the published page, each with a narrow contract. Understanding this chain answers the question "if I re-run analysis X, what must I re-run to update the site?"

**`atlas_assemble.py`** builds `atlas_full_notf.json`, the one file the site embeds. It chooses a spine — `matrix_alllayer.json` if present, falling back to `matrix_ts3_string.json`, asserting if neither exists — then derives the coverage, universality, similarity (Jaccard), lineage, and firing blocks itself, and finally loops over a declarative list of **thirteen pull-through blocks** (depth, tissue_layers, cka, cka_layers, nonlinearity, module_themes, flow, celltype, topn, gsea, controls, depth_calibrated, findings), copying each verbatim if its file exists and printing a skip notice if not. The SVD block is merged incrementally: it starts from the previous atlas JSON and updates per-model entries from `svd/<M>_L<NN>_svd.json` globs, which is how a tenth model gets added without re-deriving the other nine.

> [!TIP]
> Missing input files never crash the assembler — a missing file means the corresponding block is absent from the output, not a failed run. This fault-tolerance pattern means partial regenerations produce a coherent (if incomplete) atlas, and the skip notices in stdout are the audit trail for what did not make it in.

**`atlas_hypothesis_block.py`** exists because of a documented drift incident: the site's prediction panels were once assembled by hand, and when the literature null was made reproducible the page kept serving an old z = 40.48 while the manuscript said 34.7. The script now derives the entire `hypothesis` block from six canonical files (`hypothesis_trrust2`, `hypothesis_final`, `hypothesis_robust`, `hypothesis_sizematched`, `hypothesis_pubmed`, `hypothesis_perturb`) and edits only that key of `atlas_full_notf.json`. Its `--check` mode recomputes without writing and reports drift, which turns the public site into just another auditable artifact.

**`inject_atlas.py`** performs the final substitution: it reads `atlas_template.html` — editable markup whose data blocks are empty `<script id="…-data" type="application/json">` placeholders — and injects six files: `modules_alllayers.json`, `genes_ts3.json`, `atlas_full_notf.json`, `sae_health.json`, `programme_table.json`, and the explorer maps. It produces three builds: a LIGHT variant embedding the capped `explorer_slim_light.json` (5.4 MB), a FULL local variant, and the published `index.html`, which carries only a stub and fetches the heavy maps from `data/explorer.json` on first explorer use — cutting the served page to roughly a fifth of the naive size.

Sources: [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L2-L8), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L64-L70), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L281-L301), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L303-L318), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L2-L12), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L29-L31), [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L22-L32), [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L42-L56), [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L81-L86)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph COMP["component files in outputs/atlas/comparative/"]
        SPINE["matrix_alllayer.json<br/>or matrix_ts3_string.json"]
        DERIVED["freq_ts3 - alllayer_concepts<br/>genes_ts3 - cka_ts3 - tissue_alllayers<br/>circuits_adjacent - hardcell_agreement"]
        PULL["13 pull-through blocks<br/>depth - controls - flow - cka_layers<br/>module_themes - topn - gsea ..."]
        SVDF["svd/M_L-NN-_svd.json"]
        HYP6["hypothesis_* x6"]
    end
    ASM["atlas_assemble.py<br/>derive + merge, skip missing"]
    ATLAS["atlas_full_notf.json<br/>356 KB - the site's spine"]
    HYPB["atlas_hypothesis_block.py<br/>rewrite one key - --check for drift"]
    INJ["inject_atlas.py<br/>substitute 6 placeholders"]
    TPL["atlas_template.html<br/>__DATA__ placeholders"]
    SITE["index.html<br/>+ data/explorer.json"]
    SPINE --> ASM
    DERIVED --> ASM
    PULL --> ASM
    SVDF --> ASM
    ASM --> ATLAS
    ATLAS --> HYPB
    HYP6 --> HYPB
    HYPB --> ATLAS
    ATLAS --> INJ
    TPL --> INJ
    INJ --> SITE
```

| Chain stage | Inputs (count) | Output | Failure behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| `atlas_assemble.py` | spine (1, asserted) + derived inputs (~7, optional) + pull-through list (13, optional) + previous atlas for SVD merge | `atlas_full_notf.json` | missing optional file → block skipped with notice; missing spine → assert |
| `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` | 6 hypothesis files + current `atlas_full_notf.json` | rewritten `hypothesis` key | `--check` mode reports drift without writing |
| `inject_atlas.py` | 6 data blocks + template | `index.html`, `data/explorer.json`, 2 local builds | hard dependency: `atlas_full_notf.json` must exist |

## Drift Control: One Invariant, Six Checks

The inventory's contract — "the manuscript, the supplement and the site's data blocks are built from these files and nothing else" — is enforced, not aspirational. `audit_all.py` runs six modules covering the three drift surfaces the project has actually been bitten by: text versus results (a fold range left at 166× where the source said 166.7), supplement versus results (tables keeping stale permutation counts), and figures versus results (a figure shipping four days of replaced numbers). The sixth check is precisely the site: `atlas_hypothesis_block.py --check` against `atlas_full_notf.json`. The command's exit code is framed as a submission gate — all six passing means it is safe to submit, and the failure instruction is architectural in spirit: *"Fix the source of the disagreement, not the check."* The figure checks close their own loop by hashing inputs: `audit_figures.py` stamps `.sources.json` with the hashes of each plotting script's inputs, so a figure can be verified against the data it was drawn from. The design principle behind all of this is the same one this page documents: a claim is true if, and only if, it can be re-derived from the result files — [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks) covers the check internals.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L3), [audit_all.py](pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L4-L8), [audit_all.py](pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L19-L26), [audit_all.py](pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L44-L48), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L71-L73)

## Reproducing the Map on Your Machine

The minimal path touches every layer of the flow without downloading anything: clone the repository, `pip install -r requirements.txt`, `export ATLAS_BASE=$(pwd)`, drop the manuscript files next to the results, and run `python pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py` — the result files ship in the repository, so all 312 checks re-derive every published number from them locally. Rebuilding the site from the same files is one more command (`python pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py`, which writes `index.html` and `data/explorer.json`), served with any static file server. To go further and *re-run* the analyses rather than check them, `bash pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh` materializes the per-run catalogues into `outputs/atlas/` first; what those archives contain, their sizes, and the checksum scheme are covered in [Release Archives and Checksummed Fetching](19-release-archives-and-checksummed-fetching), and why the catalogues were re-extracted (the v1 positional-sampling fault) is the story of [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run).

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L19-L34), [fetch_runs.sh](pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh#L1-L9), [atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L48-L58)

## Where to Go Next

The natural continuation of this page follows the flow's terminus and its enforcement. [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks) details the six verification modules summarized above; [Release Archives and Checksummed Fetching](19-release-archives-and-checksummed-fetching) unpacks the bridge between the GPU host and your checkout; [Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files) goes deeper into `inject_atlas.py` and the template placeholder mechanics; and [Layer Explorer Feature Maps](23-layer-explorer-feature-maps) explains what the lazily-fetched 50 MB `explorer_slim_full.json` actually renders.


# Audit System and Manuscript Checks



This page documents the six-module consistency audit that gates every release of the atlas comparison: an orchestrator (`audit_all.py`) that dispatches manuscript, supplement, figure, and site checks against the result JSONs each artifact claims to describe. The suite exists because this project repeatedly observed the same failure mode — prose, tables, and figures silently diverging from the data that produced them — and each module encodes a specific incident. We cover the architecture, the shared numeric-matching primitive, the distinction between verbatim and derived claims, and the content-hash stamping protocol that closes the figure gap.

## Three Surfaces That Drift

The system design starts from a partition of failure surfaces rather than a list of bugs. The orchestrator's docstring names exactly three things that "can drift apart, and each has bitten this project": the text versus the results (a fold range left at 166× where the source said 166.7), the supplement versus the results (Table S8 kept 20-permutation folds after the move to 250, and Table S2 printed unfiltered totals under a "5–500 genes" heading), and the figures versus the results (Fig S2 shipped for four days showing numbers that had been replaced). The manuscript auditor's own docstring adds the epistemological motivation: it was written "after three separate bugs in one session, each of which looked like a result rather than a mistake — a null taken from the wrong population, unmapped gene symbols folded into 'zero publications', and an Ensembl filter applied after truncation instead of before." The design conclusion is stated outright: reasoning about whether a number is right is what failed each time, so the audit instead re-reads every number from its source file.

This gives the audit system its shape: one check per artifact type, all reading from the single directory of result files (`outputs/atlas/comparative/`) documented in [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map).

Sources: [audit_all.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L2-L10), [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L2-L11), [README.md](/pipeline/scripts/README.md#L75-L85)

## Orchestrator: `audit_all.py`

`audit_all.py` is a 50-line subprocess dispatcher. It resolves its own directory, declares the six checks as `(label, script)` pairs, runs each with `capture_output=True`, and prints one `PASS`/`FAIL` line per module using the module's **last stdout line** as the summary — so `96/96 numbers verified against source` or `all 7 figures match the data they were drawn from` becomes the aggregate report. On failure it reprints only the diagnostic lines from the failing modules, filtered by a keyword list (`MISMATCH`, `STALE`, `MISSING`, `UNSTAMPED`, `no such sentence`, `needs a look`) — a deliberate triage view that suppresses the passing rows. Any nonzero child exit code propagates as exit code 1, which the docstring frames as the actual output: a plain statement of "whether it is safe to submit."

The six registered checks divide by artifact and by claim type:

| # | Check module | Scope | Artifact audited |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `audit_manuscript.py` | Results 3.4–3.5, Discussion, Limitations | `MANUSCRIPT.md` |
| 2 | `audit_manuscript_core.py` | Results 3.1–3.3 and Methods | `MANUSCRIPT.md` |
| 3 | `audit_manuscript_derived.py` | Numbers derived, not read off a result | `MANUSCRIPT.md` |
| 4 | `audit_supplement.py` | Hand-written tables vs data, code, environment | `SUPPLEMENTARY.md` |
| 5 | `audit_figures.py` | Rendered figures vs source hashes | `figures/*.png` |
| 6 | `atlas_hypothesis_block.py --check` | Public site vs same results | `index.html` data block |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources["Result JSONs (outputs/atlas/comparative)"]
        J1["controls.json"]
        J2["hypothesis_*.json"]
        J3["sae_health.json<br/>depth_backbone.json"]
        J4["cka_svd_null.json"]
    end
    ORCH["audit_all.py<br/>subprocess x6, exit 1 on any fail"]
    subgraph Artifacts["Published artifacts"]
        M["MANUSCRIPT.md"]
        S["SUPPLEMENTARY.md"]
        F["figures/*.png<br/>(.sources.json manifest)"]
        W["index.html hypothesis block"]
    end
    M --> A1["audit_manuscript.py"]
    M --> A2["audit_manuscript_core.py"]
    M --> A3["audit_manuscript_derived.py"]
    S --> A4["audit_supplement.py"]
    F --> A5["audit_figures.py"]
    W --> A6["atlas_hypothesis_block --check"]
    J2 --> A1
    J1 --> A2
    J3 --> A2
    J4 --> A3
    J1 --> A4
    J3 --> A5
    J2 --> A6
    A1 & A2 & A3 & A4 & A5 & A6 --> ORCH
```

The one design subtlety: check 6 is not an `audit_*` file at all. The site-assembly script `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` (see [Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files)) ships a `--check` mode that reports drift between the embedded prediction block and the hypothesis files, and the orchestrator simply invokes it as a sixth subprocess — reusing the generator's own logic as its auditor rather than duplicating it.

Sources: [audit_all.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L18-L49), [README.md](/pipeline/scripts/README.md#L60-L62)

## The `check()` Primitive: Matching Text-Implied Precision

All three manuscript auditors share one comparison function, and its contract is documented in `audit_manuscript.py`'s docstring: matching is **numeric, not textual**. Each check is a regex over the whitespace-flattened manuscript with exactly one capture group holding the number, e.g. `rf"{re.escape(disp)} {N}×"` for a per-model fold claim. The function then derives the tolerance from the text itself: it counts how many decimals the sentence shows and applies `tol = 0.5 * 10**(-dec)`, so a manuscript that writes "13.3" is compared to a source value of 13.29 within ±0.05 — rounding is not reported as an error, but a genuine divergence is.

The primitive absorbs the manuscript's typographic conventions so they never produce false alarms:

| Convention in text | Handling in `check()` |
|---|---|
| Thousands separators (`4,111`) | Stripped before parsing |
| Unicode minus (`−`) | Normalized to ASCII `-` |
| En/em-dash ranges (`166–284×`) | Range endpoints checked as two separate captures; `audit_manuscript_core.py` defines `D = r"[-–—]"` explicitly |
| Spelled-out counts ("two of the five models") | `WORDS` dict maps `one`…`ten`; capture group `[A-Za-z]+` |
| Prose precision ("about one in every 480") | Optional `tol_rel` widens tolerance relative to the expected value (`tol_rel=0.02` for a two-significant-figure claim) |
| Computed forms (`100 × precision`, `1/(N+1)` p-value floor) | Expected value is an expression over source fields, not a stored copy |

Every row lands in a `rows` list as `(claim, source, "expected vs got", status, ok)`. The report prints a fixed-width table and the tally line (`{passed}/{total} numbers verified against source`), then lists failures under a `needs a look:` heading.

The single most consequential rule lives in the final comment block: **a check that could not find its sentence did not run at all, which is worse than a mismatch** — rewording a sentence would otherwise switch its check off in silence. So `re.search` returning `None` records a `"no such sentence"` failure, and *any* failed row exits 1. This makes the audit failure-closed against prose edits, not just numeric edits.

> [!TIP]
> When extending the suite, resist the temptation to make missing sentences a warning. The "no such sentence = fail" rule is what prevents the audit from decaying into a checklist of assertions that pass vacuously — the exact anti-pattern that let the 28.4× artefact survive (see next section).

Sources: [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L46-L66), [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L249-L263), [audit_manuscript_core.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_core.py#L47-L65), [audit_manuscript_derived.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_derived.py#L43-L63)

## Verbatim Claims: `audit_manuscript.py` and `audit_manuscript_core.py`

The two verbatim auditors split the manuscript by section provenance. `audit_manuscript.py` covers Results 3.4–3.5, Discussion, and Limitations — the sections built from the hypothesis-testing campaign — and loads `hypothesis_trrust2.json`, `hypothesis_final.json`, `hypothesis_robust.json`, `hypothesis_pubmed.json`, `hypothesis_perturb.json`, and `hypothesis_studybias.json` up front, then navigates them with a `dig(d, *path)` helper that returns `default=None` for any missing path. `audit_manuscript_core.py` covers Results 3.1–3.3 and Methods — the sections "whose numbers predate today's work" — reading `controls.json`, `alllayer_null.json`, `depth_backbone.json`, `kegg_robust.json`, and `sae_health.json`; its `dig` additionally accepts integer list indices, and it replaces the two-capture range idiom with the en-dash-aware `D` pattern.

Three structurally interesting claim families show how far the pattern is pushed:

- **Range endpoints as paired checks.** A manuscript sentence like "five variants give a↔b×" produces two checks (`robustness min`, `robustness max`), where each expected value is `min()`/`max()` *recomputed from the result file's list* — the text is audited against derived extrema even inside the verbatim module.
- **Permutation counts read from each test's own file.** A dedicated block checks every `N = ...` in Methods against the producing file's `n_perm` field, with the comment explaining why: the text said 200 for tests that actually ran 500 and 100, and "a script default that changes shows up here rather than in a reviewer's recomputation of the p-value floor."
- **Boolean invariants as rows.** `audit_manuscript_core.py` appends raw `rows.append(...)` entries for non-numeric claims — e.g., that the CKA-vs-floor ratio exceeds tenfold for every pair, that the SAE is ahead of PCA in all ten models, and that a negative random-dictionary variance holds across the board.

One cross-artifact leak is intentional: two checks in `audit_manuscript.py` leave the manuscript — one parses `SUPPLEMENTARY.md`'s Table S11 code block and counts its keyword rows against a "full list of N strings" claim, and another reads `atlas_full_notf.json`'s `depth` map to verify the Intro's "a transformer of N–M layers" range is exactly the min/max across the ten models.

Sources: [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L32-L33), [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L101-L110), [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L163-L179), [audit_manuscript_core.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_core.py#L1-L9), [audit_manuscript_core.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_core.py#L136-L157), [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L207-L214)

## Derived Claims: Recompute, Don't Compare

`audit_manuscript_derived.py` closes a coverage hole the other two modules cannot see. Its docstring reports that a coverage measurement over the Results and Discussion found **33 numbers that do not appear verbatim in any JSON**: minima and medians over a list, ratios of two stored figures, a correlation across models, a reciprocal. Nothing verified those, "so a stale one would have survived every re-run — which is exactly how the 28.4× selection artefact lasted as long as it did."

The module's answer is a strict rule stated in its header: each check **recomputes the quantity from the stored primitives instead of comparing it to a second stored copy of itself**, because "a copy can go stale in step with the text, a recomputation cannot." The recomputed quantities include:

| Derived claim | Recomputation from primitives |
|---|---|
| r(graph size, hits) across models | `np.corrcoef` over `per_model[m]["n_pairs"]` vs `["hits"]` for all ten models |
| CKA span, median, shuffle floor, min ratio | `min`/`max`/`np.median`/`real/shuf` over the 45-entry `cka_null` pair list |
| Corroboration gain (ge2/ge1) | `curve["2"]["fold"] / curve["1"]["fold"]` from `hypothesis_trrust2.json` |
| "About one correct edge in every N pairs" | `n_pairs / hits`, with `tol_rel=0.02` for the word "about" |
| Backbone specific % | `100 * triviality["specific"] / triviality["n_ge8"]` |
| Dedup arithmetic consistency | `max(\|hits_block_carried + hits_rest − hits_dedup\|) <= 2` across models |

Two claims in this family expose a hazard worth naming. The corroboration-gain check deliberately reads the all-ten curve from `hypothesis_trrust2.json` and *not* the five-model version in `hypothesis_final.json` (5.3×/28.4×), because the manuscript reports the five-model figure only as a direction check — "reading the gain off that file would silently restate the selected numbers as the headline." And the Fig 4 caption check verifies a *bound*, not a value: the caption states "every pair exceeds its floor >N-fold," so the check requires the recomputed minimum ratio to fall in `[N, N+10)`. The comment records that the caption read ">10-fold" for weeks while the text said fortyfold — an inconsistency invisible to value-equality checks.

Where a derived number had no primitives to recompute from at all, the fix was upstream, not in the auditor: the two affected figures are now *written by their producing scripts* (`hypothesis_pubmed`'s uncapped co-mention rate; `study_bias_coverage.py`), so the audit can read them like verbatim values.

Sources: [audit_manuscript_derived.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_derived.py#L2-L13), [audit_manuscript_derived.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_derived.py#L74-L81), [audit_manuscript_derived.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_derived.py#L100-L104), [audit_manuscript_derived.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_derived.py#L120-L136), [audit_manuscript_derived.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript_derived.py#L216-L238)

## Supplement: Generated or Verified, Nothing Else

`audit_supplement.py` enforces a binary property over the supplementary tables: **every number is either generated or verified**. The motivating incidents are in the docstring — Table S3 contradicted itself on dead-feature fractions, Table S5 kept a fold range the main text had corrected, Table S2's heading lied about its filter — and the structural fix split the supplement in two:

- **Generated tables** (S2, S3, S5, S8, S9, S10 — the report line says exactly this) are regenerated from the result JSONs by `make_supp_tables.py` and "cannot drift." That script's docstring records the trigger: S8 still carried 20-permutation folds after the manuscript moved to 250, and S9/S10 — including the paper's actual deliverable, the released prediction list — "had never been written at all." S2's generator now emits *both* filter columns (5–500 and 5–200) because the permissive annotator admits 5–500 gene sets while the calibrated one admits 5–200, with a parenthetical confession of the earlier mislabeling preserved in the output.
- **Hand-written tables** (S1, S4, S6, S7) are audited by `audit_supplement.py`, which parses each `## Table S…` section and re-derives every cell from a different authority than the prose.

The four verified tables each check against a distinct ground truth, which is the table's design lesson:

| Table | Verified against | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| S1 per-model spec | `sae_health.json` + `controls.json:svd_null` | Row regex → layers, `d_sae = 4 × d_model` arithmetic, variance explained; plus a coverage check that all models appear |
| S4 annotator parameters | **The source code itself** | Regex-extracts `ALPHA, TOP, AMIN, MX = ...` from `degree_null.py` and compares to the table cells; asserts "no PPI" in the databases column |
| S6 software environment | **The running interpreter** | Compares live `platform.python_version`, `numpy.__version__`, `scipy.__version__`, `h5py.__version__` to the table's local column |
| S7 SAE vs PCA at k=32 | `controls.json:svd_null` | Per-model PCA/SAE/gap with tolerance `5e-4`; coverage check over all models |

Two finer checks extend the same principle to captions: the Fig S2 caption's fold range and permutation count are compared against `depth_backbone.json`, and the supplementary figure list is asserted to be in order "1,2" — a cheap guard against reordering that would silently orphan in-text references.

Sources: [audit_supplement.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_supplement.py#L2-L16), [audit_supplement.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_supplement.py#L42-L77), [audit_supplement.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_supplement.py#L79-L113), [audit_supplement.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_supplement.py#L115-L140), [make_supp_tables.py](/pipeline/scripts/make_supp_tables.py#L2-L9), [make_supp_tables.py](/pipeline/scripts/make_supp_tables.py#L44-L60)

## Figures: Staleness by Content Hash

`audit_figures.py` addresses the surface the manuscript audit is structurally blind to: a rendered PNG carries no link to the JSON it was drawn from. The docstring gives the incident — Fig S2 shipped for four days showing superseded folds with a "N=20 perms" legend — and the design principle: staleness is detected **by content, not by timestamp**, so "a figure re-rendered with no change to its data is not stale, and a figure whose data changed is, whatever the file dates say."

The mechanism has three parts. First, a static registry (`FIGURES`) maps each of the five plotting scripts (`make_figures.py`, `make_fig14.py`, `make_fig5.py`, `make_figS1.py`, `make_figS2.py`) to the figures it owns — seven PNGs total. Second, `sources_of()` scans each script's source for `json.load(open(...))` calls and extracts the `.json` filenames, so a newly added plotting script "is picked up automatically" if it loads data conventionally. Third, each source file's SHA-256 (first 16 hex chars) is recorded in a manifest, `figures/.sources.json`, whenever figures are stamped.

The lifecycle runs through two modes. In `--check` mode, the current hashes are compared to the manifest and each figure receives one of four statuses: `MISSING` (never rendered), `UNSTAMPED` (no manifest entry — run `--update` after rendering), `STALE` (some source hash changed since render, with the offending filenames listed), or `ok`. In `--update` mode, the stamp is *earned*, not granted: before writing the manifest, the script refuses if any figure is missing **or has an mtime older than the newest of its sources** — "a figure older than a source it is drawn from was not re-rendered, whatever the person stamping believes." The motivating failure is preserved in the comment: `make_fig14.py` once died on a typo *after* writing Fig 4 and *before* Fig 1, and a `--update` run immediately afterward certified the un-rendered Fig 1 as current.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R["Run plotting script<br/>(make_fig*.py)"] --> D{"Rendered all<br/>owned figures?"}
    D -- "died mid-script" --> X["Fig older than its data:<br/>refuse to stamp"]
    D -- yes --> U["audit_figures.py --update"]
    U --> S["Stamp SHA-256 of each<br/>source JSON into .sources.json"]
    S --> C["Later: audit_figures.py --check"]
    C --> H{"Source hashes<br/>match manifest?"}
    H -- yes --> OK["ok"]
    H -- no --> ST["STALE + offending files"]
    H -- "no entry" --> US["UNSTAMPED"]
    ST --> R
    US --> U
```

> [!TIP]
> The mtime guard on `--update` is the subtle piece: stamping is a claim about *causality* ("these figures were rendered from these sources"), and file-content hashes alone cannot verify ordering. Comparing figure mtime against the max source mtime is the cheapest sufficient check that the render actually happened after the data existed in its current form.

Sources: [audit_figures.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_figures.py#L2-L17), [audit_figures.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_figures.py#L31-L57), [audit_figures.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_figures.py#L73-L98), [audit_figures.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_figures.py#L100-L128)

## Site Drift and the Exit-Code Contract
