The sixth check binds the published site to the same discipline. `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` rebuilds the prediction block embedded in `index.html` (via `inject_atlas.py` and `data/explorer.json`, covered in [Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files)) from the hypothesis result files; its `--check` mode reports drift between the embedded block and those files. `audit_all.py` registers it under the label "The public site against the same results," which closes the loop: manuscript, supplement, figures, and site are all audited against one shared source directory, so a result-file change that propagates to any published surface must either be re-rendered everywhere or fail the gate.

The contract binding the whole suite is uniform and strict:

| Property | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Individual module failure | Prints diagnostics, `sys.exit(1)` |
| Sentence removed/rewritten | `"no such sentence"` → treated as a failure, not a skip |
| Missing source file | `"source missing"` → failure (`check(expected=None)`) |
| Any child failure in `audit_all.py` | Aggregate exit 1; details printed for failing modules only |
| Success | Tally line, e.g. "All checks pass: text, supplement and figures agree with the results they report" |

The orchestrator closes its failure path with a policy statement that functions as the system's constitution: **"Fix the source of the disagreement, not the check."** Checks are derived from the artifacts' real provenance, so the correct response to a failure is to re-render, regenerate, or correct the number — never to loosen a pattern. Operationally, all modules resolve their data root from the `ATLAS_BASE` environment variable (defaulting to the authors' local path), so the suite runs unchanged against any checkout that has fetched the result files — the fetching mechanics are covered in [Release Archives and Checksummed Fetching](19-release-archives-and-checksummed-fetching), and the policy rationale for recording analysis decisions alongside is in [Decision Log Design](20-decision-log-design).

Sources: [audit_all.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L19-L26), [audit_all.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L37-L49), [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L25-L29), [audit_manuscript.py](/pipeline/scripts/audit_manuscript.py#L17), [README.md](/pipeline/scripts/README.md#L3-L5)

## Where This Fits

The audit suite is the enforcement layer for the provenance chain described across the Reproducibility Engineering section: upstream, [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map) documents every JSON these checks read; downstream, [Release Archives and Checksummed Fetching](19-release-archives-and-checksummed-fetching) covers how the GPU-extraction outputs those JSONs depend on are retrieved verifiably, [Decision Log Design](20-decision-log-design) records the methodological choices the audit numbers must reflect, and [Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files) explains the assembly pipeline whose `--check` mode serves as the suite's sixth module. For the statistical machinery behind the numbers being audited — nulls, permutation counts, and calibration — see [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim) and [Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation); the robustness variants checked in section 3.4 are documented in [Reviewer Robustness Analyses](16-reviewer-robustness-analyses).

# Release Archives and Checksummed Fetching



This page documents how the per-run analysis outputs and external gene-set inputs travel with this repository. The result *summaries* live in `outputs/atlas/comparative/` inside the git checkout, but the raw per-run artifacts — the feature catalogues every downstream script reads — total about 1.2 GB unpacked, so they ship as GitHub release assets instead. A single 37-line shell script, `pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh`, downloads them, verifies each archive's SHA-256 digest against a manifest fetched from the same release, and unpacks everything into exactly the directory layout the local analysis stage expects. The release currently in force is `runs-v2`, the corrected extraction; the superseded `runs-v1` remains reachable through a flag.

Sources: [fetch_runs.sh](pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh#L1-L9), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L47-L51), [scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L86-L87)

## Why the Per-Run Data Ships as Release Assets

The repository keeps two distinct data tiers deliberately separated. The small tier — the comparative result files, nulls, calibration grids and site data — is committed directly, because section 1 of the reproduce guide verifies every published number from it *without any downloads*. The large tier — per-layer feature catalogues for all ten models across three corpus draws, plus the external gene-set databases — is only needed when you want to re-run the analysis rather than check it, and at 1.2 GB unpacked it would bloat every clone. That tier therefore lives in release assets: you fetch it on demand, verify it, unpack it, and the standard scripts consume it transparently via `ATLAS_BASE`.

One boundary is worth stating precisely: the fetch covers catalogues and inputs, not model internals. The GPU extraction stage writes `feature_catalog_L<NN>.json` per layer — the files that get archived — alongside SAE weights (`sae_L<NN>.pt`, about 17 GB total) and activations, which stay on the GPU host and are deliberately not redistributed, since no published number reads them directly.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L18-L28), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L49-L51), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L152-L158)

## The Archive Manifest

Each archive has a defined unpack target under `outputs/atlas/`, and the reproduce guide publishes both the size and the exact SHA-256 digest of every asset. The current tag `runs-v2` holds the corrected extraction (every model reads all 6,000 cells); `runs-v1` keeps the superseded catalogues plus the legacy first cluster run, which exists *only* in v1.

| archive | MB | unpacks to | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `runs-ts3_out.tar.gz` | 70 | `outputs/atlas/ts3_out/` | feature catalogues on the shared corpus: five depth-matched layers for seven models, every layer for GeneCompass, scFoundation and Tahoe-x1; the permissive annotations of the seven models' five layers |
| `runs-alllayer_cat.tar.gz` | 57 | `outputs/atlas/alllayer_cat/` | every-layer catalogues for AIDO.Cell, C2S-Scale, Geneformer-V2, MaxToki, UCE, scGPT, tGPT |
| `runs-heldout_cat.tar.gz` | 23 | `outputs/atlas/heldout_cat/` | catalogues on the held-out draw (5,581 cells, none shared with the corpus), all ten models, five depth-matched layers |
| `runs-seeds.tar.gz` | 24 | `outputs/atlas/seeds/` | the SAE-seed control (three seeds, mid layer and every layer), read by `controls_import.py` |
| `inputs-genesets.tar.gz` | 101 | `outputs/atlas/genesets/` | GO_BP, KEGG, Reactome sets (Enrichr via gseapy, 2026-08-17), STRING v12 edges and aliases, TRRUST edges, the 16,205-gene background; unchanged from v1 |
| `legacy-cluster-run.tar.gz` (v1 only) | 76 | `outputs/atlas/cluster/` | the first cluster run (AIDO, UCE, tGPT, scGPT on an earlier corpus); superseded, read by no published number |

The published manifest itself is short enough to quote in full — this is the digest block your download will be checked against:

```
4dc9f0c1928fc8d0121cf01efbf1eba38dc53c675b835dfcd960324c405fd122  inputs-genesets.tar.gz
738b694e31f0502cd0e66dc72a83c8199730bde0b799e8168df4cd1c4147b4ee  runs-alllayer_cat.tar.gz
295df6e717d991984515cbc8c5ed82505dce67fcab1b1d7c3c44ec12b66bc55c  runs-heldout_cat.tar.gz
41382c8f762c3bae686f63029ec897d51061f1a26b10d87174e4542dd6e83a7c  runs-seeds.tar.gz
898c5e9471ba315e2da30792c7e226f4bc2f641b46f295d89b080d4fa933f0f1  runs-ts3_out.tar.gz
bdffaf0042bf4abc03d62dd23294cb898d5f197230281914dc783d69706e5866  legacy-cluster-run.tar.gz (v1)
```

Note the deliberate immutability signal on `inputs-genesets.tar.gz`: "unchanged from v1" means the external gene-set snapshot is pinned across the v1→v2 release boundary, so only the model catalogues changed when the extraction was corrected. The `legacy-cluster-run.tar.gz` provenance is also recorded in the legacy code's README — it is the output of a run no published number depends on.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L57-L77), [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L130-L135), [legacy/README.md](pipeline/legacy/README.md#L16-L25)

## Anatomy of the Fetch Script

The script is structured as a flat sequence guarded by `set -euo pipefail` — any failed download, checksum mismatch or extraction aborts the whole run immediately. Conceptually it executes the following flow:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["bash pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh"] --> B["Resolve repo + tag<br/>ATLAS_RELEASE_REPO · ATLAS_RELEASE_TAG"]
    B --> C["mkdir -p outputs/atlas/"]
    C --> D["curl SHA256SUMS from the release"]
    D --> E{"next archive<br/>of the 5 listed"}
    E --> F["curl the .tar.gz"]
    F --> G["grep its single manifest line<br/>pipe into shasum -a 256 -c -"]
    G -->|mismatch| H["abort<br/>set -e stops everything"]
    G -->|verified| I["tar xzf, then rm the archive"]
    I --> E
    E -->|all five done| J{"--legacy flag?"}
    J -->|yes| K["curl SHA256SUMS.legacy<br/>from the runs-v1 tag"]
    K --> L["verify + unpack<br/>legacy-cluster-run.tar.gz<br/>then rm archive + manifest"]
    L --> M["print the unpacked contents"]
    J -->|no| M
```

Two implementation details carry the integrity guarantee. First, the manifest is fetched *once* before the loop begins (`curl -sSL -o SHA256SUMS "$BASE/SHA256SUMS"`), establishing the expected digests before any payload arrives. Second, verification is *streamed per file*: `grep " $f\$" SHA256SUMS | shasum -a 256 -c -` extracts exactly the manifest line ending in the archive's name and pipes it straight into `shasum`'s check mode via stdin, so the digest comparison happens against freshly downloaded bytes with no intermediate trust state. The `$` anchor in the grep pattern matters — it prevents a file named as a prefix of another from matching the wrong line.

> [!TIP]
> The verification pattern protects against truncated or corrupted transfers and against an archive that silently drifted from its published digest — it does not defend against a compromised release origin, since the manifest and the archive travel over the same channel from the same repository. Its job is reproducibility of the *bytes*, which is what the audit system downstream depends on.

Third, extraction is destructive-by-design: `tar xzf "$f" && rm "$f"` deletes each archive the moment it unpacks. The pipeline never holds both the compressed (~275 MB total) and unpacked (~1.2 GB) copies, trading re-download cost for disk — a reasonable trade given the release URL is deterministic and checksummed.

Sources: [fetch_runs.sh](pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh#L10-L27), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L61-L67)

## Configuration Surface and the Legacy Branch

The script exposes a deliberately minimal configuration: two environment variables and one positional flag. Path resolution is self-anchoring — `ROOT` is derived from the script's own location (`$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)`), so the destination is always `<repo-root>/outputs/atlas/` regardless of where you invoke it from.

| knob | default | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `ATLAS_RELEASE_REPO` | `Biodyn-AI/atlas-comparison` | redirect downloads to a fork's releases |
| `ATLAS_RELEASE_TAG` | `runs-v2` | pin to `runs-v1` to reproduce the superseded catalogues |
| `--legacy` (argument) | off | additionally fetch `legacy-cluster-run.tar.gz` from the hard-coded `runs-v1` tag |

The legacy branch is structurally interesting because it demonstrates *tag mixing*: the five current archives come from whatever `ATLAS_RELEASE_TAG` resolves to (v2 by default), while the legacy cluster run is always fetched from `runs-v1`, which is hard-coded as `LEGACY_TAG`. It follows the same manifest-verify-extract discipline but with a separately named manifest (`SHA256SUMS.legacy`), and it cleans up both the archive and its manifest afterward so the destination directory contains only unpacked data. This asymmetry exists because the corrected v2 extraction deliberately left the old cluster run behind: it was produced by the earlier corpus and reads into no published number, yet is preserved for provenance.

Sources: [fetch_runs.sh](pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh#L11-L17), [fetch_runs.sh](pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh#L28-L36), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L54-L59)

## What Lands Where — and the Two Inputs You Must Fetch Yourself

After a successful run, `outputs/atlas/` contains the five unpacked directories and the script prints a final `ls` of the result so you can eyeball the layout. This lands in exactly the structure the local analysis stage expects, since every script reads and writes under `$ATLAS_BASE/outputs/atlas/` — the reproduce guide's setup step exports `ATLAS_BASE` to the repository root precisely so the fetched archives slot in without path configuration.

However, two evidence inputs are **not redistributed** at all, for licensing/practical reasons, and must be fetched from their original sources:

| input | source | lands in | consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gene2pubmed.gz`, `Homo_sapiens.gene_info.gz` | NCBI Gene FTP (ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/DATA/), snapshot as of 2026-09-11 | `outputs/atlas/pubmed/` | `hypothesis_pubmed.py`, `hypothesis_studybias.py`, `study_bias_coverage.py` |
| Replogle et al. 2022 pseudobulk Perturb-seq (`K562_gwps_normalized_bulk_01.h5ad`, `rpe1_normalized_bulk_01.h5ad`) | plus.figshare.com | `outputs/atlas/perturb/` | `hypothesis_perturb.py`, `hypothesis_studybias.py`, `study_bias_coverage.py` |

This split means a full re-run of the held-out prediction tests needs the fetch script *plus* two manual downloads, whereas everything else — matrices, nulls, calibration, site assembly, figures, audits — runs purely from the fetched archives and the committed result files. The scripts that consume these inputs will fail loudly if the directories are empty, and the per-script docstrings name their own reads and writes.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L8-L13), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L79-L88), [scripts/README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L1-L5)

## Failure Semantics and Reproduction Discipline

Because the script runs under `set -euo pipefail`, every failure mode terminates at the exact point of fault: a failed `curl` aborts before checksum comparison, a checksum mismatch aborts before `tar`, and a failed extraction aborts before the archive is deleted. The consequence is a clean resume property — re-running the script simply re-downloads and re-verifies everything, and since archives are removed only after successful extraction, a partially failed run leaves at most one stale archive on disk with no half-unpacked state. Seeds inside the downstream scripts are fixed, so once the archives are in place, the numbers reproduce exactly.

The whole fetch step is one line in the reproduce guide's stage 2, positioned *before* the local pipeline order — the catalogue-consuming builders (`atlas_build_ts3`, `alllayer_matrix`, and everything downstream) cannot start without `ts3_out/` and `alllayer_cat/` on disk, and the seed control import reads `seeds/`. If your intent is only to verify published numbers rather than re-run anything, you do not need the archives at all: section 1 of the reproduce guide runs the full audit from the committed result files alone.

> [!TIP]
> Before trusting a re-run built on fetched archives, check the release lineage first: catalogues fetched from `runs-v1` will not reproduce v2 numbers — the entire correction history (AIDO.Cell reading only 32 cells under the old position cap, the 419 overlapping held-out cells) is a property of the tag, not the code, since the analysis scripts themselves are identical across both releases.

Sources: [fetch_runs.sh](pipeline/scripts/fetch_runs.sh#L10-L27), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L47-L55), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L90-L132), [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L130-L135)

## Where to Go Next

The fetch mechanism is one link in a three-layer reproducibility chain. To understand how the fetched catalogues flow into the result files the audit checks, read [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map). To understand *why* `runs-v2` exists — the extraction faults that made v1 catalogues unusable — read [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run). For how the fixed-seed re-run discipline is recorded over time, continue to [Decision Log Design](20-decision-log-design).

# Decision Log Design



`docs/DECISIONS.md` is the rationale ledger of the atlas-comparison project: sixteen numbered entries that record, for every consequential choice in the pipeline, what was decided, why, what it cost, and where the implementation lives. This page documents the *design* of that log — its entry format, its numbering and cross-reference system, its contract with the automated audit, and its deliberate policy of preserving retractions and failures. It sits in the Reproducibility Engineering chapter between the audit machinery and the corrected re-run, because the log is the document both of those processes write into.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L1-L4), [README.md](README.md#L20-L24)

## The Entry Contract: Four Questions, in Work Order

The preamble defines the entire format in three lines: *"What was decided, why, what it cost, and where it lives in the code. In the order the work was done."* Every entry is therefore an anatomy of a single engineering trade-off rather than a specification. Decision 1 (one shared corpus) is the canonical example: the *what* states the protocol exactly (6,000 Tabula Sapiens cells, 2,000 per tissue, raw counts, seed 0, held-out seed 1), the *why* explains the rejected alternative (earlier single-model atlases ran on different corpora, so "any difference between them could be the data"), the *cost* names what the choice forecloses (cross-species models read on human cells only; no claim about other tissues or platforms), and a final `Code:` line pins the decision to `pipeline/atlas_h100/build_ts_corpus.py`. The chronological ordering is a deliberate choice — the log reads as a lab notebook of decisions in the sequence they were actually made, which is why late corrections (decisions 11 and 16) appear at the bottom rather than being folded back into earlier entries.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    T["## N. Title<br/>permanent numbered anchor"] --> W["What<br/>the choice, with exact parameters<br/>and seeds"]
    W --> Y["Why<br/>the alternative rejected,<br/>and the evidence for rejecting it"]
    Y --> C["Cost<br/>what the choice gives up,<br/>confounds it introduces"]
    C --> P["Code:<br/>the scripts that implement it"]
    P -.->|numbers re-derived from<br/>result files| AUD["audit_all.py"]
```

The `Cost:` field is what distinguishes this log from a changelog or an ADR collection. Decision 3 (the SAE) spends more words on costs than on configuration: it admits the hyperparameters "was not swept" (seed variance was measured instead — the permissive mid-layer core varies by 12 %), that surplus capacity "fills with near-copies of the strongest signal" in eight of ten models, and that tGPT's 21.3 % dead features are "a confound for every tGPT-specific result… not corrected for." Decisions are recorded as priced trades, not wins.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L6-L19), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L36-L59)

| Field | Question answered | Example (decision 1) | Example (decision 3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What** | The exact choice | 6,000 cells, seed 0; held-out seed 1 | TopK, k = 32, dict 4×d_model, Adam 3e-4, 4 epochs |
| **Why** | Alternative rejected + reason | Different corpora would confound model comparison | Matches earlier atlases' bio-sae config, so features are comparable |
| **Cost** | What it gives up or risks | No cross-species or other-tissue claims | Near-copy feature blocks; tGPT dead-feature confound, uncorrected |
| **Code:** | Where it is implemented | `build_ts_corpus.py` | `common/sae.py`, `scripts/sae_health.py` |

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L1-L4)

## The Sixteen Decisions: A Catalog

The entries are not homogeneous; the format admits structural variance wherever a table or a bullet list communicates better than prose. Decision 5 is a claim-to-null coverage matrix — a three-column table mapping every headline claim to the specific null built against it and its permutation count. Decision 16 is a bullet list of the extraction faults. The catalog below classifies all sixteen by what kind of knowledge each preserves:

| # | Entry | Kind | Cross-references |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | One corpus for all ten models | Design choice | — |
| 2 | Every layer, five depth-matched read-outs | Design choice + **invariant rule** | paper §3.1 |
| 3 | The SAE | Configuration + measured costs | → decision 16 |
| 4 | Two annotators, which one counts | Method selection, grid-search provenance | — |
| 5 | A null behind every claim | Claim/null/permutations matrix | — |
| 6 | What was retracted | Negative results, kept reproducible | — |
| 7 | What survived | Positive results | → decision 8 |
| 8 | Held-out prediction test | Test design + **iteration notes** | — |
| 9 | Two more evidence kinds (literature, perturbation) | Supporting evidence | — |
| 10 | Why no new biology | Negative-result analysis | — |
| 11 | Model facts corrected against papers | Late correction | ← decision 15 |
| 12 | What the site reads from data | Interface contract | — |
| 13 | Things that did not go to plan | Failure disclosure | → decision 16 |
| 14 | KEGG | Scope + licensing state | — |
| 15 | The audit | Process boundary | → decision 11 |
| 16 | The extraction was wrong; re-run (2026-10) | Major correction | ← decisions 3, 13 |

Two entry types deserve note. Decision 2 encodes an **invariant**, not just a choice: "feature counts are never summed across layers and never read as concepts coexisting in one representation, because each layer is its own space with its own dictionary." And decision 8's "Two design points that took iteration" records *process* guardrails — the corroboration curve is reported over all ten models rather than the four that passed, "because the four were selected on TRRUST and would then be re-scored against it," with the selected set "read from `hypothesis_trrust2.json` (p < 0.05), not typed in." The log thus carries anti-selection-bias rules alongside configuration facts.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L21-L34), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L85-L107), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L163-L173)

## Decision Numbers as Permanent Cross-References

The numbering is the log's addressing scheme, and the references run in both directions. Inside the document, decision 3 cites decision 16 ("decision 16 explains why it is not a position cap"), decision 7 points to decision 8 for the regulatory-prediction result, decision 13's failure list ends with "the extraction itself was wrong… decision 16," and decision 15's audit boundary invokes decision 11 as the example of a fact found outside the audit's scope. Outside the document, the top-level `README.md` closes its account of the October re-extraction with "what changed and why is in `docs/DECISIONS.md` (decision 16)," and `docs/CHANGELOG.md`'s 2026-10-11 entry records the coordinated update: "README, DECISIONS (16), METHODS, RESULTS, REPRODUCE updated."

The maintenance consequence is an **append-only discipline**: because both internal entries and external documents cite decisions by number, a new decision must be appended at the end — never inserted or renumbered. Entry 16 exists as a number precisely because decisions 3 and 13 could not predict that the extraction faults would need their own entry when they were first written.

> [!TIP]
> Treat the decision numbers as a public API. Any edit that renumbers or splits an entry breaks four internal references, the README pointer, and the changelog record simultaneously — the log is only safe to extend, in order.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L41), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L145), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L246), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L262), [README.md](README.md#L32-L35), [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L134-L135)

## The Numbers Contract with the Audit

The preamble's final sentence — *"Numbers are the ones the audit checks against the result files"* — makes `DECISIONS.md` a party to the machine-verified claims pipeline. Decision 15 spells out both sides of that contract: `audit_all.py` re-derives every number in the paper, supplement, figures and site from the result file that produced it (312 checks, six modules), with figures stamped against the hashes of their inputs "so a figure older than its data fails." What the log deliberately records beyond that envelope is equally explicit: "The audit does not check prose claims, architecture facts (decision 11 was found by reading the model papers) or whether a figure is legible. Those were checked by hand, three passes."

This boundary explains why decision 11 exists at all. The three corrected model facts (MaxToki's rank-value encoding, GeneCompass's rank-plus-value input with four knowledge priors, tGPT's ~120 M parameter count) are exactly the class of claim the audit cannot reach — they describe external papers, not result files. The decision log is therefore the *ledger of last resort* for truths no script can verify: after the corrections, "everything that reads model size or the rank/non-rank split was recomputed… No conclusion changed," and the log records that re-derivation even though the audit only covers its numbers. The audit's own failure philosophy — "Fix the source of the disagreement, not the check" — is the same instinct the log embodies: documentation and data must agree, and when they disagree, the documentation entry names the source of truth.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L256-L262), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L208-L223), [audit_all.py](pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L19-L26), [audit_all.py](pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py#L44-L46)

## Keeping Negatives, Costs, and Failures

The log's most distinctive design policy is that discarded and failed work is a first-class entry type, not deleted history. Decision 6 lists four retracted claims — the "universal core" of ~2,000 shared concepts (which fails the random-gene null at 365 real against 582 random), annotation rate as an interpretability score, the "100 % SVD-invisible" claim, and the new-biology shortlist (0 of 207 candidates survive its nulls) — and closes with the reproducibility commitment: "The scripts and result files for all four are kept so the negatives are reproducible." Decision 13, "Things that did not go to plan," discloses operational mishaps in single lines that pair failure with fix: "`controls.py` used to overwrite the shared `controls.json` and once wiped fourteen blocks… It merges now."

Costs get the same permanence. Decision 10 closes its negative result with a scope statement the project stands behind: "the atlas ranks testable links; it cannot confirm or refute a link about an unstudied gene with these resources, and neither could anything else." Decision 14 records forward-looking administrative state alongside analysis — "the copyright form is to be cleared before publication" — showing the log also tracks obligations, not just measurements. For an intermediate developer the transferable pattern is: **a decision log that only survives successes is marketing; keeping the nulls, the confounds, and the wiped files is what makes it engineering documentation.**

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L109-L125), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L234-L246), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L198-L206), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L248-L254)

## Corrections Without Erasure

Decisions 11 and 16 define how the log absorbs post-release corrections. Decision 16 is the only dated entry — "(2026-10)" — marking the epoch boundary between the two extraction generations: the position cap that let AIDO.Cell see 32 cells while tGPT saw all 6,000, the non-stable sort that padded top-gene lists with zero-activation filler, the unseeded torch RNG, UCE's cache keyed on a fixed directory, and the 419 held-out cells shared with the corpus. The entry records both the faults and the consequence: "Everything downstream of the catalogues was re-run from scratch… the backbone grew from 78 to 96 concepts… TRRUST prediction holds in four models instead of five (scGPT drops out)." Critically, the superseded state is preserved, not purged: release `runs-v2` holds the corrected catalogues while "`runs-v1` keeps the superseded ones," a split `docs/REPRODUCE.md` mirrors in its archive table and `docs/CHANGELOG.md` mirrors in its dated entries.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph DOC["docs/"]
        D["DECISIONS.md<br/>why + cost"] --- M["METHODS.md<br/>how, in brief"]
        D --- R["RESULTS.md<br/>file → written by → read by"]
        D --- P["REPRODUCE.md<br/>run order + runs-v1/v2"]
        D --- C["CHANGELOG.md<br/>commit subjects, dated"]
    end
    D -->|Code: pointers| S["pipeline/<br/>atlas_h100/ + scripts/"]
    S --> F["outputs/atlas/comparative/<br/>result files"]
    F --> A["audit_all.py<br/>312 checks"]
    A --> MAN["manuscript + supplement"]
    A --> SITE["index.html site"]
```

Each document answers a different question, and the decision log's `Code:` lines are what make the set navigable as a system: a reader starts at a decision, jumps to its implementing scripts, and from there `RESULTS.md` resolves which result file those scripts write and which audit modules read it.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L264-L298), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L57-L59), [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L130-L135), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L1-L3), [METHODS.md](docs/METHODS.md#L1-L4)

| Document | Question it answers | Form |
|---|---|---|
| `DECISIONS.md` | Why this, and what it cost | 16 numbered chronological entries |
| `METHODS.md` | How, in brief | Short sections with code pointers |
| `RESULTS.md` | Which file holds what | Table: file → written by → read by |
| `REPRODUCE.md` | What to run, in what order | Commands + checksummed archive table |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | What happened, when | Dated commit subjects, oldest first |

## Reading On

The decision log is the narrative layer over machinery documented elsewhere in this chapter. To see how the numbers it cites are machine-verified, continue to [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks); to walk through the faults decision 16 summarizes, see [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run); for the result files that the `Code:` pointers and the audit both resolve against, see [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map). For the statistical reasoning behind decisions 4, 5 and 8, [Null Models Behind Every Claim](10-null-models-behind-every-claim) and [Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test) cover the methods the log only prices and records.


# Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run



This page documents the most consequential event in the repository's history: the discovery that the first GPU feature extraction (release `runs-v1`) was internally inconsistent across models, the eight faults that were found and fixed, and the full re-run that produced `runs-v2` — the catalogues behind every published number. It is the engineering complement to the scientific retraction story told in [Key Findings and Retracted Claims](4-key-findings-and-retracted-claims); here the focus is on what was mechanically wrong in the extraction code, how each fault is now guarded in code, and the exact order in which everything was re-computed.

The authoritative narrative lives in the decision log: decision 13 lists process incidents ("things that did not go to plan") and decision 16 is the extraction itself. Per the log, an external read of the code found three faults in the first release; re-running on the fixes exposed more.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L234-L246), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L264-L299), [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L130-L136)

## How the Faults Were Found and Contained

The faults entered through the GPU extraction stage ([Model Adapter Contract](6-model-adapter-contract), [TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training)) and were surfaced late: the changelog's first correction commit is dated 2026-10-05, roughly three weeks after the repository's public revisions began. Three faults were found by reading the code; the remaining five appeared only when the corrected extraction was executed and downstream analyses were rebuilt. The containment strategy is visible in the changelog itself — each fault got its own fix commit, followed by staged re-runs (GPU analyses on 2026-10-07, local stage from scratch on 2026-10-11, release `runs-v2` the same day, and a pair-list correction on 2026-10-14).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["External code review<br/>finds 3 faults"] --> B["Fixes committed<br/>2026-10-05"]
    B --> C["Re-run exposes<br/>5 more faults"]
    C --> D["GPU analyses re-run<br/>on corrected SAEs<br/>2026-10-07"]
    D --> E["Local stage re-run<br/>in documented order<br/>2026-10-11"]
    E --> F["Release runs-v2<br/>corrected catalogues"]
    F --> G["Pair-list + null-tie<br/>hardening 2026-10-14"]
```

Sources: [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L130-L136), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L264-L266)

## The Fault Catalogue

Decision 16 enumerates the faults precisely. The unifying theme of the first group is that the ten models were not actually compared under equal conditions — the thing the whole atlas exists to guarantee ([Ten Foundation Models Compared](3-ten-foundation-models-compared)).

| # | Fault | Symptom in v1 | Fix in code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Position cap in corpus order** | `extract()` stopped at 500,000 gene-token positions taken in corpus order. Models that read many genes per cell saw very few cells: AIDO.Cell 32, scFoundation ≈160, Geneformer-V2 and MaxToki ≈270, UCE 492; tGPT (64 tokens/cell) saw all 6,000 | `--per-cell 168`: every cell read, ≤168 positions kept per cell, seeded draw |
| 2 | **Zero-activation filler in top-gene lists** | A non-stable descending sort padded features that fire on few genes with arbitrary zero-activation genes | `kind="stable"` sort; genes with zero mean activation dropped before truncation |
| 3 | **SAE seeded NumPy but not torch** | Weight init and per-epoch shuffling were unseeded (the published seed control was unaffected — its scripts seeded torch themselves) | `torch.manual_seed(cfg.seed)` at the top of `train_sae` |
| 4 | **UCE preprocessing cache reuse** | UCE's processor skips preprocessing when output files exist; a fixed work-directory name meant every UCE run after the first silently reused 2,000 corpus cells — including the held-out UCE catalogue, which was built on corpus cells | Work dir keyed on a SHA-1 fingerprint of `obs_names` + `var_names` |
| 5 | **Held-out draw not disjoint** | The seed-1 held-out corpus shared 419 of 6,000 cells with the seed-0 training corpus | `make_heldout_disjoint.py` drops them (held-out catalogue now holds 5,581 cells) |
| 6 | **Site CKA heatmap mislabelled blocks** | The site labelled SVD/CKA blocks 0–4 as 0–100% depth; it now reads each model's depth-matched blocks (the paper's CKA numbers came from another file and were correct) | CKA matrix reads depth-matched blocks from all-layer embeddings |
| 7 | **Hand-pasted `controls.json` blocks** | Five blocks of `controls.json` were pasted in by hand from other result files, so the audit compared old text against old copies | `controls_import.py` derives all five blocks from their source files |
| 8 | **Undocumented local steps** | The `--merge` run of `alllayer_concepts.py`, the slow `depth_backbone.py`, and `depth_calibrated.py` were missing from the documented order; the cross-model set was typed in; the full pair list came from a one-off command | All three steps, the model list (read from `hypothesis_trrust2.json`), and the pair list (`hypothesis_trrust3.py`) are now scripts + `REPRODUCE.md` |

Fault 1 deserves emphasis because of its asymmetry: the corpus-order cap did not merely reduce sample size uniformly, it produced a **hidden per-model design matrix**. Any cross-model difference in the v1 catalogues conflated model behaviour with which cells each model had actually seen — the exact confound the shared-corpus decision (decision 1) was designed to eliminate.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L266-L288), [atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L67-L71), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L57-L59)

## Inside the Fixes

### Per-cell extraction replaces the corpus-order cap

The corrected `extract()` keeps the legacy code path deliberately — `per_cell = 0` reproduces the published v1 runs — but the corrected path (`per_cell > 0`) streams activations to disk while the model runs and samples at most `per_cell` positions per cell via a seeded `np.random.default_rng`. Two engineering details are worth noting: per-position **cell IDs are threaded through every adapter yield**, so the sampler can group positions by cell and the held-out control can later split by cell; and each layer is stored as float16 when its values fit (float32 where they exceed the range, which happens for tGPT). The run writes an `extraction.json` manifest recording positions, unique cells, `per_cell`, seed, and per-layer dtype — the audit trail that would have caught fault 1 had it existed in v1.

```python
# pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py (corrected path)
for c in np.unique(cids):
    pos = np.flatnonzero(cids == c)
    keep.append(pos if len(pos) <= per_cell
                else np.sort(rng.choice(pos, per_cell, replace=False)))
```

Sources: [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L11-L31), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L36-L48), [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L81-L87)

### Stable, filler-free top-gene lists

In `build_catalog()`, the per-feature gene ranking uses `np.argsort(..., kind="stable")` for tie determinism, then masks out genes whose mean activation is zero *before* taking the top 20. A feature that fires on fewer than 20 genes now simply gets a shorter list instead of arbitrary filler — which matters downstream, because the calibrated annotator counts overlaps among a feature's top-10 genes ([Calibrated versus Permissive Annotation](9-calibrated-versus-permissive-annotation)); zero-activation filler could only dilute or spuriously pad those overlaps.

Sources: [pipeline.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/pipeline.py#L107-L119)

### Torch seeding and the cache fingerprint

The SAE fix is one line with a comment anchoring it to the fault: `torch.manual_seed(cfg.seed)` covers both Kaiming weight initialisation and the per-epoch `torch.randperm` shuffle. The UCE fix is structural rather than a parameter change: instead of a fixed work directory, the adapter hashes the cell and gene names actually passed in and derives `uce_work/<fingerprint>` from them, so any different corpus or subsample — main vs held-out — is guaranteed its own preprocessing cache.

Sources: [sae.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/common/sae.py#L68-L80), [uce.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/adapters/uce.py#L83-L95)

> [!TIP]
> The DONE-marker resumability in `run_full_fixed.sh` (skip any model with `$OUT/$m/DONE` present) is what made the re-run tractable: a mid-run crash on model 7 of 10 does not force re-extracting the first six. If you port these scripts, keep the marker-per-model pattern — a single global marker would forfeit that property.

### Making the held-out draw actually held out

`make_heldout_disjoint.py` addresses fault 5 with a set-difference on cell barcodes: read the seed-0 corpus backed, drop held-out cells whose `obs_names` appear in it, report the compartment composition of what remains, and write the disjoint h5ad. This is what restored the meaning of "held-out replication" ([Held-Out Regulatory Prediction Test](11-held-out-regulatory-prediction-test), [Shared Corpus and Held-Out Draw](8-shared-corpus-and-held-out-draw)): the released held-out catalogue is built on 5,581 cells, none of which any SAE was trained on.

Sources: [make_heldout_disjoint.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/make_heldout_disjoint.py#L1-L28), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L63-L65)

### Deriving `controls.json` instead of pasting it

`controls_import.py` is the anti-fault-7: it maps every previously hand-pasted block to its source file — `seeds` and `seeds_alllayer` from the GPU-side seed-control JSONs, `heldout` from `heldout.json`, `random_null`/`survivor_nulls`/`stats_final`/`degree_null` as verbatim copies of their result files, and `recalibration` assembled from both recalibration grids plus the robustness sweep — and merges them into `controls.json`. The result is that the audit ([Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks)) now compares freshly derived text against the sources, not a snapshot against a copy.

Sources: [controls_import.py](pipeline/scripts/controls_import.py#L1-L13), [controls_import.py](pipeline/scripts/controls_import.py#L28-L71)

## The Corrected Re-Run

The re-run is a two-stage cascade: everything downstream of the catalogues was re-run from scratch in the documented order ([Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map)), and the GPU-side analyses were re-run on the corrected SAEs first. The GPU stage builds the corpus and the disjoint held-out draw once, then runs three suites — full extraction, held-out extraction, seed control — followed by the downstream GPU analyses (CKA, probes, SVD, explorer maps). A fourth model environment exists only for Tahoe-x1 (torch 2.6.0, flash-attn 2.7.4), and scGPT loads under torch 2.13 through a vocabulary-only torchtext stand-in added during the same correction wave.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C0["build_ts_corpus.py seed 0<br/>6,000 cells, 3 tissues"] --> C1["build_ts_corpus.py seed 1<br/>held-out draw"]
    C1 --> C2["make_heldout_disjoint.py<br/>drop 419 shared cells → 5,581"]
    C0 --> R1["run_full_fixed.sh<br/>--all-layers --per-cell 168 --seed 0"]
    C2 --> R2["run_heldout_fixed.sh<br/>5 depth-matched layers"]
    R1 --> R3["run_seeds_fixed.sh<br/>seeds 0-2"]
    R1 --> R4["run_downstream_fixed.sh<br/>CKA, probes, SVD, explorer"]
    R1 --> X1["out_fixed/&lt;M&gt;/feature_catalog_L*.json"]
    R2 --> X1
    X1 --> L1["Local stage: matrices → concepts → controls →<br/>predictions → assembly → figures → audit_all"]
```

Before/after, the extraction semantics that every consumer of the catalogues inherits:

| Dimension | v1 (superseded) | v2 (published) |
|---|---|---|
| Cells seen per model | 32 (AIDO.Cell) to 6,000 (tGPT) | 6,000 for all ten models |
| Position selection | First 500,000 in corpus order | ≤168 per cell, uniform without replacement, seed 0 |
| Positions per layer | ≤500,000, unequally weighted by model | ≈1M, cells weighted equally |
| Top-gene lists | Unstable sort, zero-activation filler | Stable sort, filler dropped |
| Held-out corpus | 6,000 cells, 419 shared with corpus | 5,581 cells, disjoint |
| Archive | `runs-v1` (kept, superseded) | `runs-v2` (release) |

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L139-L158), [atlas_h100/README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L48-L74), [run_full_fixed.sh](pipeline/atlas_h100/run_full_fixed.sh#L1-L24), [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L131-L133)

> [!TIP]
> One re-run hazard is documented but easy to miss: `hypothesis_trrust3.py` and `hypothesis_sizematched.py` cache co-firing graphs in `comparative/.cofire_cache.pkl`. If you swap catalogues under a fetched `runs-v2` tree — or compare against `runs-v1` via `fetch_runs.sh --legacy` — delete that cache or the local stage will silently score graphs built from the old catalogues.

## What Changed in the Published Numbers

The re-run changed conclusions, not just files — and the decision log states the deltas explicitly. The calibrated backbone grew from 78 to 96 concepts (≥8 of 10 models) and stayed far above both its nulls; held-out replication now holds on **all ten models** rather than a subset, on the genuinely disjoint draw; the TRRUST prediction test passes in four models instead of five — **scGPT drops out** (11.9x on the superseded catalogues, 1.7x with p = 0.27 on the corrected ones, as recorded in decision 8); and the literature and perturbation corroboration got slightly stronger. Post-release hardening continued on the local stage: the released pair list was rebuilt with a pairwise gene-family rule after the per-symbol pattern let 399 same-family pairs through (now 4,485 pairs), and `degree_null.py` sorts equal-degree genes stably so the degree-matched null no longer depends on platform tie order.

The result-file map reflects the new provenance: `heldout_calibrated.json` is annotated "passes, ten models, no cell shared with the corpus", `hypothesis_final.json` holds "the validated models and the released prediction list", and `hypothesis_pairs_full.json` carries the 4,485 pairs with their same-family flags. `runs-v1` remains fetchable (`fetch_runs.sh --legacy`) but is read by no published number — the superseded catalogues are kept precisely so the negative results remain reproducible, mirroring the repository's retraction philosophy.

Sources: [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L290-L295), [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md#L153-L161), [CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md#L135-L138), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L36-L38), [REPRODUCE.md](docs/REPRODUCE.md#L53-L59)

## Where This Page Leaves You

If you are auditing the extraction itself, the code anchors are `common/pipeline.py` (`extract` and `build_catalog`), `common/sae.py` (seeding), `adapters/uce.py` (cache fingerprint), `make_heldout_disjoint.py`, and the `run_*_fixed.sh` scripts. If you want to verify that the current numbers are consistent with the corrected catalogues, run `audit_all.py` per [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks). To fetch the corrected archives with checksum verification, follow [Release Archives and Checksummed Fetching](19-release-archives-and-checksummed-fetching); for how decisions like this one are recorded — including this decision's own numbering — see [Decision Log Design](20-decision-log-design). Continue with [Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files) to see how `runs-v2` catalogues flow into the interactive atlas.


# Site Assembly from Result Files



This page documents how the interactive Comparative SAE Atlas — a single self-contained HTML page with no build framework — is generated from the ~50 result files in `outputs/atlas/comparative/`. It covers the two data lines that feed the site (the concept/statistics object and the Layer-Explorer feature maps), the three build targets produced by one injector script, and the drift checks that keep the public page synchronized with the analyses behind it. The site itself is plain markup with data embedded as `<script type="application/json">` blocks, described by its own meta tags as "Sparse-autoencoder features of ten single-cell foundation models on one 6,000-cell corpus."

Sources: [atlas_template.html](pipeline/atlas_template.html#L1-L11), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L3)

## The Assembly Line at a Glance

Site assembly is a four-stage chain of three local, CPU-only scripts. `atlas_assemble.py` merges component result files into one embedded object; `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` regenerates the prediction/evidence panels of that object from the hypothesis result files; `build_explorer_slim.py` (GPU side) compiles the per-feature maps into two payload sizes; and `inject_atlas.py` pushes everything into the template's placeholder slots, emitting a light build, a full build, and the published page with lazily fetched explorer data.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph COMP["outputs/atlas/comparative/ — component JSONs"]
        MAT["matrix_alllayer.json<br/>(fallback: matrix_ts3_string.json)"]
        PASS["depth / tissue / cka / controls /<br/>findings … (13 pass-through files)"]
        HYP["hypothesis_*.json +<br/>agreement_curve.json + pair_redundancy.json"]
    end
    subgraph GPU["pipeline/atlas_h100/ — GPU-side inputs"]
        EXP["explorer/&lt;M&gt;_explorer.json<br/>(x, y, tx, ty, freq, svd)"]
        CAT["feature_catalog_L*.json"]
        MOD["modules_alllayers.json"]
        ANN["annotations/&lt;M&gt;_L*.json"]
    end
    A["atlas_assemble.py"] --> AF["atlas_full_notf.json (~356 KB)"]
    MAT --> A
    PASS --> A
    AF --> HB["atlas_hypothesis_block.py"]
    HYP --> HB
    HB --> AF2["atlas_full_notf.json<br/>(hypothesis + controls patched)"]
    EXP --> BS["build_explorer_slim.py"]
    CAT --> BS
    MOD --> BS
    ANN --> BS
    BS --> EF["explorer_slim_full.json (~50 MB)"]
    BS --> EL["explorer_slim_light.json (~5 MB)"]
    T["atlas_template.html<br/>(script-data placeholders)"]
    AF2 --> INJ["inject_atlas.py"]
    EF --> INJ
    EL --> INJ
    T --> INJ
    INJ --> IDX["index.html (published)"]
    INJ --> EX["data/explorer.json<br/>+ explorer_stub.json"]
    INJ --> LB["atlas_ts3_light.html (local)"]
    INJ --> FB["atlas_ts3_full.html (local)"]
```

The scripts-README groups exactly these three under "Assemble the site": `atlas_assemble.py` "builds `atlas_full_notf.json`, the one file the site embeds, from the component results", `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` "rebuilds its prediction block from the hypothesis files; `--check` reports drift", and `inject_atlas.py` "embeds the data blocks into `../atlas_template.html` and writes `index.html` and `data/explorer.json`". Everything upstream (matrices, nulls, hypothesis tests) belongs to the pages on the Local Analysis Stage; this page starts where those results already exist as JSON.

Sources: [README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L54-L62)

## Stage 1: `atlas_assemble.py` — Deriving the One Embedded Object

`atlas_assemble.py` re-derives the site's core object `atlas_full_notf.json` for **all models present in the component JSONs** — its docstring specifies it runs "after `reannotate_string.py` (8-model matrix) + the all-layers downstream (with Tahoe added)". The model roster is never hardcoded: it is filtered from a canonical `ORDER` list by whichever models the concept matrix actually contains, so a new model appears on the site purely by appearing in the data.

Sources: [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L1-L14)

Derivation versus pass-through is the script's core split. The **derived** blocks are computed from the concept matrix: coverage (features, annotation rate, concepts per source), the universality spectrum (how many models share each concept), Jaccard similarity, per-model exclusive concepts, totals, lineage (scaling correlations, a scipy dendrogram from `1 − J`, model signatures), firing-rate splits, and the inductive-axis taxonomy with per-programme category universality. The **pass-through** blocks are simply pulled from their own result files if present — and if a file is missing, the block is skipped with a log line rather than crashing, exactly as the docstring promises ("Robust to missing pieces (keeps a block absent rather than crashing)").

| derived in-script | pulled through from own file |
|---|---|
| coverage, universality, similarity, specific, totals, firing | `depth` ← depth_alllayers.json |
| lineage (scaling, dendrogram, signature) | `tissue_layers` ← tissue_alllayers.json |
| axes (taxonomy, category universality) | `cka` ← cka_ts3.json, `cka_layers` ← cka_layers.json |
| extra (economy, rare frontier, gene universality, tissue tradeoff, circuits, hardcells) | `nonlinearity`, `module_themes`, `flow`, `celltype`, `topn`, `gsea`, `controls`, `depth_calibrated`, `findings` |

Sources: [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L1-L7), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L282-L301)

Two merge behaviors matter for reproducibility. First, the script prefers the **all-layer** concept matrix (`matrix_alllayer.json`, the union over every layer) and falls back to the depth-matched `matrix_ts3_string.json`, asserting if neither exists. Second, the SVD block is merged incrementally: it starts from the previous `atlas_full_notf.json`'s `svd` block (an older subset of models) and updates it with any per-model `svd/<M>_L*_svd.json` files, and the cross-layer `flow` block is preserved from the old file if it was not recomputed this round — so re-running the assembler on a partial analysis set degrades gracefully instead of erasing sections.

Sources: [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L55-L62), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L303-L316), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L318-L320)

## Stage 2: `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` — Regenerating the Panels That Once Drifted

The site's prediction, independent-evidence and novelty panels have their own builder, and its existence is an incident report. The block feeding those panels "was assembled by hand. Nothing regenerated it and nothing checked it, so when the literature null was made reproducible the page kept serving the old z = 40.48 while the manuscript said 34.7 — the same class of drift the manuscript audit exists to catch, on the public half of the project." The fix: every field of the `hypothesis` block is now derived from the canonical result files, so "re-running an analysis and re-injecting is enough to keep the site true."

Sources: [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L2-L11)

| result file | feeds on the site |
|---|---|
| `hypothesis_trrust2.json` | per-model recovery bars, recurrence curve, permutation count (500, matching what the bars are drawn from) |
| `hypothesis_final.json` | ground truth, validated models, worked examples (capped at `N_EXAMPLES = 18`) |
| `hypothesis_pairs_full.json` | `pairs_all` — **every** released pair as compact rows `[gene_a, gene_b, n_models, weight, co_mentions, same_family]`, so the page lists, filters and exports all pairs instead of fourteen examples |
| `agreement_curve.json` | the many-draw agreement estimate quoted where the 100-draw null is too sparse |
| `hypothesis_robust.json` / `hypothesis_sizematched.json` | robustness variants and the equal-budget re-scoring |
| `hypothesis_pubmed.json` / `hypothesis_perturb.json` | literature co-mention and Perturb-seq panels, novelty counts |
| `pair_redundancy.json` | the near-duplicate check behind the prediction panel's reading |
| `cka_svd_null.json`, `backbone_composition.json`, `backbone_terms.json` | controls patches: `survivor_nulls` (replacing an early four-model subset with the full ten-model null), backbone composition, and the full ≥8-sharing term list (the original page had only 40 of 78 terms) |

Sources: [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L29-L31), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L54-L70), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L111-L127)

The builder encodes presentation-judgment rules that raw numbers would get wrong. A fold value against a null that produced **no edge at all** is set to `null` — the comment explains that "1.5e9 rendered as '1520000000x' would be the most confident claim on it". The permutation count printed beside the per-model bars comes from `trrust2` (500 rewirings), not `hypothesis_final` (200), because "the page said 200 for a while" while drawing its bars from the other file. A `diffs()` helper yields **every changed leaf**, so a rebuild reports exactly which fields moved, and `--check` mode prints the drift and exits `1` without writing — usable as a CI-style gate.

> [!TIP]
> Run `python scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py --check` after any analysis re-run: a non-zero exit is the signal that the committed `atlas_full_notf.json` has drifted from the result files, and the final print tells you the required next action verbatim — "==> now run scripts/inject_atlas.py and deploy index.html".

Sources: [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L37-L43), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L129-L136), [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L158-L166)

## Stage 3: `build_explorer_slim.py` — Two Payloads for the Feature Maps

The Layer Explorer's per-feature data comes from the GPU side, where `layer_explorer.py`, `tsne_coords.py` and `coact_embed.py` produce the coordinates and firing statistics, and `build_explorer_slim.py` compiles them into the flat format the page renders. Each feature collapses to one **`pts` row of ten numbers** — `[x*100, y*100, module, svd, geneIdx, freqKey, id, tf, tx*100, ty*100]` — where `(x, y)` are decoder-UMAP and `(tx, ty)` t-SNE coordinates. Merging happens at build time: the top gene per feature comes from the feature catalogues, module colour and TF flags from `modules_alllayers.json` (features outside the top-degree co-activation graph are left uncoloured/grey), and the per-layer annotation rate from the annotations files, with a shared per-model gene dictionary (`genes`) keeping the payload small.

Sources: [build_explorer_slim.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L1-L13), [build_explorer_slim.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L44-L63), [README.md](pipeline/atlas_h100/README.md#L31-L36)

Two sizes are emitted from the same pass: `explorer_slim_full.json` (~50 MB, **every alive feature**) for the local, no-size-limit build, and `explorer_slim_light.json` (~5.3 MB), which keeps only the top 500 features per layer ranked by firing rate for the published artifact. This size discipline is why the GPU README lists the pair as "the feature maps of the site's Layer explorer", and why the result-file map notes the full file is "served to the site as data/explorer.json".

Sources: [build_explorer_slim.py](pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L64-L80), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L26-L27)

## Stage 4: `inject_atlas.py` — Placeholders, Patches, and Three Builds

The template (`pipeline/atlas_template.html`) is the "canonical editable markup (data blocks are `__DATA__` placeholders)". The injector reads it, finds every `<script id="...-data" type="application/json">` line with a regex that captures the indentation, and replaces the placeholder with the contents of the mapped file — six slots: `modules-data`, `genes-data`, `atlas-data`, `health-data`, `programme-data`, and `explorer-data`. The slot comments document why each block exists; for example, `health-data` (dead-feature fractions) is embedded "so a model whose lead rests on the roster's weakest dictionaries (tGPT) carries that caveat next to its recommendation".

| slot id | source file | size | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `atlas-data` | atlas_full_notf.json | 356 KB | everything: coverage, universality, similarity, depth, tissue, CKA, SVD, controls, hypothesis block |
| `genes-data` | genes_ts3.json | 2,769 KB | gene-search index |
| `modules-data` | modules_alllayers.json | 9,036 KB | co-activation graphs and communities |
| `health-data` | sae_health.json | 1 KB | dead-feature caveat beside model recommendations |
| `programme-data` | programme_table.json | — | programmes × models with untrained-SAE, co-expression and random-gene baselines |
| `explorer-data` | explorer_slim_*.json **or** the lazy stub | 5–50 MB | the Layer Explorer maps |

Sources: [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L18-L31), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L10), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L32), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L52), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L64)

One `build()` call produces each target, and the **SITE build differs in exactly one mechanism: lazy loading**. When `lazy="data/explorer.json"` is passed, the injector writes the full explorer JSON to `data/explorer.json` next to the page and embeds only a stub in the `explorer-data` slot — `{"lazy": "data/explorer.json", "models": [...], "mb": <size>}` — so "the published HTML is a fifth of the size and the maps are fetched the first time someone opens the explorer". The light and full builds instead embed their payloads inline for offline use.

| build | explorer payload | destination | role |
|---|---|---|---|
| LIGHT | explorer_slim_light.json (inline) | `atlas_ts3_light.html` | local, size-capped artifact |
| FULL | explorer_slim_full.json (inline) | `atlas_ts3_full.html` | local, no size limit |
| SITE | stub + `data/explorer.json` (lazy) | `index.html` in the repository root | the published page |

Sources: [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L41-L55), [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L78-L83)

The injector also keeps the prose honest as the model roster grows. `N_MODELS` is read from `atlas_full_notf.json` itself; two hardcoded readouts are patched (`${rows.length}/7 models` becomes a dynamic denominator, "7 models (Tahoe pending)" becomes "8 models"), and `__BUILT__` is stamped with the build date. Crucially, model-count words are rewritten only on short lines — "never touch the multi-MB data blocks, where a concept like 'seven-transmembrane' must not be mangled" — and a previously blanket word substitution was removed outright after it rewrote legitimate prose ("at least eight of the ten" → "ten of the ten"). Paths are controlled by `ATLAS_BASE` (data root), `ATLAS_REPO` (site repository, auto-detected by checking for `../atlas_template.html`), and `ATLAS_OUT` (build directory), so the chain runs outside the authors' machine.

> [!TIP]
> The lazy stub is the reason `index.html` and `data/explorer.json` must be deployed together: the page boots from a few-kilobyte stub and resolves the ~50 MB map bundle on first explorer use, so shipping the HTML without the `data/` folder silently breaks only that one feature.

Sources: [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L1-L4), [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L33-L38), [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L63-L75), [inject_atlas.py](pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L12-L19)

## The Re-Build Loop and the Shipped Artifacts

The full refresh sequence is short and strictly ordered, and each step names the next: re-run any analyses (component JSONs update) → `python scripts/atlas_assemble.py` (re-derive the embedded object) → `python scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py` (re-patch hypothesis + controls, or `--check` first) → `python scripts/inject_atlas.py` (re-emit `index.html` + `data/explorer.json`). No step reads anything outside `outputs/atlas/comparative/`, which is what makes the invariant checkable: "The manuscript, the supplement and the site's data blocks are built from these files and nothing else; `pipeline/scripts/audit_all.py` checks that."

Sources: [atlas_hypothesis_block.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_hypothesis_block.py#L158-L166), [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L3), [README.md](pipeline/scripts/README.md#L84-L88)

The repository's published set is correspondingly minimal: the single-page `index.html`, `data/explorer.json` (the lazy map bundle), and `data/hypothesis_pairs_full.json` (all 4,485 released regulatory pairs with models, weight, co-mentions and the same-family flag — the complete counterpart to the compact `pairs_all` rows embedded in the atlas object). The site derives its discipline from the same philosophy as the rest of the project: the assembler's own comments record that a "new biology" analysis block was removed from the object entirely after both nulls came back negative, with the note "Do not reinstate without a null" — the public page refuses to carry a claim the result files cannot defend.

Sources: [RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md#L38), [atlas_assemble.py](pipeline/scripts/atlas_assemble.py#L207-L213)

## Where to Go Next

For the complete file-side inventory that this assembly consumes — every JSON with its writer, readers and size — continue to [Result Files and Data Flow Map](17-result-files-and-data-flow-map). For how drift between prose, figures and result files is systematically caught (the audit machinery `atlas_hypothesis_block.py` mirrors), see [Audit System and Manuscript Checks](18-audit-system-and-manuscript-checks), and for why the underlying catalogues were re-extracted before the site could be rebuilt, see [Extraction Faults and Corrected Re-Run](21-extraction-faults-and-corrected-re-run). Finally, to see what the lazy-loaded `data/explorer.json` actually renders once fetched, continue to the next page, [Layer Explorer Feature Maps](23-layer-explorer-feature-maps).

# Layer Explorer Feature Maps



The Layer Explorer is the atlas's per-layer, per-model map of every sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature: a 2-D scatter of decoder directions, the co-activation structure behind module colouring, SVD-alignment flags, and firing statistics — all precomputed offline into compact JSON so the browser renders tens of thousands of dots without ever loading a model. This page traces the feature map's full life cycle: GPU-side extraction (`layer_explorer.py`), module-graph construction (`modules_alllayers.py`), lossless compaction into the "pts" format (`build_explorer_slim.py`), and the three-build delivery strategy with lazy loading (`inject_atlas.py` + `atlas_template.html`).

## What Each Feature Dot Encodes

Every dot in the explorer is one SAE latent direction, and four derived signals are attached to it. **Position** is a UMAP (and a parallel t-SNE) projection of the feature's *decoder direction* — the axes carry no meaning, and the cloud is near-uniform because features are close to orthogonal. **Colour** follows a user toggle: co-activation community (grey = not in the top-degree graph) or SVD alignment. **Size/opacity** relates to firing frequency, and a **TF flag** marks features whose annotations include TRRUST transcription factors. The site's own help glossary summarizes this contract for readers: position is decoder-direction UMAP/t-SNE, and a feature is "one direction learned by a sparse autoencoder on a model's residual stream," summarised by its top decoder genes.

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L1-L10), [atlas_template.html](/pipeline/atlas_template.html#L1238-L1241)

## Pipeline Architecture

The feature map is produced by a four-stage pipeline. The GPU stage reads *saved* SAE checkpoints and memory-mapped activation matrices — it never re-runs the foundation models — and emits one raw explorer JSON per model. Two sibling consumers then branch off that JSON: the module-graph builder derives per-layer co-activation communities, and the slim builder fuses coordinates, module assignments, top genes and annotation rates into the two deployment-sized files. Finally, the injector splices those files into the HTML template's `__DATA__` placeholders, producing three builds that differ only in *how* the explorer payload is shipped.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph GPU["Extraction stage (per model, per depth-matched layer)"]
        SAE["sae_L*.pt<br/>TopK SAE checkpoints"]
        ACT["layer_LL_activations.npy<br/>memory-mapped activations"]
        LE["layer_explorer.py"]
        SAE --> LE
        ACT --> LE
    end
    LE --> EXPL["explorer/&lt;M&gt;_explorer.json<br/>features · edges · freq · svd"]
    EXPL --> MA["modules_alllayers.py"]
    EXPL --> SL["build_explorer_slim.py"]
    CAT["feature_catalog_L*.json<br/>(top genes)"] --> MA
    CAT --> SL
    ANN["annotations/&lt;M&gt;_L*.json<br/>(annotation rate)"] --> MA
    ANN --> SL
    MA --> MODS["modules_alllayers.json"]
    SL --> FULL["explorer_slim_full.json<br/>(every alive feature)"]
    SL --> LIGHT["explorer_slim_light.json<br/>(top 500/layer)"]
    subgraph SITE["Site assembly"]
        INJ["inject_atlas.py"]
        TPL["atlas_template.html"]
        FULL --> INJ
        LIGHT --> INJ
        MODS --> INJ
        TPL --> INJ
        INJ --> B1["atlas_ts3_light.html"]
        INJ --> B2["atlas_ts3_full.html"]
        INJ --> B3["index.html<br/>lazy: data/explorer.json"]
    end
```

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L44-L62), [build_explorer_slim.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L6-L13), [modules_alllayers.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/modules_alllayers.py#L1-L10), [inject_atlas.py](/pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L22-L33)

## Extraction Stage: `layer_explorer.py`

The script discovers layers by globbing `sae_L*.pt` in the model's output directory and sorts them numerically, so it automatically covers *all* depth-matched layers rather than a hand-picked subset. For each layer it loads the checkpoint's config (`d_model`, `expansion`, `k`), reconstructs the `TopKSAE`, and opens the activation matrix with `mmap_mode="r"` — the corpus never has to fit in RAM.

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L58-L67)

The statistical core is a single streaming pass over the activations that accumulates three float64 tensors on the GPU: `S1` (feature sums), `S2` (the Gram matrix `Hᵀ H`), and `S0` (firing counts). From these it derives everything the map needs in O(1) extra memory: firing frequency `freq = S0/N`, the alive mask (`freq > 0`), and the full Pearson correlation matrix `cov / √(var·var)` with the diagonal zeroed. This is why edge computation scales to `d_sae`-sized dictionaries on an H100 without materialising per-pair passes.

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L69-L80)

Two embeddings are computed from the same material — the column-normalised decoder weight matrix restricted to alive features (`W_dec` is stored as `[d_model, d_sae]`, so alive columns are transposed to `[n_alive, d_model]`). UMAP runs with cosine metric, `n_neighbors=15`, `min_dist=0.1`, `random_state=0`; t-SNE runs with cosine metric, PCA init, and an adaptive perplexity of `min(30, max(5, n/20))`. Both fall back to plain PCA if the library is missing, guaranteeing the map always renders.

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L16-L41), [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L82-L87)

SVD alignment and edge mining complete the per-layer payload. For alignment, up to 120,000 activation rows are sampled, centred, decomposed, and each alive feature is flagged if its maximum absolute cosine to a top right-singular vector exceeds 0.5. For edges, each alive feature keeps its top-k correlated alive neighbours, pairs below `min_corr` are dropped, pairs are deduplicated as `(min(i,j), max(i,j))` keeping the stronger correlation, and the list is sorted descending and capped at 9,000. Coordinates from both embeddings are min-max normalised to [0, 1] before serialization.

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L89-L107)

The raw output schema is `{model, layers: {L: {n_alive, dead, d_sae, n_svd_aligned, features: [{id, x, y, tx, ty, freq, svd}], edges: [[i, j, corr]]}}}` written to `explorer/<M>_explorer.json`.

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L109-L122)

**Extraction parameters:**

| Flag | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--topk` | 10 | correlated neighbours retained per feature during edge mining |
| `--min-corr` | 0.15 | minimum Pearson correlation for an edge to survive |
| `--max-edges` | 9000 | per-layer cap after strength-sorted deduplication |
| `--svd-cos` | 0.5 | \|cos\| threshold for the SVD-alignment flag |
| `--sample` | 120000 | activation rows sampled for the SVD basis |
| `--batch` | 65536 | streaming batch size for the correlation accumulators |

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L50-L56)

## Module Colouring: `modules_alllayers.py`

Module colouring reuses — never recomputes — the co-activation edges from the explorer JSON. Per layer, the builder constructs a `networkx` graph over the strong edges, keeps only the top-260 highest-degree nodes (the co-activating core, kept "for a legible layout"), runs greedy modularity clustering, and lays the surviving subgraph out with a seeded spring layout (`seed=7`, `k=1.6/√n`, 120 iterations). Each node carries its community id, degree, a display label (dominant annotation concept, else top gene), its top-6 decoder genes, and a TF flag derived from TRRUST source annotations; module labels themselves are the most common concept per community. Edges are re-encoded as `[nodeIndexA, nodeIndexB, weight]`, strength-sorted, and capped at 600.

Sources: [modules_alllayers.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/modules_alllayers.py#L36-L84)

Crucially, the output deliberately matches the pre-existing `modules_ts3.json` node/edge schema (indices into nodes; x, y in 0..1), so the site's canvas renderer only gained a layer selector rather than a new code path — the same design pattern as the explorer itself: heavy geometry computed once offline, the browser only animating and hit-testing.

Sources: [modules_alllayers.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/modules_alllayers.py#L1-L10), [modules_alllayers.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/modules_alllayers.py#L110-L112)

## Slimming Stage: `build_explorer_slim.py`

The slim builder is a lossless-enough repackager that turns verbose per-feature objects into fixed 10-slot integer arrays (`pts`), deduplicating gene strings into a per-model shared dictionary. Positions are rescaled by ×100 and rounded to 0.1 so JSON numbers stay short; firing frequency becomes a ×1000 integer key that preserves ordering. Features absent from the top-degree module graph get `module = n_mod` and `tf = 0`, which the renderer treats as grey.

| Slot | Content | Encoding | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–1 | `x, y` | `round(v*100, 1)` | decoder-direction UMAP, 0–100 |
| 2 | `module` | int | co-activation community; `n_mod` = uncoloured |
| 3 | `svd` | 0/1 | aligned to a top SVD axis (cos > 0.5) |
| 4 | `geneIdx` | int | index into shared `genes` array (top decoder gene) |
| 5 | `freqKey` | int | `round(freq*1000)` — firing-rate rank key |
| 6 | `id` | int | SAE latent index (joins back to catalog/annotations) |
| 7 | `tf` | 0/1 | TRRUST transcription-factor flag |
| 8–9 | `tx, ty` | `round(v*100, 1)` | t-SNE fallback view |

Sources: [build_explorer_slim.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L10-L11), [build_explorer_slim.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L37-L60)

Each layer also carries a metadata block — `alive`, `dead`, `svd_aligned`, `n_mod`, `mod_labels`, and `rate` (the percentage of shown features with any annotation) — so the UI can print per-layer summary lines without extra requests. Two sizes are emitted: `explorer_slim_full.json` with every alive feature for the size-unlimited local atlas, and `explorer_slim_light.json` keeping only the top `--cap` (default 500) features per layer sorted by `freqKey`, tuned so the published artifact stays within a ≤16 MB budget.

Sources: [build_explorer_slim.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L61-L66), [build_explorer_slim.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L71-L75)

> [!TIP]
> The grey convention is positional: slot 2 equal to `n_mod` is not a real community — it is the sentinel meaning "this feature never made the top-degree module graph." Any consumer that colours by community id must treat `id === n_mod` as uncoloured, or unclustered features will silently inherit the last module's hue.

## Delivery: Three Builds and Lazy Loading

`inject_atlas.py` performs placeholder surgery on `atlas_template.html`: it finds `<script id="…-data" type="application/json">` blocks and replaces their contents with the corresponding result files (`modules-data`, `genes-data`, `atlas-data`, `health-data`, `programme-data`, and `explorer-data`). Because the explorer payload dominates page weight, the injector supports a **lazy mode**: instead of inlining the JSON, it writes the full payload to `data/explorer.json` beside the page and embeds a tiny stub `{lazy, models, mb}` in the `explorer-data` block — explicitly so "the published HTML is a fifth of the size and the maps are fetched the first time someone opens the explorer."

Sources: [inject_atlas.py](/pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L22-L33), [inject_atlas.py](/pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L42-L56)

The three builds differ only in the explorer strategy:

| Build | Explorer payload | Output | Intended use |
|---|---|---|---|
| LIGHT | `explorer_slim_light.json` inlined | `atlas_ts3_light.html` | size-budgeted artifact (≤16 MB) |
| FULL | `explorer_slim_full.json` inlined | `atlas_ts3_full.html` | local browsing, no size limit |
| SITE | stub + lazy `data/explorer.json` | `index.html` | the published page |

Sources: [inject_atlas.py](/pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L81-L87)

On the client, the explorer section is wired into the tab shell under the **Genes** tab (mapped via `TABMAP` and ordered after gene search and the prediction test), and `exRender()` is invoked only when that tab becomes active — the render trigger that makes the lazy fetch pay off, since users who never open the explorer never download the multi-megabyte map.

Sources: [atlas_template.html](/pipeline/atlas_template.html#L1483-L1493), [atlas_template.html](/pipeline/atlas_template.html#L1500-L1503)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Reader
    participant P as index.html (stub: lazy/models/mb)
    participant F as data/explorer.json
    participant R as exRender() canvas
    U->>P: opens the Genes tab / #explorer section
    P->>F: first visit — fetch full slim payload once
    F-->>R: layers[] pts arrays (coords, module, svd, gene, freq)
    R->>U: scatter render, module/SVD colour toggle, hover tooltips
```

Sources: [inject_atlas.py](/pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L42-L56), [atlas_template.html](/pipeline/atlas_template.html#L1500-L1503)

> [!TIP]
> The explorer's navigation entry is `#explorer` in the template nav, but the tab shell re-homes the section under the Genes tab at runtime — deep links like `#explorer` resolve through the `TABMAP` routing, so bookmarking the section anchor still opens the right tab and scrolls to the map.

## Schema Quick Reference

**Raw explorer JSON (per layer):** `n_alive` / `dead` (firing vs never-fired counts), `d_sae` (expansion × d_model), `n_svd_aligned`, `features[]` with `id, x, y, tx, ty, freq, svd` in unit coordinates, and `edges[]` as `[i, j, corr]` among alive features.

Sources: [layer_explorer.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/layer_explorer.py#L109-L116)

**Slim JSON (per model):** a shared `genes[]` dictionary plus `layers{}` whose entries hold the metadata block and `pts` arrays; the injector's stub adds `{lazy, models, mb}` so the page can display payload size before fetching.

Sources: [build_explorer_slim.py](/pipeline/atlas_h100/build_explorer_slim.py#L61-L68), [inject_atlas.py](/pipeline/scripts/inject_atlas.py#L53-L56)

## Where to Go Next

The explorer consumes artifacts produced upstream: how the SAEs it reads were trained is covered in [TopK Sparse Autoencoder Training](7-topk-sparse-autoencoder-training), and how features acquire their top genes and concept labels is [Concept Matrices and Backbone Detection](13-concept-matrices-and-backbone-detection). The SVD-alignment flag ties into [Cross-Model Geometry: CKA and SVD](12-cross-model-geometry-cka-and-svd). For the rest of the delivery chain — placeholder injection, gene search, and the other data blocks the site embeds — continue to [Site Assembly from Result Files](22-site-assembly-from-result-files).
